docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• WorldPop: RuntimeError during school_age=True data availability check:
    • Resolved a RuntimeError: Could not ensure data availability for loading that occurred when school_age=True and WorldPop data was not yet present in the data store.
    • WPPopulationConfig.get_data_unit_paths now correctly returns the original .zip URLs to trigger the download/extraction process when filtered .tif files are missing.
    • After successful download and extraction, it now accurately identifies and returns the paths to the local .tif files, allowing BaseHandler to confirm availability and proceed with loading.

  • WorldPop: list index out of range when no datasets found:

    • Added a RuntimeError in WPPopulationConfig.get_relevant_data_units_by_country when self.client.search_datasets returns no results, providing a clearer error message with the search parameters.

  • WorldPop: Incomplete downloads with min_age/max_age filters for non-school-age age_structures:

    • Fixed an issue where load_data with min_age or max_age filters (when school_age=False) resulted in incomplete downloads.
    • WPPopulationConfig.get_data_unit_paths now returns all potential .tif URLs for non-school-age age_structures during the initial availability check, ensuring all necessary files are downloaded.
    • Age/sex filtering is now deferred and applied by WPPopulationReader.load_from_paths using WPPopulationConfig._filter_age_sex_paths after download, guaranteeing data integrity.

  • HealthSitesFetcher

    • Ensured correct Coordinate Reference System (CRS) assignment (EPSG:4326) when returning GeoDataFrame from fetched health facility data.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: • Added s2sphere as a new dependency for S2 geometry operations

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Healthsites.io API Integration (HealthSitesFetcher):

    • New class HealthSitesFetcher to fetch and process health facility data from the Healthsites.io API.
    • Supports filtering by country, bounding box extent, and date ranges (from_date, to_date).
    • Provides methods for:
      • fetch_facilities(): Retrieves health facility locations, returning a pd.DataFrame or gpd.GeoDataFrame based on output format.
      • fetch_statistics(): Fetches aggregated statistics for health facilities based on provided filters.
      • fetch_facility_by_id(): Retrieves details for a specific facility using its OSM type and ID.
    • Includes robust handling for API pagination, different output formats (JSON, GeoJSON), and nested data structures.
    • Integrates with OSMLocationFetcher and pycountry to standardize country names to OSM English names for consistent querying.
    • Configurable parameters for API URL, API key, page size, flat properties, tag format, output format, and request sleep time.

  • OSMLocationFetcher Enhancements:

    • Historical Data Fetching (fetch_locations_changed_between):
      • New method fetch_locations_changed_between() to retrieve OSM objects that were created or modified within a specified date range. This enables historical analysis and change tracking.
      • Defaults include_metadata to True for this method, as it's typically used for change tracking.
    • Comprehensive OSM Country Information (get_osm_countries):
      • New static method get_osm_countries() to fetch country-level administrative boundaries directly from the OSM database.
      • Supports fetching all countries or a specific country by ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 code.
      • Option to include various name variants (e.g., name:en, official_name) and ISO codes.
    • Metadata Inclusion in Fetched Locations:
      • Added include_metadata parameter to fetch_locations() to optionally retrieve change tracking metadata (timestamp, version, changeset, user, uid) for each fetched OSM element.
      • This metadata is now extracted and included in the DataFrame for nodes, relations, and ways.
    • Flexible Date Filtering in Overpass Queries:
      • Introduced date_filter_type (newer, changed) and start_date/end_date parameters to _build_queries() for more granular control over time-based filtering in Overpass QL.
    • Date Normalization Utility:
      • Added _normalize_date() helper method to convert various date inputs (string, datetime object) into a standardized ISO 8601 format for Overpass API queries.

  • TifProcessor

    • Comprehensive Memory Management:
      • Introduced _check_available_memory(), _estimate_memory_usage(), and _memory_guard() methods for proactive memory assessment across various operations.
      • Added warnings (ResourceWarning) for potentially high memory usage in batched operations, with suggestions for optimizing n_workers.
    • Chunked DataFrame Conversion:
      • Implemented to_dataframe_chunked() for memory-efficient processing of large rasters by converting them to DataFrames in manageable chunks.
      • Automatic calculation of optimal chunk_size based on target memory usage via _calculate_optimal_chunk_size().
      • New helper methods: _get_chunk_windows(), _get_chunk_coordinates().
    • Raster Clipping Functionality:
      • clip_to_geometry(): New method to clip rasters to arbitrary geometries (Shapely, GeoDataFrame, GeoSeries, GeoJSON-like dicts).
      • clip_to_bounds(): New method to clip rasters to rectangular bounding boxes, supporting optional CRS transformation for the bounds.
      • New helper methods for clipping: _prepare_geometry_for_clipping(), _validate_geometry_crs(), _create_clipped_processor().

  • WorldPopDownloader Zip Handling:

    • Modified download_data_unit in WPPopulationDownloader to correctly handle .zip files (e.g., school age datasets) by downloading them to a temporary location and extracting the contained .tif files.
    • Updated download_data_units to correctly flatten the list of paths returned by download_data_unit when zip extraction results in multiple files.
    • Adjusted WPPopulationConfig.get_data_unit_paths to correctly identify and return paths for extracted .tif files from zip resources. It is now intelligently resolves paths. For school-age datasets, it returns paths to extracted .tif files if available; otherwise, it returns the original .zip path(s) to trigger download and extraction.
    • Added filter support to WPPopulationConfig.get_data_unit_paths hence to the WPPopulationHandler for:
      • School-age datasets: supports sex (e.g., "F", "M", "F_M") and education_level (e.g., "PRIMARY", "SECONDARY") filters on extracted .tif filenames.
      • Non-school-age age_structures: supports sex, ages, min_age, and max_age filters on .tif filenames.

  • WorldPop: Filtered aggregation in GeometryBasedZonalViewGenerator.map_wp_pop:

    • map_wp_pop now enforces a single country input when handler.config.project is "age_structures".
    • When predicate is "centroid_within" and the project is "age_structures", individual TifProcessor objects (representing age/sex combinations) are loaded, sampled with map_rasters(stat="sum"), and their results are summed per zone, preventing unintended merging.

  • PoiViewGenerator: Filtered aggregation in PoiViewGenerator.map_wp_pop:

    • map_wp_pop now enforces a single country input when handler.config.project is "age_structures".
    • When predicate is "centroid_within" and the project is "age_structures", individual TifProcessor objects (representing age/sex combinations) are loaded, sampled with map_zonal_stats(stat="sum"), and their results are summed per POI, preventing unintended merging.

  • TifProcessor Multi-Raster Merging in Handlers and Generators:

    • Extended _load_raster_data in BaseHandlerReader to support an optional merge_rasters argument. When True and multiple raster paths are provided, TifProcessor now merges them into a single TifProcessor object during loading.
    • Integrated merge_rasters argument into GHSLDataReader and WPPopulationReader's load_from_paths and load methods, enabling control over raster merging at the reader level.
    • Propagated merge_rasters to GHSLDataHandler's load_into_dataframe, and load_into_geodataframe methods for consistent behavior across the handler interface.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• TifProcessor

    • Unified DataFrame Conversion:
      • Refactored to_dataframe() to act as a universal entry point, dynamically routing to internal, more efficient methods for single and multi-band processing.
      • Deprecated the individual _to_band_dataframe(), _to_rgb_dataframe(), _to_rgba_dataframe(), and _to_multi_band_dataframe() methods in favor of the new unified _to_dataframe().
      • to_dataframe() now includes a check_memory parameter.
    • Optimized open_dataset Context Manager:
      • The open_dataset context manager now directly opens local files when LocalDataStore is used, avoiding unnecessary rasterio.MemoryFile creation for improved performance and reduced memory overhead.
    • Enhanced to_geodataframe and to_graph:
      • Added check_memory parameter to to_geodataframe() and to_graph() for memory pre-checks.
    • Refined sample_by_polygons_batched:
      • Included check_memory parameter for memory checks before batch processing.
      • Implemented platform-specific warnings for potential multiprocessing issues on Windows/macOS.
    • Improved Multiprocessing Initialization:
      • The _initializer_worker() method now prioritizes merged, reprojected, or original local file paths for opening, ensuring workers access the most relevant data.
    • Modular Masking and Coordinate Extraction:
      • Introduced new private helper methods: _extract_coordinates_with_mask(), _build_data_mask(), _build_multi_band_mask(), and _bands_to_dict() to centralize and improve data masking and coordinate extraction logic.
    • Streamlined Band-Mode Validation:
      • Moved the logic for validating mode and band count compatibility into a dedicated _validate_mode_band_compatibility() method for better code organization.

  • GigaSchoolLocationFetcher

    • fetch_locations() method:
      • Added process_geospatial parameter (defaults to False) to optionally process geospatial data and return a gpd.GeoDataFrame.
    • _process_geospatial_data() method:
      • Modified to return a gpd.GeoDataFrame by converting the pd.DataFrame with a geometry column and EPSG:4326 CRS.

  • OSMLocationFetcher Refactoring:

    • Unified Query Execution and Processing: Refactored the core logic for executing Overpass queries and processing their results into a new private method _execute_and_process_queries(). This centralizes common steps and reduces code duplication between fetch_locations() and the new fetch_locations_changed_between().
    • Enhanced _build_queries: Modified _build_queries to accept date_filter_type, start_date, end_date, and include_metadata to construct more dynamic and feature-rich Overpass QL queries.
    • Updated fetch_locations Signature:
      • Replaced since_year parameter with since_date (which can be a str or datetime object) for more precise time-based filtering.
      • Added include_metadata parameter.
    • Improved Logging of Category Distribution:
      • Modified the logging for category distribution to correctly handle cases where categories are combined into a list (when handle_duplicates='combine').
    • since_year Parameter: Removed since_year from fetch_locations() as its functionality is now superseded by the more flexible since_date parameter and the _build_queries enhancements.

  • PoiViewGenerator Mapping Methods (map_zonal_stats, map_nearest_points, map_google_buildings, map_ms_buildings, map_built_s, map_smod):

    • Changed map_zonal_stats and map_nearest_points to return pd.DataFrame results (including 'poi_id' and new mapped columns) instead of directly updating the internal view.
    • Updated map_google_buildings, map_ms_buildings, map_built_s, and map_smod to capture the pd.DataFrame returned by their respective underlying mapping calls (map_nearest_points or map_zonal_stats) and then explicitly call self._update_view() with these results.
    • This enhances modularity and allows for more flexible result handling and accumulation.

  • ZonalViewGenerator.map_rasters Enhancements:

    • Modified map_rasters to accept raster_data as either a single TifProcessor or a List[TifProcessor].
    • Implemented internal merging of List[TifProcessor] into a single TifProcessor before performing zonal statistics.
    • Replaced sample_multiple_tifs_by_polygons with the TifProcessor.sample_by_polygons method.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• TifProcessor:
    • to_graph() Sparse Matrix Creation:
      • Corrected the sparse matrix creation logic in to_graph() to ensure proper symmetric graph representation when graph_type="sparse".
    • Coordinate System Handling in _initializer_worker:
      • Ensured that _initializer_worker correctly handles different data storage scenarios to provide the correct dataset handle to worker processes, preventing RuntimeError due to uninitialized raster datasets.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text:
• OSMLocationFetcher
    • Redundant Category Distribution Logging: Removed the explicit category distribution logging for handle_duplicates == "separate" since the value_counts() method on the 'category' column already provides this.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• TifProcessor Revamp

    • Explicit Reprojection Method: Introduced reproject_to() method, allowing on-demand reprojection of rasters to a new CRS with customizable resampling_method and resolution.
    • Reprojection Resolution Control: Added reprojection_resolution parameter to TifProcessor for precise control over output pixel size during reprojection.
    • Advanced Raster Information: Added get_raster_info() method to retrieve a comprehensive dictionary of raster metadata.
    • Graph Conversion Capabilities: Implemented to_graph() method to convert raster data into a graph (NetworkX or sparse matrix) based on pixel adjacency (4- or 8-connectivity).
    • Internal Refactoring: _reproject_to_temp_file: Introduced _reproject_to_temp_file as a helper for reprojection into temporary files.

  • H3 Grid Generation

    • H3 Grid Generation Module (gigaspatial/grid/h3.py):
      • Introduced H3Hexagons class for managing H3 cell IDs.
      • Supports creation from lists of hexagons, geographic bounds, spatial geometries, or points.
      • Provides methods to convert H3 hexagons to pandas DataFrames and GeoPandas GeoDataFrames.
      • Includes functionalities for filtering, getting k-ring neighbors, compacting hexagons, and getting children/parents at different resolutions.
      • Allows saving H3Hexagons to JSON, Parquet, or GeoJSON files.
    • Country-Specific H3 Hexagons (CountryH3Hexagons):
      • Extends H3Hexagons for generating H3 grids constrained by country boundaries.
      • Integrates with AdminBoundaries to fetch country geometries for precise H3 cell generation.

  • Documentation

    • Improved tif.md example to showcase multi-raster initialization, explicit reprojection, and graph conversion.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• TifProcessor
  • Improved Temporary File Management: Refactored temporary file handling for merging and reprojection using tempfile.mkdtemp() and shutil.rmtree for more robust and reliable cleanup. Integrated with context manager (__enter__, __exit__) and added a dedicated cleanup() method.
  • Reprojection during Initialization: Implemented automatic reprojection of single rasters to a specified target_crs during TifProcessor initialization.
  • Enhanced open_dataset Context Manager: The open_dataset context manager now intelligently opens the most up-to-date (merged or reprojected) version of the dataset.
  • More Flexible Multi-Dataset Validation: Modified _validate_multiple_datasets to issue a warning instead of raising an error for CRS mismatches when target_crs is not set.

  • Optimized _get_reprojection_profile: Dynamically calculates transform and dimensions based on reprojection_resolution and added LZW compression to reprojected TIFF files to reduce file size.

  • ADLSDataStore Enhancements

    • New copy_file method: Implemented a new method for copying individual files within ADLS, with an option to overwrite existing files.
    • New rename method: Added a new method to rename (move) files in ADLS, which internally uses copy_file and then deletes the source, with options for overwrite, waiting for copy completion, and polling.
    • Revamped rmdir method: Modified rmdir to perform batch deletions of blobs, addressing the Azure Blob batch delete limit (256 sub-requests) and improving efficiency for large directories.

  • LocalDataStore Enhancements

    • New copy_file method: Implemented a new method for copying individual files.

docs.text: • Removed deprecated tabular property and get_zoned_geodataframe method from TifProcessor. Users should now use to_dataframe() and to_geodataframe() respectively.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• OSMLocationFetcher Enhancements
  • Support for querying OSM locations by arbitrary administrative levels (e.g., states, provinces, cities), in addition to country-level queries.
  • New optional parameters:
    • admin_level: Specify OSM administrative level (e.g., 4 for states, 6 for counties).
    • admin_value: Name of the administrative area to query (e.g., "California").

  • New static method get_admin_names(admin_level, country=None):

    • Fetch all administrative area names for a given admin_level, optionally filtered by country.
    • Helps users discover valid admin area names for constructing precise queries.

  • Multi-Raster Merging Support in TifProcessor

  • Added ability to initialize TifProcessor with multiple raster datasets.
  • Merges rasters on load with configurable strategies:
    • Supported merge_method options: first, last, min, max, mean.
  • Supports on-the-fly reprojection for rasters with differing coordinate reference systems via target_crs.
  • Handles resampling using resampling_method (default: nearest).
  • Comprehensive validation to ensure compatibility of input rasters (e.g., resolution, nodata, dtype).
  • Temporary file management for merged output with automatic cleanup.
  • Backward compatible with single-raster use cases.

New TifProcessor Parameters: - merge_method (default: first) – How to combine pixel values across rasters. - target_crs (optional) – CRS to reproject rasters before merging. - resampling_method – Resampling method for reprojection.

New Properties: - is_merged: Indicates whether the current instance represents merged rasters. - source_count: Number of raster datasets merged.

  • WorldPop Handler Refactor (API Integration)

  • Introduced WPPopulationHandler, WPPopulationConfig, WPPopulationDownloader, and WPPopulationReader.
  • Uses new WorldPopRestClient to dynamically query the WorldPop REST API.
  • Replaces static metadata files and hardcoded logic with API-based discovery and download.
  • Country code lookup and dataset filtering now handled at runtime.

  • Improved validation, extensibility, logging, and error handling.

  • POI-Based WorldPop Mapping

  • PoiViewGenerator.map_wp_pop() method:

    • Maps WorldPop population data around POIs using flexible spatial predicates:
    • "centroid_within", "intersects", "fractional" (1000m only), "within"
    • Supports configurable radius and resolution (100m or 1000m).
    • Aggregates population data and appends it to the view.

  • Geometry-Based Zonal WorldPop Mapping

  • GeometryBasedZonalViewGenerator.map_wp_pop() method:
    • Maps WorldPop population data to polygons/zones using:
    • "intersects" or "fractional" predicate
    • Returns zonal population sums as a new view column.
    • Handles predicate-dependent data loading (raster vs. GeoDataFrame).

  • AdminBoundariesViewGenerator New generator class for producing zonal views based on administrative boundaries (e.g., districts, provinces) with flexible source and admin level support.

  • Zonal View Generator Enhancements

  • _view: Internal attribute for accumulating mapped statistics.
  • view: Exposes current state of zonal view.
  • add_variable_to_view(): Adds mapped data from map_points, map_polygons, or map_rasters with robust validation and zone alignment.

docs.title: Contribution Guidelines
docs.text: Thank you for considering contributing to Giga! We value your input and aim to make the contribution process as accessible and transparent as possible. Whether you're interested in reporting bugs, discussing code, submitting fixes, proposing features, becoming a maintainer, or engaging with the Giga community, we welcome your involvement.

docs.title: Adding a dataset
docs.text:
A dataset published as files is a handler. A dataset served as a query is a fetcher. The handler base, including the search key and the search geometry, is documented in the API reference: Handler base. That section is for contributors to this repository. It is not a stable API for other packages.

Where a new dataset goes:

  • A handler goes in gigaspatial/handlers/. Add its config, downloader, reader, and handler to the dictionary in gigaspatial/handlers/__init__.py, and the handler alone to the one in gigaspatial/__init__.py.
  • A fetcher goes in gigaspatial/fetchers/ and its class name ends in Fetcher. Register it in gigaspatial/fetchers/__init__.py and gigaspatial/__init__.py.
  • An image downloader goes in gigaspatial/image_downloaders/. Add it to that package's __all__ and to gigaspatial/__init__.py.

Those __init__.py files load names lazily. Each one also repeats its names in an if TYPE_CHECKING: block, and tests/test_public_api.py fails if the two lists differ. Code inside the package uses absolute imports (from gigaspatial.handlers.ghsl import ...). The reasons are in Public import paths.

docs.title: With a coding agent
docs.text:
Team members can install agent skills for this repository from the team's skills repository, a submodule at .agents/vendor/di-applied-science-skills. From the repository root:

git submodule update --init
python .agents/vendor/di-applied-science-skills/install.py giga-spatial

The skills land in .agents/skills/, which Cursor and Codex read and git ignores. Invoke them by name:

  • build-handler probes a dataset's source, interviews you on the design, and writes the handler, its registrations, and its tests.
  • judge-handler-base reviews a new handler, or a change to the handler base, against the contract in .agents/reference/handler-contract.md.

The contract lives here because it describes this repository's code; update it with any change to the handler base. The skills themselves are edited in the skills repository. After the submodule moves to a newer commit, run install.py again with no arguments.

Tests marked live reach real data sources and are skipped by default. Run them with pytest -m live.

docs.title: How to Contribute to our Giga Project?
docs.text:
1. Familiarize Yourself: Before contributing, familiarize yourself with the project by reviewing the README, code of conduct, and existing issues or pull requests.
  2. Issues and Feature Requests: Check the issue tracker for existing issues or create a new one to report bugs, suggest improvements, or propose new features.
  3. Fork and Branch: Fork the repository and create a branch for your contribution. Branch names should be descriptive (e.g., feature/add-new-functionality, bugfix/issue-description).
  4. Code Changes: Make changes or additions following our coding conventions and style guide. Ensure to write clear commit messages that explain the purpose of each commit.
  5. Testing: If applicable, include tests for the changes made to ensure code reliability. Ensure existing tests pass.
  6. Documentation: Update relevant documentation, including README files or any other necessary guides.
  7. Pull Request: Open a pull request (PR) against the main branch. Clearly describe the changes introduced, referencing any related issues.

docs.title: Report a Bug or Suggestion
docs.text:
• Bug Reports: Help us understand and address issues by submitting detailed bug reports via GitHub issues. Include as many relevant details as possible in the provided template to expedite resolutions.
  • Suggestions: Share your ideas, feedback, or stay updated on Giga by joining our Discord channel.

docs.title: Making Changes and Pull Requests
docs.text:
To contribute code changes:

  1. Fork the repository and create a new branch for your contribution

    git checkout -b 'my-contribution'.

  2. Make your changes on the created branch.
  3. Commit with clear messages describing the updates.
  4. Submit a pull request in the main repository, ensuring the following:
  5. Clear use case or demonstration of bug fix/new feature.
  6. Inclusion of relevant tests (unit, functional, and fuzz tests where applicable).
  7. Adherence to code style guidelines.
  8. No breaking changes to the existing test suite.
  9. Bug fixes accompanied by tests to prevent regression.
  10. Update of relevant comments and documentation reflecting code behavior changes.

docs.title: Contributing with an Issue
docs.text: If you encounter a bug but aren't sure how to fix it or submit a pull request, you can create an issue. Issues serve as avenues for bug reports, feedback, and general discussions within the GigaSpatial GitHub repository.

docs.title: Other Ways to Contribute
docs.text:
Beyond code contributions:

  • Feedback and Insights: Share your expertise and experiences related to cash transfer by contacting us at giga@unicef.org.
  • Documentation: Contribute to our journey by sharing reports, case studies, articles, blogs, or surveys. Contact us to contribute and learn more via giga@unicef.org.

docs.title: About
docs.text: GigaSpatial started inside UNICEF's Giga initiative. Development began in January 2025.

docs.title: How GigaSpatial compares to other tools
docs.text:
• Hand-built geopandas, rasterio, rasterstats, pyrosm, and osmnx pipelines: GigaSpatial uses geopandas, rasterio, and h3 under the hood, and replaces custom per-dataset download scripts, tile stitching, CRS projection, and buffer or zonal loops with handlers, fetchers, and generators that run in a few lines of Python.
  • Grid libraries (h3-py, h3ronpy, h3-toolkit): h3-py indexes coordinates and geometries into H3 cell IDs. H3ViewGenerator, S2ViewGenerator, MercatorViewGenerator, AdminBoundariesViewGenerator, and GeometryBasedZonalViewGenerator in GigaSpatial acquire published country datasets (WorldPop, GHSL, Google and Microsoft buildings, Relative Wealth Index) into your data store and map them directly onto H3 hexagons, S2 cells, Mercator tiles, administrative boundaries, or custom polygons.
  • Cloud catalogs and spatial engines (Google Earth Engine, Microsoft Planetary Computer, PostGIS, DuckDB, Apache Sedona): Cloud platforms and spatial databases run queries inside their own infrastructure. GigaSpatial downloads and caches published datasets into a data store you control (local disk, Azure Data Lake Storage, or Snowflake) and also provides optional GEEProfiler (giga-spatial[gee]), BigQueryClient (giga-spatial[bq]), and DuckDB or Trino integrations when you want them.

docs.text:
• January 2025. Development began.
  • 7 February 2025. v0.1.0, the first public release, and the first handlers.

Releases after that are in the changelog.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text: This page says what the project is aiming at. It has no dates. A line here is not a promise to ship. What has shipped is in the changelog.

docs.title: More datasets
docs.text: Publish more datasets through the library, including climate data. A dataset published as files becomes a handler. A dataset served as a query becomes a fetcher.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: Finish the documentation site: the tutorial, the user guide, and the API reference.

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
Two stages.

An MCP server whose tools run GigaSpatial. An agent calls a tool, such as population for a country or the nearest buildings to a set of points. The library downloads what is missing, runs the operation, and returns a view or a table. The model sees that result. It does not see the files.

Later, retrieval sits in front of those tools. The agent retrieves which dataset and which operation fit the question. The tool runs, and the computed result is what enters the context. The rasters are not embedded.

docs.title: Design decisions
docs.text:
These records explain decisions that are hard to reverse or surprising without context: what was decided, why, and which alternatives were rejected. Read them before proposing to change one of these areas. A new decision gets the next number.

Record Decision 0001 Handlers separate the search key, which finds the files to fetch, from the search geometry, which crops the loaded data. 0002 The handler base is documented in the API reference, but it is not a stable API for other packages. 0003 Users import from the top level or a public subpackage, which load lazily. Every other module path is internal. 0004 A spatial network is held as node and edge tables; networkx and pandana are exports, and edits return a new network. 0005 A saved spatial network is a folder with a nodes Parquet file, an edges GeoParquet file, and a JSON metadata file. 0006 OSM extracts are stored by date, and the network built from each is saved uncropped beside it; cropping happens at load. 0007 OSM extracts are chosen by polygon, with ISO codes only as a fast path and a curated list of multi-country extracts. 0008 Connecting points to an existing network is a rooted Steiner tree with the existing network as one virtual root, solved by ConnectionPlanner.

docs.title: Separate the search key from the search geometry in dataset handlers
docs.text: Handlers resolve a source in two ways that used to share one method, extract_search_geometry: finding the data units to fetch, and finding the area to crop loaded data to. Half the handlers overrode it to return something that is not a geometry (a country code for WorldPop, OpenCellID and Google-Microsoft combined; a filter dict for HDX; the raw source for Microsoft Buildings), so cropping silently did nothing or broke for them, and the CRS of the geometry was never stated. We split the two: get_search_key(source) is the override point and returns whatever the dataset's unit lookup understands (by default the search geometry), while extract_search_geometry is owned by the base, always returns a geometry in the config's CRS, and is the only thing cropping uses.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Keep one method and let cropping type-check its result. Rejected: a country code still cannot be cropped to, and the method's name keeps lying to the next handler author.
  • Let each handler override cropping. Rejected: it spreads CRS handling across eleven handlers, which is how GHSL ended up with its own meaning of the crs option.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Datasets published per country (units_match_country = True) skip the crop for country sources, since their files already match the country. Small leftovers are accepted: WorldPop rasters cover the country's bounding rectangle, OpenCellID files include towers near the borders of the country's mobile country codes, and Microsoft Buildings falls back to tiles overlapping the country when it is missing from the location mapping.
  • Path sources are never cropped, and sources with no geometry (an HDX filter dict) raise when cropping is requested.

docs.title: Document the handler base in the API reference
docs.text: The handler base is internal: this repository is its only subclasser, and the hooks are not a stable API for other packages. People adding a dataset still have to see how a source becomes files and how cropping uses a geometry. The API reference documents that once, in a last section named "Handler base." The README, the getting started, and the user guide do not use search key or search geometry. Contributing links to that section and does not explain it again.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Leave the base in the contributor notes and out of the API reference. Rejected: a contributor looks up the classes in the reference, and the notes would be a second copy that drifts.
  • Explain the base on each handler's page. Rejected: someone loading GHSL would have to read the orchestration.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Documenting the base does not make it a public extension point. The hooks can still change without a compatibility alias.
  • Caller pages show the class a user imports, its constructor, and the methods they call.

docs.title: Public import paths and lazy loading
docs.text:
Users import from three tiers. The top level, from gigaspatial import X, holds what a script creates: every handler, fetcher, image downloader, view generator, grid, data store, and client, plus TifProcessor, read_dataset, write_dataset, and the main processing.geo helpers. The public subpackages hold the building blocks: gigaspatial.handlers (each handler's config, downloader, and reader, plus AdminBoundaries and the GeoRepo and WorldPop clients), gigaspatial.fetchers, gigaspatial.image_downloaders, gigaspatial.generators, gigaspatial.grid, gigaspatial.processing, gigaspatial.core.io, gigaspatial.core.http, and gigaspatial.core.schemas. Every other module path is internal and may move between minor releases, including gigaspatial.core, gigaspatial.config, and the handler base (ADR 0002). The packages follow the glossary: a fetcher never lives in handlers, whatever its class name.

The top level, gigaspatial.handlers, gigaspatial.fetchers, and gigaspatial.processing.elevation load their names lazily (PEP 562). Importing every dataset eagerly made import gigaspatial take about six seconds and load every optional integration that was installed, including Earth Engine, Snowflake, and BigQuery. Lazy loading keeps the flat top-level imports and makes a bare import take milliseconds.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Eager imports in __init__.py. Rejected: the cost above, paid by every user for datasets they never touch.
  • The lazy_loader package (SPEC 1). Rejected: one more dependency, and .pyi stubs that have to be kept in sync with the code. gigaspatial._lazy.attach is a few lines, and each lazy __init__.py repeats its names in an if TYPE_CHECKING: block for IDEs, type checkers, and mkdocstrings. A test checks that the two lists match.
  • Keep the gigaspatial.io, gigaspatial.elevation, and gigaspatial.algorithms aliases, with or without a deprecation warning. Rejected: they were made by writing to sys.modules, which type checkers and IDEs cannot see, and io in __all__ replaced the standard library's io on from gigaspatial import *. They were removed in 0.10.0 without a shim. The library is before 1.0.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Adding a public class means adding it to the dictionary passed to attach, to the TYPE_CHECKING block, or to the subpackage's __all__.
  • The API reference renders each class from its defining module but shows only the class name, and each page opens with the imports to use.

docs.title: Spatial networks are held as tables, not as networkx graphs
docs.text: A SpatialNetwork keeps its nodes and edges as two columnar tables. The adjacency matrix that scipy's graph routines need is built from them on demand and cached. networkx and pandana are export formats, not the representation, and every edit returns a new network so that cached structures never go stale. We measured this on the simplified Rwanda drive network (125,058 nodes, 332,535 edges). The networkx graph held 731 MB, against 229 MB for the tables. Node coordinates took 43 ms from the graph and 0.6 ms from the table. The edges of a sub-region took 1.6 to 3 s from the graph and 0.03 s from the tables. scipy computed shortest paths about 12 times faster than networkx.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• A networkx MultiDiGraph, as osmnx returns. Rejected: it costs three times the memory, and every accessor loops in Python. Building one from the tables takes 0.8 to 2.5 s on the network above, so users who need networkx pay that once, only when they ask for it.
  • igraph. Rejected as the representation: it is one more compiled dependency, and its many-to-many shortest paths (13 µs per pair) were between scipy (24 µs) and pandana (1.9 µs).
  • An inplace= option on edits. Rejected: it saves no memory, because unchanged columns are shared between the old and new network, and every in-place edit would have to invalidate the cached adjacency matrix, KD-tree, spatial index, and pandana network. Missing one gives wrong shortest paths without an error.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Adding or removing edges one at a time in a Python loop is slow. The editing methods take many nodes or edges at once.
  • pandana takes the tables directly. Its contraction-hierarchy build took 1.4 s on the network above and then answered origin-destination pairs at about 1.9 µs each. That makes pandana the faster backend for very large sets of pairs, while scipy needs no build step.

docs.title: A saved spatial network is a folder of Parquet files
docs.text: SpatialNetwork.save writes a folder to the data store: nodes.parquet, edges.parquet as GeoParquet with WKB geometry and zstd compression, and network.json with whether the network is directed, its CRS, the default weight, the fetch parameters, and the library version. On the unsimplified Rwanda drive network (4.5 million edges) this is 73 MB and loads in 0.18 s, against 1.4 GB and 437 s for GraphML and 532 MB and 25 s for pickle. List-valued OSM attributes are normalised before saving: osmid becomes a list of integers on every edge, and text attributes are joined with ;, because GeoParquet cannot store a column that mixes lists and single values.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• GraphML or pickle of a networkx graph. Rejected: the sizes and load times above, and pickle cannot be read safely from an untrusted data store or by other tools.
  • Feather (Arrow IPC). Rejected: it was no faster than Parquet on these networks, and geopandas, DuckDB, and QGIS do not read it as widely. The library's write_dataset already writes Parquet.
  • One zip file holding both tables. Rejected: it read no faster than a folder, and it stops users from reading edges.parquet on its own.
  • GeoPackage with two layers. Rejected: 167 MB and 0.47 s on the simplified network, against 64 MB and 0.17 s for Parquet, and it stringifies list attributes.

docs.title: OSM extracts are stored by date, with uncropped networks beside them
docs.text: OSMRoadsHandler stores each Geofabrik extract under the date of the extract, in Geofabrik's own folder structure: osm/geofabrik/2026-10-27/africa/rwanda.osm.pbf, with a country's sub-regions under the country, as in .../south-america/brazil/nordeste.osm.pbf. The road network built from an extract is saved beside it, one folder per network type and simplification (rwanda.networks/drive_service-simplified/), and always covers the whole extract with every connected part. Cropping to a source and keeping the largest connected part happen only at load. A network cropped for one source and saved next to the extract would otherwise be taken for the whole extract on the next load.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Country folders first, dates below. Rejected: a dated snapshot is what users keep, compare, or delete together, and Geofabrik deletes its daily files after about a week, so the date is the first thing a user needs to see.
  • Store only extracts and build the network on every load. Rejected: building a country takes a minute or more, and loading a saved network takes under a second.
  • Store the network cropped to each source. Rejected for the reason above; the stored network must stand for the file it came from.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The base's availability check covers the extract only. The network folder is a cache derived from the extract's path; a missing network is built from the extract, never downloaded again.
  • Old dates are never deleted automatically, and the guide states the space extracts take (Nigeria is 680 MiB, Brazil 2 GiB).
  • Reproducing an old result needs the stored extract, since Geofabrik keeps daily files for about a week.

docs.title: OSM extracts are chosen by polygon, not by ISO code
docs.text: OSMRoadsHandler chooses the smallest Geofabrik extract whose polygon covers the source's area, using the polygons in Geofabrik's index-v1.json. A country's ISO code is only a fast path, and a country source skips the crop only when the extract is that country's own file: exactly that one code in the index, and not on a curated list of extracts that hold several countries. The index's codes cannot be trusted alone. In October 2026, five French and Pacific territories were coded VU, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, and Brunei had no extract of their own, and malaysia-singapore-brunei carried only Malaysia's code.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Look extracts up by ISO code only. Rejected for the errors and gaps above.
  • Treat every country source as matching its file (units_match_country = True). Rejected: a country inside a multi-country or regional extract would come back with its neighbours' roads.
  • Compare the extract's area with the country's to detect multi-country files. Rejected: Geofabrik's polygons run past national borders by varying amounts, so no ratio separates the cases reliably.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A country's own file and its sub-region files are returned uncropped, with the small leftovers across borders that ADR 0001 accepts for datasets published per country. Passing the country's boundary geometry as the source gives an exact crop.
  • The curated list lives in the module and is tested against a stored copy of the index, so a new multi-country extract shows up as a failing test.
  • Continent extracts (Africa is 7.4 GiB) are used only when named.

docs.title: Connecting points to an existing network is a rooted Steiner tree, solved by a planner object
docs.text:
Connecting schools, clinics, or villages to an existing network, such as fibre, a power grid, or water mains, at the smallest shared cost is the Steiner tree problem once the existing network is treated as one root. Every root node (a fibre node, or a place already connected) joins a virtual root at zero cost, and the plan is a minimum Steiner tree over the terminals and that virtual root. Removing it leaves a forest whose every tree reaches the existing network, so a terminal may connect directly or through other terminals, and a trench used by several terminals is paid once. ConnectionPlanner holds the problem (network, terminals, roots, weight, and later prizes, demands, and capacities) and its solvers; SpatialNetwork.connecting_subnetwork stays as a thin wrapper that returns the planned network.

On the concept note's example (197 schools and 5 fibre nodes in Kigali), the rooted tree is 258 km. Joining each school to its nearest fibre node, the old meaning of sources=, takes 355 km, because it shares only overlapping routes. Joining the schools and the fibre nodes in one unrooted tree takes 265 km, because it also pays to connect fibre nodes that the backbone already connects.

The existing network's nodes are called roots, not sources, because "Source" already means the place a dataset is requested for across the handlers and fetchers. connecting_subnetwork's sources= and method="nearest_source" become roots= and "nearest_root" before their first release.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Shortest paths to the nearest root. Kept as method="nearest_root", but not the default: it never lets a terminal connect through another one, and it was 38% longer on the example.
  • An unrooted Steiner tree over terminals and roots. Rejected for this question: it pays to join the roots to each other. The gap grows with how far apart the roots are.
  • Methods on SpatialNetwork only. Rejected: prize-collecting and capacitated versions need prizes per terminal, demands, capacities per root, solver options, and a result with more than a network. A problem object takes them without growing SpatialNetwork's API, and new solvers are added to it.
  • A fibre-specific planner. Rejected: the same problem arises for power grids, water, and evacuation routes. The planner uses generic terms (terminals, roots, bridges), and the docs use fibre as their main example.
  • An exact solver as a dependency. Rejected: SCIP-Jack solves instances of this size exactly, but it is a compiled external program. It is used only to validate the heuristics, in the benchmarks.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• connecting_subnetwork(terminals, sources=...) becomes connecting_subnetwork(terminals, roots=...) and changes meaning before its first release: with roots and method="steiner", it is the rooted tree.
  • The problem is NP-hard. The planner returns approximations (Mehlhorn's algorithm, at most twice the optimum) and a lower bound, so every plan can state how far from the optimum it can be at most.
  • Cost per cable, which grows with the number of terminals behind an edge, is out of scope; it makes the problem a fixed-charge network design problem, with very different solvers.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
These pages list the classes and functions a caller imports. Each entry is one class or function, generated from its docstring.

Each page opens with the imports to use. Classes you create in a script, such as handlers, fetchers, generators, grids, and data stores, import from gigaspatial. Their building blocks, such as a handler's config, downloader, and reader, import from the subpackage: gigaspatial.handlers, gigaspatial.fetchers, gigaspatial.image_downloaders, gigaspatial.generators, gigaspatial.grid, gigaspatial.processing, gigaspatial.core.io, gigaspatial.core.http, or gigaspatial.core.schemas. Any other module path is internal and may change between releases.

The handler base is last. It is for adding a dataset to this library, and it is the page that explains a search key and a search geometry.

docs.title: Boundaries
docs.text:
AdminBoundaries loads administrative boundaries for a country. It is not a handler and not a fetcher. Handlers use it when a country source needs a geometry.

from gigaspatial import AdminBoundaries
from gigaspatial.handlers import GeoRepoClient

Bases: AdminBoundaryTable

Handler for administrative boundary data from multiple external sources.

Extends AdminBoundaryTable with factory methods that resolve and ingest boundaries from GADM, GeoRepo (UNICEF), geoBoundaries (HDX), Natural Earth, and internal data stores.

Examples:

>>> boundaries = AdminBoundaries.create("BRA", admin_level=1)
>>> gdf = boundaries.to_geodataframe()

docs.title: Clients
docs.text:
A client is a connection used to query a database, a warehouse, or a web API. It is not a data store, and it is not a dataset: a fetcher or a handler may use one.

from gigaspatial import BigQueryClient, BigQueryClientConfig, DBConnection

A generalizable Google BigQuery client for GigaSpatial.

Provides generic, dataset-agnostic methods for schema inspection and query execution. Dataset-specific fetchers (e.g. MLabFetcher) should compose this client rather than reimplement it.

Bases: BaseModel

Configuration for authenticating and initializing a BigQuery client.

Defaults are resolved from GigaSpatial's global_config, mirroring the pattern used by the Google Earth Engine profiler.

Credential resolution priority: 1. Service account key file (service_account_key_path) 2. Application Default Credentials (ADC) — for GCP-hosted environments

A unified database connection class supporting both Trino and PostgreSQL.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: config : BigQueryClientConfig, optional Validated configuration object. If not provided, a default config is constructed from global_config.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
client = BigQueryClient() # uses global_config defaults client.list_datasets() df = client.query_to_dataframe("SELECT * FROM project.dataset.table LIMIT 10")

custom = BigQueryClient(BigQueryClientConfig(project="my-gcp-project"))

docs.title: Data stores
docs.text:
A data store is where a handler keeps its files. LocalDataStore is the default. A client is not a data store.

read_dataset and write_dataset read and write a file through whichever store you pass.

from gigaspatial import LocalDataStore, ADLSDataStore, read_dataset, write_dataset
from gigaspatial.core.io import DataStore

Every store implements the abstract DataStore. To support another storage service, subclass it.

Bases: DataStore

Implementation for local filesystem storage.

Bases: DataStore

An implementation of DataStore for Azure Data Lake Storage.

Bases: DataStore

An implementation of DataStore for Snowflake internal stages. Uses Snowflake stages for file storage and retrieval.

General-purpose Delta Sharing data accessor.

Read data from various file formats stored in local or cloud-based storage.

Supports plain and compressed formats. For compound extensions such as .csv.gz or .geojson.gz, the inner format is detected automatically.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default path str

Path to the file in data storage.

required data_store DataStore

DataStore instance for accessing storage. If None, local storage is used.

None compression str

Explicit compression type ("gzip", "bz2", "xz"). If None, inferred from the file extension.

None validate_crs bool

If True, emit a UserWarning when a GeoDataFrame has no CRS.

True **kwargs

Additional arguments forwarded to the underlying reader function (e.g., sep, encoding, driver).

{}

Returns:

Type Description Union[DataFrame, GeoDataFrame]

The data read from the file as a DataFrame or GeoDataFrame.

Raises:

Type Description FileNotFoundError

If the file does not exist in the storage backend.

ValueError

If the file type is unsupported or the file cannot be parsed.

RuntimeError

For unexpected errors during the read process.

Write DataFrame, GeoDataFrame, or a generic object to various file formats.

Supported formats include .csv, .xlsx, .json, .parquet for DataFrames, and .geojson, .gpkg, .parquet for GeoDataFrames.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data

The data to write. Can be pd.DataFrame, gpd.GeoDataFrame, or a JSON-serializable object.

required data_store DataStore

Instance of DataStore for accessing data storage. If None, local storage is used.

None path

Path where the file will be written.

None **kwargs

Additional arguments passed to the specific writer function (e.g., index=False).

{}

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the file type is unsupported or if there's an error writing the file.

TypeError

If input data type is incompatible with the file extension.

RuntimeError

For unexpected errors during the write process.

docs.title: map_to_points(gdf, band=None, reducer=None, buffer_radius_m=None, start_date=None, end_date=None, temporal_reducer=None, chunk_size=None, scale=None)
docs.text:
Map GEE values to point locations with optional circular buffers.

This method extracts values from the Earth Engine image/collection at point locations. If buffer_radius_m is provided, circular buffers are created around points and spatial reduction is applied within each buffer.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: gdf : GeoDataFrame Point locations to enrich (must have Point geometries) band : str, optional Band to extract (uses config default if None) reducer : str, optional Spatial reducer: mean, median, min, max, sum, etc. (uses config default if None) buffer_radius_m : float, optional Buffer radius in meters around each point. If None or 0, point values are extracted directly. start_date : str, optional Start date YYYY-MM-DD for temporal filtering (uses config if None) end_date : str, optional End date YYYY-MM-DD for temporal filtering (uses config if None) temporal_reducer : str, optional How to aggregate over time if multiple images: mean, median, max, etc. (uses config default if None) chunk_size : int, optional Features per chunk for API rate limiting (uses config default if None) scale : float, optional Spatial resolution in meters (uses config/dataset default if None)

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: GeoDataFrame Enriched GeoDataFrame with new column: {band}_{reducer}

docs.title: Extract nightlight values at school points with 1km buffers
docs.text: profiler = GEEProfiler(dataset_id="nightlights") enriched = profiler.map_to_points( ... gdf=schools, ... band="avg_rad", ... reducer="mean", ... buffer_radius_m=1000, ... start_date="2020-01-01", ... end_date="2020-12-31" ... ) print(enriched[["school_id", "avg_rad_mean"]].head())

docs.title: Fetchers
docs.text:
A fetcher queries an API or a database and returns records. It does not store the dataset as files.

from gigaspatial import OSMLocationFetcher, OSMRoadsFetcher, GigaSchoolLocationFetcher
from gigaspatial.fetchers import MLabConfig, GEEConfig

MLabFetcher queries M-Lab speed tests in BigQuery. GEEProfiler is also a fetcher and has its own page.

docs.title: OpenStreetMap
docs.text:
Fetcher for OpenStreetMap POIs and boundaries using the Overpass API.

Handles high-level queries for diverse OSM categories (amenities, buildings, shops, etc.) within specific administrative regions or countries.

Attributes:

Name Type Description country Optional[str]

ISO country code or name.

admin_level Optional[int]

OSM administrative level for the search area.

admin_value Optional[str]

Name of the administrative area.

location_types Union[List[str], Dict[str, List[str]]]

Mapping of category keys (e.g., 'amenity') to values.

base_url str

Overpass API endpoint URL.

timeout int

Overpass server-side query timeout, in seconds. The actual HTTP client timeout used for requests will be this value plus a small buffer, so we don't give up locally right as the server is about to respond.

max_retries int

Number of retry attempts for failed requests.

retry_delay int

Delay between retries in seconds.

OSMRoadsFetcher returns a road network rather than records: a SpatialNetwork. It needs pip install "giga-spatial[roads]", and the road networks guide says which area sizes suit Overpass.

Fetch the road network of a source from OpenStreetMap, through osmnx and the Overpass API.

The source is turned into an area to query: a country's boundary, a geometry as given, the union of a frame's polygons, or for points the convex hull (area="hull"), bounding box ("bbox"), or union of buffers ("buffers"), buffered by buffer meters. The result is a directed :class:SpatialNetwork, with list-valued OSM attributes normalised so it can be saved; the fetcher saves nothing itself.

Needs pip install 'giga-spatial[roads]'.

Attributes:

Name Type Description network_type str

osmnx network type, such as "drive_service", "drive", "walk", "bike", or "all".

custom_filter Optional[Union[str, List[str]]]

Overpass way filter replacing network_type, such as '["highway"~"primary|secondary"]'.

simplify bool

Join edges between junctions, as osmnx does.

retain_all bool

Keep every disconnected part, not only the largest.

truncate_by_edge bool

Keep edges that leave the area at one end.

buffer float

Meters around point and line sources.

area Literal['hull', 'bbox', 'buffers']

How points become an area: "hull", "bbox", or "buffers".

overpass_url Optional[str]

Overpass endpoint, such as a mirror when the main server is down. The OVERPASS_URL setting otherwise.

timeout int

Seconds for each Overpass request.

max_retries int

Retries after a failed request, with growing pauses.

retry_delay float

Seconds before the first retry.

docs.title: UNICEF
docs.text:
Fetch UNICEF child welfare indicators from the UNICEF SDMX Data Warehouse.

Wraps the unicefdata Python package, providing access to 700+ indicators across categories such as child mortality, education, nutrition, immunisation, WASH, and SDGs.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: indicator : str SDMX indicator code, e.g. "CME_MRY0T4" (Under-5 mortality rate). Use :func:search_indicators or :func:list_categories from unicefdata to discover available codes. countries : list of str, optional ISO 3166 alpha-3 country codes (e.g. ["KEN", "NGA", "BRA"]). If None, fetches data for all available countries. year : str or int, optional Single year (2020), range ("2015:2023"), or list. If None, fetches all available years. sex : str, optional Sex disaggregation: "_T" (total), "F", "M", or "ALL". Defaults to "_T". format : str, optional Output format: "long" (default), "wide", or "wide_indicators". latest : bool, optional If True, keep only the most recent value per country. mrv : int, optional Keep the N most recent values per country. circa : bool, optional If True, return the closest available year when an exact match is not found. logger : logging.Logger, optional Logger instance. Defaults to the global GigaSpatial logger.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
fetcher = UnicefDataFetcher( ... indicator="ED_CR_L1", ... countries=["KEN", "NGA", "ETH"], ... year="2015:2023", ... ) df = fetcher.fetch() df = fetcher.fetch(latest=True)

docs.title: Zones
docs.text:
Bases: GeometryBasedZonalViewGenerator[T]

Generates zonal views using H3 hexagons as the zones.

Mirrors MercatorViewGenerator/S2ViewGenerator but uses H3 cells (resolutions 0-15). The input source defines the area/cells and resolution determines the granularity.

Supported sources: - Country string → CountryH3Hexagons.create - Shapely geometry or GeoDataFrame → H3Hexagons.from_spatial - List of points (shapely Points or (lon, lat) tuples) → from_spatial - List of H3 indexes (strings) → H3Hexagons.from_hexagons

Bases: GeometryBasedZonalViewGenerator[T]

Generates zonal views using Google S2 cells as the zones.

This mirrors the MercatorViewGenerator but uses S2 cells (levels 0-30) as zone units. The primary input source defines the geographic area of interest and the level determines the granularity of S2 cells.

Attributes:

Name Type Description source Union[str, BaseGeometry, GeoDataFrame, List[Union[Point, Tuple[float, float]]], List[Union[int, str]]]

Specifies the geographic area or specific cells to use. Can be: - A country name (str): Uses CountryS2Cells to generate cells covering the country. - A Shapely geometry (BaseGeometry): Uses S2Cells.from_spatial to create cells intersecting the geometry. - A GeoDataFrame (gpd.GeoDataFrame): Uses S2Cells.from_spatial to create cells intersecting geometries or from points. - A list of points (List[Union[Point, Tuple[float, float]]]): Uses S2Cells.from_points via from_spatial. - A list of cell identifiers (List[Union[int, str]]): Uses S2Cells.from_cells (accepts integer IDs or token strings).

level int

The S2 level (0-30). Higher levels produce smaller cells.

config Optional[ZonalViewGeneratorConfig]

Configuration for generation.

data_store Optional[DataStore]

Optional data store instance.

logger Optional[Logger]

Optional logger.

Bases: GeometryBasedZonalViewGenerator[T]

Generates zonal views using Mercator tiles as the zones.

This class specializes in creating zonal views where the zones are defined by Mercator tiles. It extends the GeometryBasedZonalViewGenerator and leverages the MercatorTiles and CountryMercatorTiles classes to generate tiles based on various input sources.

The primary input source defines the geographical area of interest. This can be a country, a specific geometry, a set of points, or even a list of predefined quadkeys. The zoom_level determines the granularity of the Mercator tiles.

Attributes:

Name Type Description source Union[str, BaseGeometry, GeoDataFrame, List[Union[Point, Tuple[float, float]]], List[str]]

Specifies the geographic area or specific tiles to use. Can be: - A country name (str): Uses CountryMercatorTiles to generate tiles covering the country. - A Shapely geometry (BaseGeometry): Uses MercatorTiles.from_spatial to create tiles intersecting the geometry. - A GeoDataFrame (gpd.GeoDataFrame): Uses MercatorTiles.from_spatial to create tiles intersecting the geometries. - A list of points (List[Union[Point, Tuple[float, float]]]): Uses MercatorTiles.from_spatial to create tiles containing the points. - A list of quadkeys (List[str]): Uses MercatorTiles.from_quadkeys to use the specified tiles directly.

zoom_level int

The zoom level of the Mercator tiles. Higher zoom levels result in smaller, more detailed tiles.

predicate str

The spatial predicate used when filtering tiles based on a spatial source (e.g., "intersects", "contains"). Defaults to "intersects".

config Optional[ZonalViewGeneratorConfig]

Configuration for the zonal view generation process.

data_store Optional[DataStore]

A DataStore instance for accessing data.

logger Optional[Logger]

A logger instance for logging.

Methods:

Name Description _init_zone_data

Initializes the Mercator tile GeoDataFrame based on the input source.

docs.text:
Map Google Open Buildings data to zones.

Processes Google Open Buildings dataset to calculate building counts and total building area within each zone. Can use either point centroids (faster) or polygon geometries (more accurate) for spatial operations.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default google_open_buildings_config GoogleOpenBuildingsConfig

Configuration for accessing Google Open Buildings data. Uses default configuration if not provided.

required use_polygons bool

Whether to use polygon geometries for buildings. If True, uses actual building polygons for more accurate area calculations but with slower performance. If False, uses building centroids with area values from attributes for faster processing. Defaults to False.

False

Type Description DataFrame

Note

If no Google Buildings data is found for the zones, returns the original GeoDataFrame unchanged with a warning logged.

docs.title: Grids
docs.text:
A grid system partitions geography into cells. A generator maps datasets onto those cells. H3ViewGenerator uses H3Hexagons. You only need these classes when you want the cells themselves.

from gigaspatial import H3Hexagons, S2Cells, MercatorTiles
from gigaspatial.grid import CountryH3Hexagons

Bases: BaseModel

Representation of a collection of H3 hexagons at a specific resolution.

Provides utility methods to create, filter, manipulate, and export H3 hexagonal grids for spatial analysis. Handles conversion between coordinate pairs, geometries, and H3 cell IDs.

Name Type Description resolution int

H3 resolution level (0-15).

hexagons List[str]

List of H3 cell ID strings.

data_store DataStore

Storage interface for I/O operations.

logger ClassVar

Class-level logger.

Bases: BaseModel

S2Cells class for generating and managing Google S2 cell grids.

S2 uses levels 0-30, where higher levels represent finer resolution. Level 0 covers the largest area and level 30 the smallest.

docs.title: Handler base
docs.text:
This section is for adding a dataset to this library. The classes below are internal: this repository is their only subclasser, and the hooks are not a stable API for other packages. Documenting them does not change that. See the decision.

The guides never use these names. A caller passes a source and may set crop_to_source. The classes live in gigaspatial.handlers.base, which is not a public import path.

docs.title: Search key and search geometry
docs.text:
A handler turns a source into files in two different ways.

The search key is what the dataset's index understands. It may be a country code, a filter, a geometry, or nothing, for a dataset published as one global file. get_search_key is the method a dataset overrides.

The search geometry is always a Shapely geometry in the handler's CRS. Cropping uses only that geometry. extract_search_geometry builds it. A search key that is a geometry is the search geometry.

The split, and the cases where a country source is not cropped, are recorded in Search key and search geometry.

Anything that changes which file is fetched belongs on the data unit, not in an option the downloader has to interpret.

docs.title: The classes
docs.text:
BaseHandler is what a caller holds. load_data ensures the files are stored, then reads them. BaseHandlerConfig resolves a source into data units and stored paths. BaseHandlerDownloader fetches units. BaseHandlerReader loads stored paths and may crop.

A downloader or reader declares its config class as config_type, so it can also be built on its own from a config, a dict of config fields, or nothing.

Keyword arguments stop at those public methods. Each class declares an options type: ResolveOptions, DownloadOptions, or ReadOptions. An unknown keyword raises TypeError.

Bases: ABC

Main entry point and orchestrator for dataset handlers.

Encapsulates a configuration, downloader, and reader to provide a unified API for data acquisition and access. Handlers managed by this class are intended to be the primary interface for library users.

Subclasses must implement the factory methods to provide specific component implementations.

Bases: ABC

Abstract base class for handler configurations.

Standardizes common fields used across all handlers, such as file paths, worker counts, and data store abstractions.

A source is resolved in two steps. get_search_key turns it into the value the dataset's own lookup understands (by default the search geometry), and get_relevant_data_units_by_key turns that key into data units. The search geometry, the area used for cropping, is always built by extract_search_geometry in crs.

docs.title: Handlers
docs.text:
A handler acquires a dataset published as files, stores the files, and loads them for a source. Construct the handler, then call load_data, load_into_dataframe, or the method named below. The shared machinery is documented in the handler base, not on these pages.

from gigaspatial import GHSLDataHandler, WPPopulationHandler
from gigaspatial.handlers import GHSLDataConfig, GHSLDataDownloader, GHSLDataReader

Every handler is importable from gigaspatial. Its config, downloader, and reader are in gigaspatial.handlers. A handler takes its config fields as keyword arguments, so most scripts only need the handler.

config = GoogleMSBuildingsConfig() handler = GoogleMSBuildingsHandler(config) geometry = Polygon([...]) # Your area of interest buildings = handler.load_data(geometry)

docs.title: OpenStreetMap roads
docs.text:
OSMRoadsHandler returns a SpatialNetwork built from Geofabrik's extracts, the same network OSMRoadsFetcher returns for the same area. It needs pip install "giga-spatial[roads]"; the road networks guide explains which extracts a source uses and how they are stored.

Bases: BaseHandler

OpenStreetMap road networks from Geofabrik extracts.

Stores each extract once and returns a SpatialNetwork for a country, a geometry, a frame, or points, the same network OSMRoadsFetcher returns for the same area. Suited to whole countries and regions; for a city or the area around a few schools, the fetcher downloads less.

Options, passed as keywords to load_data and the other entries:

  • choosing extracts: regions, extracts, date, refresh, max_age_days, buffer, area (OSMRoadsResolveOptions);
  • the network: network_type, tags, simplify, retain_all, truncate_by_edge, node_index (OSMRoadsReadOptions).
Example

from gigaspatial import OSMRoadsHandler handler = OSMRoadsHandler() rwanda = handler.load_data("RWA") around_schools = handler.load_data([(-1.9441, 30.0619), (-1.9536, 30.0588)], buffer=2000)

Needs pip install 'giga-spatial[roads]'.

Bases: ResolveOptions

Options that choose the extracts for a source.

Attributes:

Name Type Description regions bool

For a country source, use the country's sub-region extracts instead of its country extract.

extracts Optional[Tuple[str, ...]]

Geofabrik extract IDs to use, overriding the choice.

date Optional[str]

Use the extracts of this date (YYYY-MM-DD), stored or downloaded, instead of the newest stored ones. Geofabrik keeps daily files for about a week, then those of the 1st of each month and of January 1st.

refresh bool

Use Geofabrik's latest extracts even when older ones are stored, and download Geofabrik's index again.

max_age_days Optional[int]

Use Geofabrik's latest extracts when the newest stored one is older than this many days. Never, by default.

buffer float

Meters around point and line sources.

area Literal['hull', 'bbox', 'buffers']

How points become an area: "hull", "bbox", or "buffers".

Bases: ReadOptions

Options for building and loading road networks.

Attributes:

Name Type Description network_type str

osmnx network type, such as "drive_service", "drive", "walk", "bike", "all_public", or "all".

tags Optional[Dict[str, Optional[Sequence[str]]]]

Allowed values per OSM key, such as {"highway": ["primary", "secondary"]}, replacing network_type. A way must match every key; None allows any value of a key.

simplify bool

Join edges between junctions, as osmnx does.

retain_all bool

Keep every disconnected part, not only the largest.

truncate_by_edge bool

Keep edges that leave the area at one end.

node_index Optional[str]

pyosmium node location index, such as "flex_mem" or "sparse_file_array". Chosen from the extract's size otherwise.

docs.title: Spatial networks
docs.text:
A SpatialNetwork holds places as nodes with coordinates, joined by edges with a length in meters or another weight. A road network from OSMRoadsFetcher is one kind. The network is two tables, and every edit returns a new network. The road networks guide shows a full workflow.

from gigaspatial import SpatialNetwork, OSMRoadsFetcher

to_pandana and backend="pandana" need pip install "giga-spatial[pandana]". Why the network is held as tables, and how a saved network is laid out, are in ADR 0004 and ADR 0005.

The methods below are in this order: building, saving, and converting; reading the tables; editing; inserting points; algorithms; and reducing.

Bases: EditingMixin, AlgorithmsMixin, ReductionMixin, InsertionMixin

A spatial network held as a nodes table and an edges table.

Nodes carry coordinates in EPSG:4326, and edges carry a length in meters or another weight. A road network fetched by OSMRoadsFetcher is one kind; points joined to their nearest neighbours are another.

The nodes table is indexed by node_id and has the columns x (longitude), y (latitude), and kind, plus any attributes. The edges table has u, v, key, length (meters), kind, an optional geometry column of LineStrings, and any attributes. An edge is identified by (u, v, key).

A network never changes after it is built: methods that edit it return a new network. The tables returned by nodes and edges are shallow copies; adding columns to them does not change the network, but do not modify their values in place.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default nodes DataFrame

Node table, indexed by node ID or with a node_id column, with x and y columns or Point geometries.

required edges DataFrame

Edge table with u and v columns. A missing key is numbered per node pair, and a missing length is computed along the geometry, or between the endpoints when there is none.

required directed bool

Whether edges run from u to v only. A two-way road in a directed network is two rows, one per direction.

True crs Any

CRS of the input coordinates. They are converted to EPSG:4326. The CRS of a GeoDataFrame takes precedence for its geometries.

WGS84 weight str

Default edge column for algorithms.

'length' metadata Optional[Dict[str, Any]]

Provenance, such as the fetch parameters.

None

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If node IDs repeat, an edge references an unknown node, an edge (u, v, key) repeats, or the weight column is missing.

docs.title: save(path, data_store=None)
docs.text:
Save the network as a folder: nodes.parquet, edges.parquet, and network.json.

Edges are GeoParquet with WKB geometry, readable by geopandas, DuckDB, and QGIS; without edge geometry, edges.parquet is plain Parquet. Attributes that mix lists and single values, as osmnx produces, are normalised first (see normalize_attributes); the network itself is not changed. Existing files in the folder are overwritten.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default path Any

docs.text:
Insert points of interest as nodes, each joined to its nearest road.

Each point is joined to the nearest road edge at the foot of the perpendicular: the edge is split there, a node of kind split is added, and a connection edge joins the point (kind point) to it. When the foot is within snap_to_node meters of the edge's end, the point connects to that node instead. Points whose feet fall on the same spot share one split node. Each road edge is split once, at all of its points, and the pieces' lengths add up exactly to the original length. In a directed network, both directions of a two-way road are split at the same nodes, and connections run both ways.

docs.title: simplify(keep=None, sum_columns=('length',))
docs.text:
Remove nodes that only continue a road, joining the edges on either side.

A node is removed when it has exactly two neighbours and its edges continue through it: one edge in and one out of a one-way road, or both directions of a two-way road (in an undirected network, exactly two edges). This is the rule osmnx uses, except that osmnx also removes nodes between duplicated parallel ways and drops one of the ways, and deletes rings with no junction at all; here those nodes stay, and a ring keeps one node. Nodes of kind point or split and nodes in keep are never removed.

Joined edges get:

  • the sum of sum_columns and of the network's weight column;
  • one geometry along the joined edges;
  • text joined with ; where values differ, without repeats;
  • osmid and other list columns concatenated, without repeats;
  • oneway true only if every part is one-way, reversed true if any part is, other booleans true only if all parts are;
  • the length-weighted mean of other numeric columns;
  • the kind of their longest part.

Each direction of a two-way road is joined separately, so it stays two-way when both directions can be joined. Joined edges always get a geometry, as in osmnx, so a network without edge geometry gains a geometry column that is missing for the edges left as they were.

Parameters:

Node IDs to keep.

"steiner": Mehlhorn's approximation, faster and on roads a few percent longer. Both are Steiner tree approximations: with roots, a forest whose every tree reaches a root, so a terminal may connect through other terminals. "nearest_root": each terminal's shortest path to its nearest root. "all_pairs": the shortest paths between every terminal and every terminal and root; their number grows with the square of the terminals.
