docs.title: Connection planning
docs.text:
ConnectionPlanner plans how to connect terminals, such as schools, to roots, such as fibre nodes, along a network at the smallest shared cost, and returns a ConnectionPlan. Why it is a rooted Steiner tree and a separate object is in ADR 0008.

from gigaspatial import ConnectionPlanner

plan = ConnectionPlanner(network, school_ids, roots=fibre_ids, weight="cost").plan()

Plans how to connect terminals to roots along a spatial network at the smallest shared cost.

Terminals are the points to connect, such as schools. Roots are nodes already connected to each other through an existing network, such as fibre nodes, a power grid's substations, or water mains; reaching any root is enough. A terminal may reach a root directly or through other terminals, and an edge used by several terminals is paid once. Directions are ignored, since a cable or a pipe does not follow one-way streets.

With roots, this is the Steiner tree problem once every root is joined to one virtual root at weight 0: the plan is a forest whose every tree reaches a root. Without roots, it is the Steiner tree joining the terminals. Both are NP-hard; the planner returns approximations.

Insert the terminals and roots into the network first, with :meth:SpatialNetwork.insert_points, and pass their node IDs.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default network SpatialNetwork

The network to plan along.

required terminals Any

Node IDs to connect.

required roots Any

Node IDs already connected to each other.

() weight Optional[str]

Edge column to minimise, such as a cost. The network's weight otherwise. Zero is allowed.

None bridge_cost Optional[float]

Weight per metre of a straight-line link between parts of the network that no road joins, such as a microwave link or a planned road, in the units of weight. No bridges when None. Each part is offered links to its nearest other parts, at most five, and a plan uses a link only where it is cheaper than the roads.

None bridge_max_distance float

Longest link, in metres.

5000.0

Raises:

Type Description KeyError

If a terminal or root is not a node of the network.

ValueError

If the weight is missing or negative on some edge, or the bridge options are negative.

The result of a connection planner.

Attributes:

Name Type Description network SpatialNetwork

The connecting subnetwork, undirected, contracted to the terminals, the roots, the ends of bridges, and the nodes where paths branch, with lengths added up and geometries joined as :meth:SpatialNetwork.simplify does. Unreachable terminals and unused roots are kept without edges.

edges GeoDataFrame

The chosen edges, uncontracted, one row per pair of nodes with the attributes of its cheapest edge and a geometry (a straight line where the network has none). Bridges have kind "bridge", their great-circle length, and their weight in the weight column unless the weight is length.

terminals DataFrame

One row per terminal, indexed by node ID: status ("connected", "root" for a terminal that is itself a root, or "unreachable"); root, the root its tree reaches nearest along the plan; distance, the weight along the plan to that root; and bridged, whether that path uses a bridge. Without roots, root is missing, distance is NaN, and bridged says whether the terminal is joined to the others only through a bridge. Plans by "shortest_path" add order, when the terminal was connected (0 for a terminal that is a root, missing when unreachable), and marginal_cost, the weight of the edges its connection added.

cost float

The total weight of edges, with each bridge at bridge_cost per metre.

metadata Dict[str, Any]

The method, the weight, bridge_cost, the numbers of terminals and roots, terminals by status, bridges offered and used, and the seconds each step took.

bound Optional[float]

A lower bound on the cost of any plan connecting the same terminals, set by :meth:ConnectionPlanner.lower_bound.

gap Optional[float]

cost / bound - 1: the plan costs at most 1 + gap times the optimum.

docs.title: plan(method='shortest_path')
docs.text:
Plan the connections.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default method str

"shortest_path" (the default): Takahashi and Matsuyama's 2-approximation of the Steiner tree, and a model of a phased rollout: starting from the roots (or the first terminal), repeatedly connect the terminal nearest to anything connected so far, along its shortest path. Gives each terminal's order and marginal cost; ties go to the terminal listed first. On Kigali's roads it came within 0.7 to 6% of the optimum. "steiner": Mehlhorn's 2-approximation, with roots the rooted tree, without them the tree joining the terminals; 5 to 20 times faster, and 3 to 9% above the optimum on Kigali. :meth:improve brings either within about 1% of it. "nearest_root": each terminal's shortest path to its nearest root, and the union of those paths; needs roots, and never lets a terminal connect through another one. "all_pairs": the shortest paths between every terminal and every terminal or root; their number grows with the square of the terminals.

'shortest_path'

Returns:

Type Description ConnectionPlan

The plan. With roots, terminals that cannot reach any root, even

ConnectionPlan

through bridges, are unreachable. Without roots, the plan joins the

ConnectionPlan

terminals of the network's part that holds the most of them, and

ConnectionPlan

the others are unreachable.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the method is unknown, or is "nearest_root" without roots.

docs.title: Spatial networks: concepts and methods
docs.text:
SpatialNetwork is the library's model of a network laid out on the ground: nodes with coordinates, joined by edges that carry a length in metres. Road networks from OpenStreetMap are the main kind, but points joined to their nearest neighbours, or any network you build from your own tables, work the same way.

This note explains how it works, method by method, and what each method is good for. It is written for data scientists and statisticians who know Python, pandas, geopandas, and the basics of graphs. Where a method's result depends on how its algorithm works, the note explains the algorithm and why we chose it. The evidence behind those choices, with the benchmarks, is in design and algorithm decisions. For a ten-minute start, read the road networks guide first.

docs.title: Why a spatial network
docs.text:
Most of Giga's questions about schools are network questions. How many metres of fibre would connect these schools to the nearest fibre node, along roads? Which schools have a clinic within 5 km by road? How much longer is the road to the nearest secondary school than the straight line, and does that explain attendance? Straight-line distance answers none of them well: a river, a ridge, or a missing bridge can turn 2 km into 15.

These questions share a few building blocks: get the roads, put the schools on them, measure along them, and keep the part of the network that matters. SpatialNetwork provides those blocks and leaves the application to you.

docs.title: What it is like to use
docs.text:
A few principles run through every method:

  • Tables, not graph objects. A network is a table of nodes and a table of edges, which you can inspect, filter, and join like any pandas table. networkx and pandana are export formats, available when you need them.
  • Metres. Every length is in metres, measured on the sphere the same way osmnx measures roads, so lengths the library adds are consistent with the roads they join.
  • Directed, like OpenStreetMap. A road network follows one-way restrictions, and a two-way road is two edges. Methods that model cables or walking, where direction does not matter, take directed=False or work on the undirected network themselves.
  • Every edit returns a new network. Nothing changes in place, so a network you computed a result on stays the network you computed it on.
  • Many at once. Methods take many points, nodes, or edges in one call. A Python loop that edits one edge at a time is the slow way to use the library.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
1. Why a spatial network: this page.
  2. Getting a network: roads from OpenStreetMap, for an area or a whole country, and networks from your own tables or points. It also sets up the example used throughout.
  3. The data model: the node and edge tables, kinds, keys, lengths, and weights.
  4. Editing: selecting, clipping, attributes, weights, combining networks.
  5. Inserting points: joining schools and other points to the roads.
  6. Reduction: simplifying a network, and keeping only the roads that connect a set of points.
  7. Algorithms: shortest paths, service areas, nearest facilities, counts within a distance, components, spanning trees.
  8. Storage and interoperability: saving, loading, and converting.
  9. Worked use cases: fibre planning and accessibility, end to end.
  10. Performance and pitfalls.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
Five applications come back throughout the note. Each method's section says which it serves.

Use case Question Main methods Fibre backbone planning Which roads would carry fibre from the existing fibre to these schools, what would it cost, and in which order? insert_points, ConnectionPlanner, connecting_subnetwork, custom weights Last-mile cost How far is each school from the nearest fibre node, by road? insert_points, nearest_by_network Accessibility Which schools have a clinic within 5 km by road, and what area does a facility serve? count_within, nearest_by_network, reachable Network distance as a model feature Road distances, and how much longer they are than straight lines, as covariates or outcomes shortest_path_lengths Network diagnostics Which parts of the network are cut off, and which schools cannot be reached? connected_components, connect_components

docs.title: The example
docs.text:
Every snippet in the note runs on the same example: Rwanda's roads from OpenStreetMap, with 200 schools, 5 fibre nodes, and 10 clinics placed at random around Kigali with a fixed seed. The points are made up, so anyone can run the note without data access or credentials. Snippets build on each other, page after page, and every output shown was produced by running them in order (docs/scripts/run_concept_examples.py reruns them all).

The timings shown come from one laptop (an Apple M1 Pro), and are a guide to how costs compare rather than a promise.

docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text: Every algorithm runs on scipy's sparse graph routines (scipy.sparse.csgraph) by default. Shortest path lengths can also run on pandana, which is faster for very many pairs (see below). In a directed network, routes follow one-way roads; directed=False ignores them for one call. Unreachable pairs come back as inf, never as an error.

docs.title: The adjacency matrix
docs.text:
Every algorithm starts from a sparse matrix of the network: row and column \(i\) are the node at position \(i\) of node_index, and an entry is the weight of the edge between two nodes. Parallel edges keep their smallest weight. The matrix is built on first use and cached per weight and direction, so later calls pay nothing.

started = time.perf_counter()
matrix = network.adjacency()
print(matrix.shape, f"{matrix.nnz:,} entries", f"{time.perf_counter() - started:.2f} s")
print(list(network.node_index[:3]))

(125494, 125494) 330,649 entries 0.06 s
[271317577, 279244409, 279244410]

Results always come back with node IDs, not positions. adjacency() is there for your own sparse computations, with node_index to translate positions.

docs.title: Shortest path lengths
docs.text:
shortest_path_lengths(origins, destinations) returns a table with one row per origin and one column per destination, in metres (or in the weight you name).

started = time.perf_counter()
to_fibre = network.shortest_path_lengths(school_ids, fibre_ids)
print(to_fibre.iloc[:3].round(0))
print(f"{len(school_ids)} by {len(fibre_ids)}: {time.perf_counter() - started:.2f} s")

node_id     fibre-000  fibre-001  fibre-002  fibre-003  fibre-004
node_id                                                          
school-000     8937.0    12241.0     8273.0    17462.0    13567.0
school-001    10612.0     8455.0     4158.0    14607.0     9822.0
school-002     7944.0     6591.0     2293.0    12742.0     7957.0
197 by 5: 5.62 s

How it works. Dijkstra's algorithm, from each origin, on the cached matrix. One search costs \(O((V + E)\log V)\) and finds the distance to every node, so the cost grows with the number of origins, not with the number of destinations: about 25 ms per origin on Rwanda's roads. The library runs origins in blocks that keep the working matrix under 256 MiB, and refuses a result matrix over 1 GiB, with advice to batch, rather than run out of memory.

  • pairwise=True pairs origins[i] with destinations[i] and returns one length per pair, which is what you need for a list of trips.
  • directed=False ignores one-way restrictions, which suits walking or a cable along a road. A directed length is never shorter than the undirected one:
undirected = network.shortest_path_lengths(school_ids, fibre_ids, directed=False)
gap = (to_fibre - undirected).stack()
print(f"One-way streets add {gap.mean():.0f} m on average, {gap.max():.0f} m at most")

One-way streets add 66 m on average, 1302 m at most

Use cases. Road distance as a model feature, travel distances for cost estimates, and origin-destination matrices for planning.

docs.title: Road distance as a model feature
docs.text:
Straight-line distance understates how far a school is from anything, and by how much depends on the terrain and the roads. The ratio of the road distance to the straight-line distance, the detour index, measures that. It is a useful covariate on its own: a school with a detour index of 3 is cut off in a way its straight-line distance does not show.

def great_circle(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2, radius=6_371_009.0):
    lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2 = map(np.radians, (lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2))
    h = np.sin((lat2 - lat1) / 2) ** 2 + np.cos(lat1) * np.cos(lat2) * np.sin((lon2 - lon1) / 2) ** 2
    return 2 * radius * np.arcsin(np.sqrt(h))


nearest_clinic = network.nearest_by_network(school_ids, clinic_ids)
school_xy = network.nodes.loc[nearest_clinic["origin"], ["y", "x"]].to_numpy()
clinic_xy = network.nodes.loc[nearest_clinic["target"], ["y", "x"]].to_numpy()
features = nearest_clinic.assign(
    straight=great_circle(school_xy[:, 0], school_xy[:, 1], clinic_xy[:, 0], clinic_xy[:, 1])
)
features["detour"] = features["distance"] / features["straight"]
print(features.head(4).round(2))
print(features[["distance", "straight", "detour"]].describe().round(2))

       origin      target  distance  straight  detour

1  school-001  clinic-001   3072.66   1741.36    1.76
2  school-002  clinic-001    627.60    532.84    1.18
3  school-003  clinic-008   2857.87   1977.87    1.44
       distance  straight  detour
count    197.00    197.00  197.00
mean    4490.59   3127.79    1.50
std     2287.94   1723.44    0.34
min      207.82     88.06    1.05
25%     2967.47   1904.02    1.28
50%     4190.20   2852.59    1.41
75%     5935.87   4099.45    1.62
max    11626.62   8943.35    2.94

The straight line here is to the same clinic. The nearest clinic by road need not be the nearest in a straight line, which is one more reason to measure along the network.

docs.title: Routes
docs.text:
shortest_paths returns the routes themselves: lists of node IDs, or with geometry=True a GeoDataFrame with one line per route, drawn along the roads' geometries.

first = nearest_clinic.head(3)
routes = network.shortest_paths(first["origin"].tolist(), first["target"].tolist(), geometry=True)
print(routes[["origin", "destination", "length"]].round(0))
print(routes.geometry.iloc[0].geom_type, len(routes["nodes"].iloc[0]), "nodes")

       origin destination  length
0  school-000  clinic-005  5240.0
1  school-001  clinic-001  3073.0
2  school-002  clinic-001   628.0
LineString 48 nodes

Routes come from the same Dijkstra runs, with their predecessor arrays, walked back for all pairs at once. Drawing them along the edges' geometries costs more than the paths themselves (1.2 s against 0.34 s for 1,000 routes on Rwanda), so ask for geometry=True only when you need the lines.

docs.title: Service areas: what a facility reaches
docs.text:
reachable(origins, max_distance) lists every node within a road distance of each origin: a long table of origin, node, and distance.

started = time.perf_counter()
reach = network.reachable(clinic_ids, 5000)
print(reach.head(3).round(0))
print(f"{len(reach):,} rows, {time.perf_counter() - started:.2f} s")
served = reach[reach["node_id"].isin(school_ids)]
print(f"Schools within 5 km of a clinic: {served['node_id'].nunique()} of {len(school_ids)}")

       origin     node_id  distance
0  clinic-000  clinic-000       0.0
1  clinic-000        -184      14.0
2  clinic-000  1223026109      60.0
25,120 rows, 0.02 s
Schools within 5 km of a clinic: 125 of 197

How it works. Dijkstra from each origin, stopped at max_distance: it never looks past the limit, so it costs a fraction of a full search (0.08 s for 100 origins and 5 km on Rwanda, against 2.6 s without a limit).

Use cases. Accessibility (the schools a clinic serves), and service areas to map. Directions matter here: in a directed network the distances are from the origin outwards. For walking, pass directed=False.

docs.title: The nearest facility
docs.text:
nearest_by_network(origins, targets, k=1) gives each origin its nearest target by road and the distance to it, as in the detour example above. With k above 1, it gives the k nearest, nearest first.

three = network.nearest_by_network(school_ids, clinic_ids, k=3)
print(three.head(6).round(0))

       origin      target  distance
0  school-000  clinic-005    5240.0
1  school-000  clinic-007    5512.0
2  school-000  clinic-001    5710.0
3  school-001  clinic-001    3073.0
4  school-001  clinic-004    4405.0
5  school-001  clinic-003    5687.0

How it works. For k=1, the method does not search from every origin. One multi-source Dijkstra from all the targets at once finds, for every node, its nearest target and the distance to it, and the origins read their answer off. In a directed network the search runs on the reversed graph, so the distance is from the origin to the target. That makes it cheap however many origins there are: 0.05 s for 10,000 schools to 100 fibre nodes on Rwanda. For k above 1, it searches from each origin.

Use cases. Last-mile cost (each school's nearest fibre node), accessibility (each school's nearest clinic), and assigning facilities to the population they serve.

docs.title: Counting within a distance
docs.text:
count_within(origins, targets, max_distance) counts the targets each origin reaches within a distance: clinics within 5 km of each school, for example.

clinics_near = network.count_within(school_ids, clinic_ids, 5000)
print(clinics_near.value_counts().sort_index())

count
0    73
1    66
2    19
3    24
4    15
Name: count, dtype: int64

How it works. It runs limited Dijkstra searches from whichever side is smaller, the origins or the targets, and counts from there, reversing directions when it searches from the targets. With 10 clinics and 197 schools, it runs 10 searches.

Use cases. Accessibility indicators, such as the share of schools with at least one clinic within 5 km, or the number of other schools within reach for sharing resources.

docs.title: Connected components
docs.text:
connected_components() labels each node with its component, 0 being the largest. Weak components ignore directions; strong=True asks for components in which every node can reach every other along one-way roads.

weak = network.connected_components()
strong = network.connected_components(strong=True)
print(f"Weak components: {weak.nunique()}, strong components: {strong.nunique()}")
outside = strong[strong != 0]
print(f"Nodes outside the largest strong component: {len(outside)}")
print("Schools among them:", sorted(set(outside.index) & set(school_ids))[:5])

Weak components: 1, strong components: 11
Nodes outside the largest strong component: 11
Schools among them: []

A network loaded through OSMRoadsHandler keeps only its largest weakly connected part, so it has one weak component. Strong components show where one-way streets trap a route: a node outside the largest strong component can be reached but not left, or left but not reached, by a car that obeys the one-way signs. For a cable, that does not matter; for a delivery route, it does.

largest_component() keeps the largest component as a network.

connect_components(max_distance=None) joins disconnected parts with component_link edges between their nearest nodes. The links form a minimum spanning tree over the components, by great-circle distance, found with Borůvka's method: each round, every component finds its nearest node outside itself, and the shortest of those links join components, until one is left or the remaining gaps exceed max_distance. In a directed network each link is added in both directions.

Clipping Kigali out of Rwanda's network with clip, in Editing, left a few pieces cut off: roads that leave the box and come back into it lost the part outside.

pieces = kigali_roads.connected_components()
print(pieces.value_counts().head(4))
joined = kigali_roads.connect_components(max_distance=1000)
links = joined.edges[joined.edges["kind"] == "component_link"]
print(f"Components before: {pieces.nunique()}, after: {joined.connected_components().nunique()}")
print(f"Link edges added: {len(links)}, the longest {links['length'].max():.0f} m")

component
0    23744
1       36
2       32
3        3
Name: count, dtype: int64
Components before: 13, after: 2
Link edges added: 22, the longest 917 m

Use cases. Network diagnostics: finding where OpenStreetMap is missing a road, and bridging small gaps so that routing does not fail on data errors. The links are straight lines, not roads, and are marked as such, so they can be reported or priced differently.

docs.title: Minimum spanning tree
docs.text:
minimum_spanning_tree() keeps the edges that join every node at the smallest total weight, ignoring directions. scipy computes it with Kruskal's algorithm. Applied to the network of links between schools from Getting a network, it is the shortest set of point-to-point links that connects them all:

tree = school_links.minimum_spanning_tree()
print(school_links)
print(tree)
print(f"All links: {school_links.total_length() / 1000:.0f} km, the tree: {tree.total_length() / 1000:.0f} km")

SpatialNetwork(nodes=200, edges=488, directed=False, weight='length')
SpatialNetwork(nodes=200, edges=199, directed=False, weight='length')
All links: 531 km, the tree: 157 km

A tree over a disconnected network is a forest, one tree per component. scipy ignores zero-weight edges, so the library replaces zero weights by the smallest positive number for that call.

Use cases. Wireless or microwave backhaul between schools, where links are straight lines between towers, not roads. For fibre along roads, use connecting_subnetwork, which finds a tree through the road network instead.

docs.title: Very many pairs: the pandana backend
docs.text:
pandana answers shortest path queries with contraction hierarchies: it preprocesses the network once (about 1.4 s for Rwanda), then answers each pair in microseconds. backend="pandana" uses it for shortest_path_lengths; it needs the pandana extra.

Here it computes the road distance from every school to every clinic, as pairs:

origins = np.repeat(school_ids, len(clinic_ids))
destinations = np.tile(clinic_ids, len(school_ids))
for backend in ("scipy", "pandana"):
    started = time.perf_counter()
    lengths = network.shortest_path_lengths(origins, destinations, pairwise=True, backend=backend)
    print(f"{backend}: {len(lengths):,} pairs in {time.perf_counter() - started:.2f} s (pandana's includes its build)")
    if backend == "scipy":
        reference = lengths
print(f"Largest difference: {np.abs(lengths - reference).max():.2f} m")

scipy: 1,970 pairs in 5.09 s (pandana's includes its build)
pandana: 1,970 pairs in 1.81 s (pandana's includes its build)
Largest difference: 0.11 m

scipy's cost grows with the number of origins (about 25 ms each on Rwanda), and pandana's with the number of pairs once it is built. pandana's preprocessing costs as much as about 55 origins of scipy work, so it pays off for large origin-destination matrices, and not for a few hundred origins. It stores weights with limited precision, so its lengths differ from scipy's by a fraction of a metre. The backend works on any network; to_pandana(), which gives you pandana's network itself, indexed by node ID, needs node IDs that are all integers or all text (see Storage and interoperability).

docs.title: The data model
docs.text: A SpatialNetwork is two pandas tables and a few network-level fields. Knowing their columns, and the rules they follow, explains most of what the methods do.

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
The nodes table is indexed by node_id and has a longitude x, a latitude y, and a kind. Every other column is an attribute: OpenStreetMap tags, street_count (how many streets meet at the node, as osmnx counts them), or the columns of points you insert.

print(roads.nodes[["x", "y", "kind", "street_count", "highway"]].head())
print(roads.nodes["highway"].value_counts().head(3))

                   x         y  kind  street_count highway
node_id                                                   
271317577  29.431325 -1.620477  road             3     NaN
279244409  30.086600 -1.953869  road             3     NaN
279244410  30.085752 -1.953824  road             3     NaN
279244411  30.085278 -1.954051  road             3     NaN
279244419  30.085398 -1.956300  road             3     NaN
highway
crossing           11
traffic_signals     9
mini_roundabout     1
Name: count, dtype: int64

Node IDs keep their origin: OpenStreetMap's integer IDs for roads, your own IDs (such as "school-007") for inserted points, and negative integers for the nodes the library creates where it splits a road, as OpenStreetMap does for new objects. IDs are unique, and every method takes and returns them, never row positions.

docs.title: Edges
docs.text:
The edges table has one row per edge, identified by (u, v, key). length is in metres and kind says where the edge came from. geometry holds the road's shape as a LineString, or is missing when the edge is a straight line between its ends, which saves memory on the many short, straight road segments.

edges = roads.edges
print(edges[["u", "v", "key", "length", "kind", "osmid", "highway", "oneway", "reversed"]].head())
print(f"Edges with no geometry (straight): {edges['geometry'].isna().mean():.0%}")
