2    279245648  10130088941    0  ...  residential   True    False
3  10130088941    281686871    0  ...  residential   True    False
4   6371510564   6371497657    0  ...      primary  False    False

[5 rows x 9 columns]
Edges with no geometry (straight): 17%

osmid holds the OpenStreetMap ways an edge was made from: one way for most edges, several where simplification joined roads. Attributes that differ between those ways are joined with ;, such as "residential;tertiary".

docs.title: Directions, two-way roads, and keys
docs.text:
A road network is directed by default, as OpenStreetMap is. A two-way road is two rows, one per direction, with the second marked reversed. A one-way road is one row, with oneway true.

two_way = edges[~edges["oneway"]].iloc[0]
pair = edges[
    ((edges["u"] == two_way["u"]) & (edges["v"] == two_way["v"]))
    | ((edges["u"] == two_way["v"]) & (edges["v"] == two_way["u"]))
]
print(pair[["u", "v", "key", "length", "oneway", "reversed"]])
print(f"Parallel edges (key above 0): {(edges['key'] > 0).sum():,}")

            u           v  key    length  oneway  reversed
0  6365469082  6365469315    0  6.544992   False     False
1  6365469315  6365469082    0  6.544992   False      True
Parallel edges (key above 0): 2,780

The key tells apart parallel edges between the same two nodes, such as two roads that leave a junction and meet again. It counts from 0 for each (u, v) pair, as in osmnx and networkx.

An undirected network, such as one from from_points or to_undirected, has one row per edge, and the order of u and v has no meaning. Methods that should ignore one-way restrictions, such as measuring a cable route, take directed=False and treat a directed network as undirected for that call.

docs.title: Lengths
docs.text:
Every length is the great-circle distance in metres, with the formula and Earth radius osmnx uses for roads:

\[ d = 2R \arcsin \sqrt{\sin^2\frac{\varphi_2 - \varphi_1}{2} + \cos\varphi_1 \cos\varphi_2 \sin^2\frac{\lambda_2 - \lambda_1}{2}}, \qquad R = 6{,}371{,}009 \text{ m} \]

where \(\varphi\) is latitude and \(\lambda\) longitude, in radians. An edge with a geometry is measured along it, segment by segment. The library uses the same formula for every edge it creates (connections to inserted points, split pieces of roads, links between points), so they are consistent with the roads. The sphere is within about 0.5% of the true ellipsoid, a difference that never decides which road is nearer.

docs.title: Weights
docs.text: Algorithms minimise or add up a weight column, length by default. The network's weight field names the default, and every algorithm takes weight= to use another edge column for one call: a travel time, a cost of laying fibre, or a risk score. Weights must be present and not negative on every edge.

docs.title: Kinds and the library's terms
docs.text:
A node's or edge's kind records where it came from, so a result can always be traced back. The library's own terms:

Term Meaning node kind road A node of the road network: a junction, a dead end, or a point along a road node kind point An inserted point of interest, such as a school node kind split A node the library added where it split a road to connect a point edge kind road A road segment, or a joined chain of them edge kind split A piece of a road that was split at a split node edge kind connection The link from an inserted point to its road edge kind point_link A link between two points: from from_points, or from insert_points(chain=True) edge kind component_link A link connect_components added between disconnected parts edge kind added An edge you added with add_weighted_edges edge kind bridge A straight-line link a connection plan uses between parts of the network that no road joins insertion Adding points to a network as nodes, each joined to its nearest road connecting subnetwork The part of a network that joins a set of points, reduced to those points and the places where the paths branch key The number that tells apart parallel edges between the same two nodes weight The edge column algorithms minimise, length by default

docs.title: Coordinates and CRS
docs.text:
Nodes are stored in EPSG:4326 (longitude and latitude). Constructors convert other CRSs, and accessors take crs= to return projected output. Arrays of coordinates are ordered (y, x), which is (lat, lon), the order the rest of the library uses for point tuples.

print(roads.node_coordinates(roads.node_index[:2]))
print(roads.bounds)

[[-1.6204771 29.431325 ]
 [-1.9538695 30.0866001]]
(28.8611577, -2.866518, 30.8968143, -0.9896697)

docs.title: Metadata and summaries
docs.text:
metadata is a dictionary of provenance: the extract or the fetch parameters, how the network was built, and how it was loaded. It is saved with the network. info() summarises everything at once.

summary = roads.info()
print({key: summary[key] for key in ("nodes", "edges", "total_length_m", "edges_with_geometry")})
print(roads.metadata["build"]["network_type"], roads.metadata["load"])

{'nodes': 125095, 'edges': 332633, 'total_length_m': 106227700.31817828, 'edges_with_geometry': 274942}
drive_service {'retain_all': False, 'truncate_by_edge': False, 'cropped': False}

docs.title: A network never changes
docs.text:
Every method that edits returns a new network, and the old one stays as it was. The new network shares every column it did not change with the old one, so an edit costs only what it changes. Because a network never changes, it can cache what it derives from its tables (the adjacency matrix for routing, the spatial indexes for nearest searches, the GeoDataFrames) and never has to work out whether a cache is stale.

The one rule this asks of you: nodes and edges return copies of the tables that share their columns with the network. Adding a column to them is fine, but do not change their values in place, because another network may share the column. To change values, use the editing methods on the next page.

docs.title: Editing
docs.text: Every editing method takes many nodes or edges at once and returns a new network. The original stays as it was (see The data model).

docs.title: Finding nodes by coordinates
docs.text:
nearest_nodes returns the node closest to each point, by great-circle distance. It uses a KD-tree on the nodes' positions on the unit sphere, built once per network, so it needs no projection and is accurate everywhere. Distances come back in metres.

nearest = roads.nearest_nodes(schools, return_distance=True)
print(nearest.head(3))
print(nearest["distance"].describe().round(0))

      node_id    distance
0  1612911622  148.126799
1  6290263967  244.771110
2  2168896033   78.298345
count    200.0
mean     144.0
std      141.0
min        2.0
25%       50.0
50%       99.0
75%      201.0
max      882.0
Name: distance, dtype: float64

max_distance leaves points with no node that close without a match (a missing ID). The nearest node is not the nearest road: a school beside a long, straight road can be far from both of its ends. To join points to roads, use insert_points, which finds the nearest point on the nearest edge.

docs.title: Selecting part of a network
docs.text:
clip keeps the edges that intersect an area, and their end nodes. predicate="within" keeps only edges entirely inside it. The edges are found with an R-tree on their geometries, built once per network.

from shapely.geometry import box

kigali = box(29.98, -2.05, 30.25, -1.85)
started = time.perf_counter()
kigali_roads = roads.clip(kigali)
print(kigali_roads, f"{time.perf_counter() - started:.2f} s")
print(roads.clip(kigali, predicate="within"))

SpatialNetwork(nodes=23,833, edges=61,909, directed=True, weight='length') 0.09 s
SpatialNetwork(nodes=23,630, edges=61,453, directed=True, weight='length')

clip cuts nothing: an edge that crosses the boundary is kept whole. To cut a road network to an area the way osmnx does, keeping the nodes inside, use filter_nodes(geometry=area); to load roads for an area in the first place, pass the area to OSMRoadsHandler.load_data, which also keeps the largest connected part.

filter_edges keeps the edges you select and every node, so some nodes may be left without edges. Here, the main roads:

highway = kigali_roads.edges["highway"].astype(str)
main_roads = kigali_roads.filter_edges(mask=highway.str.contains("trunk|primary|secondary").to_numpy())
connected = main_roads.filter_nodes(mask=(main_roads.degree() > 0).to_numpy())
print(main_roads)
print(connected)

SpatialNetwork(nodes=23,833, edges=5,587, directed=True, weight='length')
SpatialNetwork(nodes=2,996, edges=5,587, directed=True, weight='length')

docs.title: Attributes and weights
docs.text:
set_edge_attribute and set_node_attribute set one column, from a single value, an array in table order, or a Series keyed by ID. update_nodes and update_edges set several columns from a table keyed by ID, and update_nodes(by="coordinates") matches rows to their nearest nodes instead.

Custom weights are edge columns like any other. For fibre planning, the cost of laying fibre depends on the road: trenching along a trunk road costs more than along a residential street, and the last stretch from the road to a school has its own price. The rates below are round, illustrative numbers per metre, not real tariffs:

cost_per_metre = {"trunk": 40, "primary": 30, "secondary": 20, "tertiary": 15}  # illustrative


def with_fibre_cost(net, other_roads=10, connections=25):
    """The network with ``rate`` (cost per metre) and ``cost`` (the edge's total) columns."""
    road_class = net.edges["highway"].astype(str).str.split(";").str[0]
    rate = road_class.map(cost_per_metre).fillna(other_roads).to_numpy()
    rate[(net.edges["kind"] == "connection").to_numpy()] = connections
    net = net.set_edge_attribute("rate", rate)
    return net.set_edge_attribute("cost", net.edges["length"].to_numpy() * rate)


costed = with_fibre_cost(kigali_roads)
print(costed.edges[["highway", "length", "rate", "cost"]].head(4).round(1))

       highway  length  rate   cost
0  residential    34.6  10.0  346.3
1  residential    23.9  10.0  238.5
2  residential    55.1  10.0  550.7
3  residential    55.1  10.0  550.7

Any algorithm can then minimise the new column with weight="cost". Attribute edits keep a column's type when nothing is lost, and text stays categorical. x, y, u, v, and key cannot be set, because they define the network.

Rates and totals. The function stores both a rate per metre and a total per edge, because they behave differently when edges are split or joined. A rate is like a speed limit: when inserting points splits a road, both pieces keep it, and when simplification joins edges, their length-weighted mean is still the right rate, so rate × length gives a joined edge's total exactly. A total is added up when edges are joined only if it is the weight of the call or named in simplify(sum_columns=...), and averaged otherwise; when a road is split, it is copied to both pieces, which counts it twice. So compute totals after inserting points, and keep a rate next to any total you will need to add up later.

docs.title: Adding nodes and edges
docs.text:
add_nodes adds nodes from a points table, without connecting them. add_weighted_edges adds edges between existing nodes, like networkx's add_weighted_edges_from but with arrays, and continues the keys of edges already between each pair. A planned road between two nodes, for example:

ends = kigali_roads.nodes.index[[0, 1]]
planned = kigali_roads.add_weighted_edges([ends[0]], [ends[1]], [1200.0], kind="added", name="planned road")
print(planned.edges[planned.edges["kind"] == "added"][["u", "v", "key", "length", "kind", "name"]])

               u          v  key  length   kind          name
61909  279244409  279244410    1  1200.0  added  planned road

A road already joins those two nodes, so the new edge gets key 1. When the weight is not length, the edges' lengths are measured from their geometry or ends, so length always means metres.

docs.title: Directions
docs.text:
to_undirected gives an undirected network with one edge per pair of nodes: the two directions of a two-way road, and any parallel edges, become the one with the smallest weight, which keeps its attributes and geometry.

undirected = kigali_roads.to_undirected()
print(kigali_roads)
print(undirected)

SpatialNetwork(nodes=23,833, edges=61,909, directed=True, weight='length')
SpatialNetwork(nodes=23,833, edges=31,443, directed=False, weight='length')

Algorithms can also ignore directions for one call with directed=False, which leaves the network as it is.

docs.title: Combining networks
docs.text:
SpatialNetwork.concat combines networks into one. Nodes with the same ID are the same node, so two areas fetched separately join where they meet. An edge whose (u, v, key) appears in several networks is kept once.

west = roads.clip(box(29.98, -2.05, 30.12, -1.85))
east = roads.clip(box(30.10, -2.05, 30.25, -1.85))
both = SpatialNetwork.concat([west, east])
print(west, east, both, sep="\n")

SpatialNetwork(nodes=13,641, edges=34,805, directed=True, weight='length')
SpatialNetwork(nodes=13,626, edges=35,616, directed=True, weight='length')
SpatialNetwork(nodes=23,833, edges=61,909, directed=True, weight='length')

The two halves overlap, and together they are exactly the Kigali box clipped earlier. concat suits networks that share nodes but not roads, such as neighbouring areas fetched from Overpass. Networks loaded from overlapping Geofabrik extracts are combined by OSMRoadsHandler itself, which matches roads by their OpenStreetMap way rather than by key (see Reduction).

docs.title: Other edits
docs.text: Method What it does filter_nodes(ids=, mask=, geometry=) Keep the selected nodes and the edges between them remove_nodes(ids=, points=, geometry=) Remove nodes and their edges; points are matched to their nearest nodes remove_edges(edges=, mask=) Remove edges by (u, v, key), by (u, v) (all parallel edges), or by mask; nodes stay filter_edges(mask=, geometry=) Keep the selected edges and every node set_node_attribute, set_edge_attribute Set one column update_nodes, update_edges Set several columns from a table add_nodes Add unconnected nodes from a points table drop_geometry() Remove edge geometry, to save memory when only the topology matters nodes_gdf, edges_gdf The tables as GeoDataFrames, built once and cached; missing edge geometries become straight lines to_geodataframes(crs=) Both GeoDataFrames, projected if asked degree(directed=) Edges per node total_length(by=) Total length in metres, optionally by a column such as kind

docs.title: Getting a network
docs.text: There are three ways to get a SpatialNetwork: OpenStreetMap roads through OSMRoadsHandler or OSMRoadsFetcher, your own node and edge tables, or points joined to their neighbours. This page shows each, and sets up the example the rest of the note uses.

docs.title: Roads for a whole country: OSMRoadsHandler
docs.text:
OSMRoadsHandler downloads Geofabrik's OpenStreetMap extract of a country, stores it, and builds the road network from it. It needs the roads extra (pip install "giga-spatial[roads]").

import time

from gigaspatial import OSMRoadsHandler

handler = OSMRoadsHandler()

started = time.perf_counter()
roads = handler.load_data("RWA")
print(roads)
print(f"First load, with the download and the build: {time.perf_counter() - started:.1f} s")

started = time.perf_counter()
roads = handler.load_data("RWA")
print(f"Later loads, from the saved network: {time.perf_counter() - started:.2f} s")
print(roads.metadata["extract"])

SpatialNetwork(nodes=125,095, edges=332,633, directed=True, weight='length')
First load, with the download and the build: 24.0 s
Later loads, from the saved network: 0.62 s
{'id': 'rwanda', 'date': '2026-10-28', 'url': 'https://download.geofabrik.de/africa/rwanda-261028.osm.pbf', 'path': 'africa/rwanda', 'replication_timestamp': '2026-10-28T21:21:02Z'}

The first call downloads Rwanda's extract (65 MiB), builds the network, and saves it beside the extract. Every later call reads the saved network. The metadata records which extract the network came from, so a result can always be traced to its data.

load_data takes any source: a country, a geometry, a GeoDataFrame, a DataFrame of points, or a list of (lat, lon) pairs. For anything but a country with its own extract, the network is cropped to the source's area, as the fetcher would crop it (see Reduction for how). The options you are most likely to need:

Option Default Effect network_type "drive_service" osmnx's network types: "drive", "drive_service", "walk", "bike", "all_public", "all" tags none Keep only these values of these OSM keys, such as {"highway": ["primary", "secondary"]}, instead of a network type simplify True Join the edges between junctions (see Reduction) buffer, area 2000, "hull" How points become an area: their convex hull, bounding box, or buffers, widened by buffer metres retain_all False Keep every disconnected part, not only the largest regions False Use a country's regional extracts, such as Brazil's five date, refresh, max_age_days Which extract date to use: a pinned date, Geofabrik's latest, or the latest when the stored one is too old

docs.title: Roads for a small area: OSMRoadsFetcher
docs.text:
For a city, a district, or the area around a few schools, OSMRoadsFetcher queries the Overpass API through osmnx and downloads only that area. It saves nothing; the network is yours to keep or discard.

from shapely.geometry import box

from gigaspatial import OSMRoadsFetcher

central_kigali = box(30.055, -1.960, 30.075, -1.940)
fetched = OSMRoadsFetcher(network_type="drive_service").fetch(central_kigali)
from_extract = handler.load_data(central_kigali)
print("Overpass:", fetched)
print("Extract: ", from_extract)

Overpass: SpatialNetwork(nodes=478, edges=1,074, directed=True, weight='length')
Extract:  SpatialNetwork(nodes=478, edges=1,074, directed=True, weight='length')

The two give the same network for the same area, built by the same rules, apart from edits made to OpenStreetMap between the extract's date and the moment of the query. Which to use depends on the area:

OSMRoadsFetcher OSMRoadsHandler Suits a city, a district, the area around a set of schools regions and whole countries Downloads only the area, from Overpass the whole country's extract, once Time for Rwanda hours, if Overpass allows it about 25 s the first time, then under a second Offline after the first run no yes Data date the moment of the query the extract's date, recorded in the metadata

docs.title: Your own tables
docs.text:
Any network with coordinates can be a SpatialNetwork: water pipes, power lines, bus routes, or roads from another source. Pass a nodes table with x (longitude) and y (latitude) and an edges table with u and v. Lengths are computed when the edges do not have them, along an edge's geometry if it has one and as a straight line between its ends otherwise.

import pandas as pd

from gigaspatial import SpatialNetwork

nodes = pd.DataFrame(
    {"node_id": ["pump", "tank", "school"], "x": [30.060, 30.070, 30.071], "y": [-1.950, -1.950, -1.942]}
)
edges = pd.DataFrame({"u": ["pump", "tank"], "v": ["tank", "school"], "material": ["PVC", "steel"]})
pipes = SpatialNetwork(nodes, edges, directed=False)
print(pipes.edges)

      u       v  key       length  kind material
0  pump    tank    0  1111.306909  road      PVC
1  tank  school    0   896.475473  road    steel

The constructor checks the tables: node IDs must be unique, every edge must reference existing nodes, and (u, v, key) must not repeat. A missing key is numbered for you. Coordinates in another CRS are converted with crs=.

docs.title: The example
docs.text:
From here on, the note works with Rwanda's roads and three sets of made-up points around Kigali: 200 schools, 5 fibre nodes, and 10 clinics. The seed makes them the same for every reader.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)


def points_around_kigali(prefix, count):
    return pd.DataFrame(
        {
            f"{prefix}_id": [f"{prefix}-{i:03d}" for i in range(count)],
            "lat": rng.uniform(-2.02, -1.90, count),
            "lon": rng.uniform(30.00, 30.18, count),
        }
    )


schools = points_around_kigali("school", 200).assign(students=rng.integers(80, 1200, 200))
fibre_nodes = points_around_kigali("fibre", 5)
clinics = points_around_kigali("clinic", 10)
print(schools.head(3))

    school_id       lat        lon  students
0  school-000 -1.944989  30.146086      1167
1  school-001 -1.912334  30.118445       448
2  school-002 -1.926918  30.109935      1025

docs.title: Points joined to their neighbours: from_points
docs.text:
SpatialNetwork.from_points builds an undirected network whose nodes are the points, joined to their k nearest neighbours (connect="knn") or to every point within max_distance metres (connect="distance"). Neighbours come from a KD-tree on the sphere, so no pair of points is compared that does not need to be, and the cost grows with the number of points, not its square.

school_links = SpatialNetwork.from_points(schools, k=4, id_column="school_id")
print(school_links)
print(school_links.edges["length"].describe().round(0))

SpatialNetwork(nodes=200, edges=488, directed=False, weight='length')
count     488.0
mean     1089.0
std       468.0
min        89.0
25%       737.0
50%      1095.0
75%      1434.0
max      2512.0
Name: length, dtype: float64

Use cases. A network of point-to-point links is the model for wireless or microwave links between schools, where the question is which towers to connect rather than which roads to follow. Its minimum spanning tree (see Algorithms) is the shortest set of links that connects every school. weight_func can give the links another weight, such as a cost that grows faster than distance.

docs.title: networkx graphs
docs.text:
SpatialNetwork.from_networkx takes any networkx graph whose nodes have x and y, which includes every osmnx graph. Use it to bring existing work into the library; to_networkx goes back (see Storage and interoperability).

graph = fetched.to_networkx()
print(type(graph).__name__, graph.number_of_nodes(), graph.number_of_edges())
print(SpatialNetwork.from_networkx(graph))

MultiDiGraph 478 1074
SpatialNetwork(nodes=478, edges=1,074, directed=True, weight='length')

docs.title: Inserting points
docs.text:
Most questions about schools start by putting the schools on the road network. insert_points does that: each point becomes a node, joined to its nearest road.

Use cases. Every road-distance question needs it: last-mile cost to the nearest fibre node, access to clinics, road distance as a model feature. It is also the first step of fibre planning.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
started = time.perf_counter()
network, skipped = roads.insert_points(schools, id_column="school_id", max_distance=500, return_skipped=True)
print(f"Schools: {time.perf_counter() - started:.2f} s, {len(skipped)} skipped")
network = network.insert_points(fibre_nodes, id_column="fibre_id", max_distance=500)
network = network.insert_points(clinics, id_column="clinic_id", max_distance=500)
summary = network.info()
print(summary["node_kinds"])
print(summary["edge_kinds"])

Schools: 1.57 s, 3 skipped
{'road': 125095, 'point': 212, 'split': 187}
{'road': 332280, 'split': 722, 'connection': 424}

For each point, the method finds the nearest road edge and the foot of the perpendicular on it: the point on the road closest to the school. It splits the road there, at a new node of kind split, and adds a connection edge from the school (kind point) to that node. The school's columns, such as students, become node attributes.

school = "school-000"
print(network.nodes.loc[[school], ["x", "y", "kind", "students"]])
connection = network.edges[network.edges["u"] == school]
print(connection[["u", "v", "length", "kind"]])
split_node = connection["v"].iloc[0]
pieces = network.edges[(network.edges["u"] == split_node) & (network.edges["kind"] == "split")]
print(pieces[["u", "v", "length", "kind"]])

                    x         y   kind  students
node_id                                         
school-000  30.146086 -1.944989  point    1167.0
                 u     v     length        kind
332942  school-000  -103  26.341664  connection
           u           v      length   kind
332675  -103  6294807498  159.216257  split
332677  -103  1612911824  177.157333  split

The split node has a negative ID, continuing below the lowest negative ID in the network, as OpenStreetMap numbers new objects. In a directed network, connections run both ways, and both directions of a two-way road are split at the same node, so a route can arrive from either side.

docs.title: Lengths are kept
docs.text:
The pieces of a split road are rescaled so they add up exactly to the road's length. Inserting a point never changes the length of a route that passes it.

by_kind = network.total_length(by="kind")
print(by_kind.round(0))
print(f"Roads before: {roads.total_length():,.0f} m")
print(f"Roads and split pieces after: {by_kind['road'] + by_kind['split']:,.0f} m")

kind
road          106043551.0
split            184149.0
connection        29550.0
Name: length, dtype: float64
Roads before: 106,227,700 m
Roads and split pieces after: 106,227,700 m

A connection's length is the great-circle distance from the point to its foot, measured with the same formula as the roads. When the network's weight is not length, connections get a weight equal to their length, and each road piece gets its share of the road's weight, in proportion to its length.

Every other attribute of the road is copied to both pieces unchanged. That is right for a road's name, class, speed limit, or cost per metre, and wrong for a total such as a cost per edge, which would then be counted twice. Compute totals after inserting points, from the pieces' lengths, as the with_fibre_cost function from Editing does. Connection edges have no road attributes at all.

docs.title: The options
docs.text:
• max_distance. A point farther than this from every road is skipped, with a warning, and return_skipped=True returns those points. Schools hundreds of metres from any mapped road are usually a sign of missing roads in OpenStreetMap, or of wrong coordinates, and are worth looking at before trusting their distances.
print(skipped)

      school_id       lat        lon  students
32   school-032 -2.018585  30.156109       343
96   school-096 -2.016976  30.169052       201
186  school-186 -2.016365  30.158554       428
  • snap_to_node. When the foot is within this many metres (5 by default) of the edge's end, the point connects to that node instead of splitting the road. This avoids slivers of road a few centimetres long next to junctions. Set it to 0 to always split.
  • chain. With chain=True, points nearest to a road are handled first, and a point joins an already inserted point (with a point_link edge) when that point is closer than any road. This reproduces how Giga's earlier code connected clusters of schools in a compound, where a school behind another school would otherwise reach the road through it anyway.
chained = roads.insert_points(schools, id_column="school_id", max_distance=500, chain=True)
print(chained.info()["edge_kinds"])

{'road': 332312, 'split': 652, 'connection': 380, 'point_link': 14}
  • id_column. The column with the point IDs; the frame's index otherwise. IDs must not repeat, and must not already be node IDs: inserting the same schools twice raises.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Joining one point to its nearest road is easy; doing it for ten thousand points at country scale is where the old approach broke down. Giga's earlier merge_points_to_graph handled points one at a time, compared each point with every earlier one, and rebuilt a table for each, so its cost grew with the square of the number of points: 292 s for 1,000 schools on Rwanda's roads. insert_points handles all points in one batch, and takes 0.6 s for the same 1,000 schools and 1.7 s for 10,000:

  1. Find each point's road. One nearest-geometry query on an R-tree of the road edges finds every point's nearest edge. The search runs in a UTM projection estimated from the network, because in degrees a road 100 m east can look farther than one 150 m north. UTM is conformal, so it ranks nearby candidates correctly even outside its zone. The projected index is built once per network (1.3 s for Rwanda) and reused by later insertions.
  2. Find the feet. line_locate_point and line_interpolate_point, vectorised over all points, give where along its edge each point's foot lies.
  3. Group by edge. Points are grouped by their edge and sorted by position along it. Points whose feet fall on the same spot share one split node.
  4. Split each road once. Each affected edge is cut at all of its points in one pass. Distances that decide anything (max_distance, snap_to_node) are measured in great-circle metres, never in the projection.
  5. Append. The new nodes and edges are added in one step.

Only step 4 loops in Python, and it loops over affected edges, not points. chain=True adds a KD-tree on the points, which asks for more neighbours only for the points whose neighbours are still closer than their road.

docs.title: Things to know
docs.text:
• Points join roads only. Connections and links from earlier insertions are never split, so inserting fibre nodes after schools does not connect a fibre node to a school's connection.
  • A point is joined to the nearest road edge, whatever it is: a service road, a track if the network type includes tracks, or a one-way street. Choose the network_type with that in mind; "drive_service", the default, includes the service roads that often lead to schools.
  • simplify never removes nodes of kind point or split, so a network with inserted points can be simplified without losing them (see Reduction).

docs.title: What things cost
docs.text:
The costs below are for Rwanda's simplified road network (125,058 nodes, 332,535 edges) on one laptop, from the library's benchmarks. They show how costs compare and grow; your machine will differ.

Paid once per network. These are built on first use and cached, so the second call is free. Since a network never changes, a cache never goes stale; but every edit makes a new network with empty caches.

Built on first use Cost Used by Adjacency matrix, per weight and direction 0.06 s every routing method KD-tree on nodes 0.03 s nearest_nodes, update_nodes(by="coordinates"), remove_nodes(points=) R-tree on edges 0.10 s clip, filter_edges(geometry=) Projected index of roads 1.3 s insert_points pandana network 1.4 s backend="pandana" edges_gdf 0.2 s maps and exports

So insert all your points in one call where you can, rather than in many calls on successive networks: each new network builds its own road index. The example inserts schools, fibre nodes, and clinics in three calls for clarity; one call with all three would be faster.

Per call.

Operation Cost Load the saved network; the topology only 0.47 s; 0.02 s insert_points, 1,000 points; 10,000 points 0.6 s; 1.7 s shortest_path_lengths, 100 origins by 1,000 destinations 2.6 s, about 25 ms per origin reachable, 100 origins within 5 km 0.08 s nearest_by_network, 10,000 origins to 100 targets 0.05 s count_within, 1,000 origins to 100 targets within 5 km 0.04 s ConnectionPlanner.plan, 1,000 schools and 20 fibre nodes: shortest_path (the default); steiner 1.1 s; 0.2 s improve, the same plan: one pass of local search; until it stops about 6 s; about 25 s lower_bound, the same schools 5 s simplify of the unsimplified network (4.5 million edges) 7 s Build Rwanda from its extract, then load it from storage about 14 s, then 0.4 s

How costs grow. Shortest path lengths grow with the number of origins, since each origin is one Dijkstra search over the whole network; destinations are almost free. Put the smaller set first, or swap origins and destinations on an undirected network. nearest_by_network with k=1 and count_within do not grow with the number of origins in the same way, because they search from the targets. A plan by steiner costs about the same for 100 or 1,000 points, and one by shortest_path grows slowly with them: 4.4 s for 10,000 schools. method="all_pairs" grows with the square. improve and lower_bound take time_limit=.

Memory. Rwanda's simplified network takes about 350 MB in memory with its tables and geometries. A shortest path matrix of 10,000 origins by 10,000 destinations is 800 MB of floats, and the library refuses matrices over 1 GiB, with advice to batch. drop_geometry() saves most of a network's memory when only routing matters, and load(columns=[]) loads only the topology.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Coordinate order. Point tuples are (lat, lon), and coordinate arrays from node_coordinates are (y, x), the order the rest of the library uses. Tables use x for longitude and y for latitude, or lat and lon columns. Swapping them puts Rwanda's schools in the Indian Ocean, and insert_points will skip them all as too far from any road.

Directed or not. A road network is directed, and its distances follow one-way streets. For walking, cycling against the flow, or a cable along a road, pass directed=False, or the distances will be longer than they should be and some pairs unreachable.

Unreachable pairs are inf. They are not errors and not missing values. Count them before you average distances, and decide whether they mean "too far" or "missing road".

Mixed node IDs. Inserting points with text IDs into a road network with integer IDs gives a network with both. Everything works with that, including saving and backend="pandana", except to_pandana(), which hands you pandana's network indexed by node ID and needs one kind. If you need pandana's own functions, give your points integer IDs (negative ones are taken by split nodes; use large positive numbers).

Totals on split and joined edges. Only the weight column is shared between the pieces of a split road and added up when edges are joined. A total such as a cost per edge is copied to both pieces when a road is split. Keep a rate per metre beside it and compute totals after inserting points (see Editing).

Do not change the tables in place. network.nodes and network.edges share their columns with the network. Assigning to a cell of them can change other networks that share the column. Use set_node_attribute, update_edges, and the other editing methods.

concat and overlapping roads. SpatialNetwork.concat keeps one edge per (u, v, key). Two networks fetched separately from Overpass for overlapping areas can number parallel edges differently, so the same road can appear twice. Load overlapping areas through OSMRoadsHandler, which combines extracts by OpenStreetMap way, or fetch one area that covers both.

Simplifying after inserting points. It is safe: simplify never removes points or split nodes. But a road between two inserted schools stays split at both, so the simplified network has more edges than before the schools were inserted.

Data, not just code. Every distance is only as good as OpenStreetMap's roads. A missing bridge makes a school look far; an unmapped track makes it look unreachable. connected_components, the skipped points of insert_points, and the schools with the largest detours are the places to look first.

docs.title: Reduction
docs.text: Two methods make a network smaller without losing what matters: simplify removes the nodes that only continue a road, and connecting_subnetwork keeps only the roads that join a set of points. ConnectionPlanner turns the second into a plan for connecting schools to existing fibre.

docs.title: Simplifying a network
docs.text:
OpenStreetMap draws a road as a chain of many short segments, so an unsimplified road network has a node at every bend. simplify removes the nodes that only continue a road and joins the edges on either side, the way osmnx's simplify_graph does. Networks from OSMRoadsHandler and OSMRoadsFetcher are simplified by default; simplify=False gives the raw network.

raw_kigali = handler.load_data(kigali, simplify=False)
started = time.perf_counter()
simple_kigali = raw_kigali.simplify()
print(raw_kigali)
print(simple_kigali, f"{time.perf_counter() - started:.2f} s")

SpatialNetwork(nodes=166,206, edges=342,706, directed=True, weight='length')
SpatialNetwork(nodes=23,722, edges=61,611, directed=True, weight='length') 0.36 s

Which nodes go. A node is removed when it has exactly two neighbours and its edges continue through it: one edge in and one out of a one-way road, or both directions of a two-way road. In an undirected network, it is a node with exactly two edges. Nodes of kind point and split, and nodes passed in keep=, are never removed, so a network with inserted schools keeps its schools.

How joined edges are made. A joined edge's attributes come from the edges it replaces:

Attribute Rule length, the weight column, and columns in sum_columns added up geometry one line along the joined edges text, such as highway and name joined with ; where the parts differ, without repeats osmid and other lists concatenated, without repeats oneway true only if every part is one-way reversed true if any part is other numbers the length-weighted mean kind the kind of the longest part 
joined = simple_kigali.edges[simple_kigali.edges["highway"].astype(str).str.contains(";")].iloc[0]
print(joined[["u", "v", "length", "osmid", "highway", "oneway"]])

u                        1224173076
v                        6370565775
length                   384.393696
osmid        [106060663, 680376414]
highway    unclassified;residential
oneway                        False
Name: 17137, dtype: object

Each direction of a two-way road is joined separately, so it stays two-way when both directions can be joined.

How it works. simplify never walks a chain of edges in Python. Each edge into a removable node is linked to the edge that continues it, which turns every chain into a linked list; pointer jumping ranks each edge's place in its chain in a logarithmic number of vectorised steps; and numpy's reduceat aggregates the attributes of every chain at once. On Rwanda's unsimplified network of 4.5 million edges this takes 7 s, against 148 s for osmnx, with the same nodes and edge lengths.

Where it differs from osmnx. osmnx also removes the nodes between two duplicated parallel ways and drops one of the ways, and it deletes rings that have no junction at all, such as a roundabout mapped on its own. simplify keeps both, so no road is lost. Neither occurs often; in Rwanda's roads, neither occurs at all.

docs.title: Keeping the roads that connect a set of points
docs.text:
connecting_subnetwork answers a fibre planner's two questions: which roads would join these schools to each other, and which roads would connect them to the fibre that already exists, at the smallest total length? It keeps the part of the network that does it, and contracts it to the points, the fibre nodes, and the places where the paths branch. It works on the undirected network, since a cable laid along a road ignores one-way restrictions. Behind it is ConnectionPlanner (see Connection plans below), which also says how each school is connected and how far the plan can be from the best one.

inserted = set(network.node_index)
school_ids = [school for school in schools["school_id"] if school in inserted]
fibre_ids = [fibre for fibre in fibre_nodes["fibre_id"] if fibre in inserted]
clinic_ids = [clinic for clinic in clinics["clinic_id"] if clinic in inserted]

for label, call in [
    ("one tree joining the schools", lambda: network.connecting_subnetwork(school_ids)),
    ("the schools connected to the fibre", lambda: network.connecting_subnetwork(school_ids, roots=fibre_ids)),
    ("each school to its nearest fibre node", lambda: network.connecting_subnetwork(school_ids, roots=fibre_ids, method="nearest_root")),
    ("all pairs, 30 schools and the fibre nodes", lambda: network.connecting_subnetwork(school_ids[:30], roots=fibre_ids, method="all_pairs")),
]:
    started = time.perf_counter()
    result = call()
    print(f"{label}: {result.total_length() / 1000:.1f} km, {len(result.edges)} edges, {time.perf_counter() - started:.2f} s")

one tree joining the schools: 254.7 km, 501 edges, 2.70 s
the schools connected to the fibre: 249.7 km, 497 edges, 1.71 s
each school to its nearest fibre node: 355.2 km, 526 edges, 0.07 s
all pairs, 30 schools and the fibre nodes: 424.7 km, 748 edges, 0.84 s

Open the interactive version of this map to zoom in on the routes.

Terminals and roots. The points to connect are the terminals. Roots, passed as roots=, are nodes already connected to each other through an existing network, such as fibre nodes, so reaching any of them is enough. Without roots, the result joins the terminals to each other.

The Steiner tree. The shortest set of roads that joins all the terminals is a Steiner tree, which may use road junctions as branching points. Finding it is NP-hard, so the library offers two approximations, each never more than twice as long as the shortest possible tree, \(2(1 - 1/\ell)\) times it for \(\ell\) leaves, and in practice within a few percent:

  • method="shortest_path" (the default) is Takahashi and Matsuyama's: start from the roots, or from the first terminal, and repeatedly connect the terminal nearest to anything connected so far, along its shortest path. After each connection, a Dijkstra from the new path updates every node's distance to the connected set, and stops wherever a distance does not fall, so it only searches the area the new path wins. 1.1 s for 1,000 schools on Rwanda's roads.
  • method="steiner" is Mehlhorn's, 5 to 20 times faster and a few percent longer:
    1. One multi-source Dijkstra from all the points gives every node its nearest point, which splits the network into one region per point (a Voronoi partition by road distance).
    2. Every edge whose ends lie in two different regions is a candidate link between those two points, with a length of the distance from each end to its point plus the edge itself. The cheapest link is kept for each pair of points.
    3. A minimum spanning tree over those links picks the pairs to join. Each chosen link is expanded back into its road path.
    4. A second minimum spanning tree over the roads in those paths removes any cycles, and leaves that are not points are pruned.

With roots, one virtual root. Joining every root to one extra node, a virtual root, at length 0 turns "connect every school to some fibre node" into a Steiner tree over the schools and that virtual root, which both methods solve as they are. Removing the virtual root leaves a forest whose every tree reaches a fibre node, so a school may connect through another school, and a road shared by several schools counts once. That is why the plan to the fibre above is much shorter than each school's own path to its nearest fibre node.

method="nearest_root". Each point takes its shortest path to its nearest root, and the result is the union of those paths. Schools share a road only where their own shortest paths overlap. One multi-source Dijkstra from the roots gives every point its nearest root and the path to it.

method="all_pairs". The shortest path between every point and every other point or root, as Giga's earlier code computed it. It shows every route that might matter, but the number of paths grows with the square of the number of points, so keep it for small sets.

In every case, the paths are collected from Dijkstra's predecessor arrays all at once, and the result is contracted with simplify(keep=points and roots), so it keeps the points, the roots, and the branching nodes, with lengths added up and geometries joined. weight="cost" minimises another column, such as the cost of laying fibre (see Worked use cases). A point that cannot be connected stays in the result as a node without edges.

docs.title: Connection plans
docs.text:
ConnectionPlanner makes the same plans, and returns a ConnectionPlan: the contracted network, the chosen road edges as they are in the network, the cost, and a table with one row per school.

from gigaspatial import ConnectionPlanner

planner = ConnectionPlanner(network, school_ids, roots=fibre_ids)
plan = planner.plan()
print(plan)
print(plan.terminals.head())

ConnectionPlan(method='shortest_path', cost=249,675.9, terminals=197 of 197 connected, edges=1,970)
               status       root      distance  bridged  order  marginal_cost
node_id                                                                      
school-000  connected  fibre-002  11592.441273    False     42     952.009015
school-001  connected  fibre-002   5065.420040    False     78    1091.600048
school-002  connected  fibre-002   3177.332951    False     21    1728.637288
school-003  connected  fibre-000   9581.415906    False    103    1530.212553
school-004  connected  fibre-000   3400.977858    False     18    1404.324554

status is connected, root for a school that is itself a fibre node, or unreachable for one that no road joins to any root. root is the fibre node its part of the plan reaches nearest, and distance the length along the plan to it. order and marginal_cost come from shortest_path: when the school was connected, and the length its connection added. They make the plan a phased rollout (see Worked use cases).

Improving a plan, and how good it is. improve shortens a plan by local search and never makes it worse, and lower_bound computes a length that no plan can go below:

started = time.perf_counter()
better = planner.improve(plan)
bound = planner.lower_bound(better)
print(f"{plan.cost / 1000:.1f} km, improved to {better.cost / 1000:.1f} km in {time.perf_counter() - started:.1f} s")
print(f"No plan is shorter than {bound / 1000:.1f} km, so this one is at most {better.gap:.1%} above the best.")

249.7 km, improved to 244.1 km in 4.7 s
No plan is shorter than 241.0 km, so this one is at most 1.3% above the best.

improve repeats two moves until neither helps. Key-path exchange removes a stretch of the plan between two schools, fibre nodes, or branching junctions, and reconnects the two halves by the cheapest path between them. Key-vertex elimination removes a branching junction and its stretches, and reconnects the pieces by their cheapest links. Either is kept only when it saves length. lower_bound is Wong's dual ascent: on the network with both directions of every road, it grows the set of nodes that reach each school at no extra cost, raising the bound by the cheapest road into that set, always for the school whose set has the fewest roads into it, until every school's set reaches the fibre. time_limit= stops either early.

How close to the best. Against exact optima, from scipy's integer programming solver on Kigali's roads, and SteinLib's published optima for 78 standard random test graphs:

Kigali's roads, 30 and 60 schools, 3 fibre nodes (10 instances) SteinLib sets B to E (78 instances, mean) steiner 3.0 to 8.8% above the optimum 3.4 to 9.9% above shortest_path 0.65 to 5.9% above 2.6 to 4.7% above either, then improve 0.00 to 0.86% above 0.4 to 2.2% above lower_bound 0.07 to 1.1% below 0.05 to 0.42% below

On Rwanda's roads with 1,000 schools, improved plans have a gap of 1.4% to the bound. The design and algorithm decisions give the benchmarks.

Bridges. In a network with parts that no road joins, such as a clipped area or one loaded with retain_all=True, schools in a part without fibre are unreachable. bridge_cost= lets the plan use straight-line links between parts, such as microwave links, at a cost per metre and up to bridge_max_distance metres; a plan uses one only where it is cheaper than the roads:

# not run
planner = ConnectionPlanner(clipped, school_ids, roots=fibre_ids, bridge_cost=3.0, bridge_max_distance=2000)
plan = planner.plan()
links = plan.edges[plan.edges["kind"] == "bridge"]
print(plan.terminals["bridged"].sum(), "schools are connected through a bridge")

Use cases. Fibre backbone planning and extension from existing fibre (with roots), a phased rollout (order and marginal_cost), and estimating the trench length or cost of a plan, which is the plan's cost, or total_length() of its network.

docs.title: How a source is cut from an extract
docs.text:
OSMRoadsHandler stores each extract's whole network, uncropped, and cuts it to a source when it loads. To give the same network OSMRoadsFetcher would, it replays the steps of osmnx's graph_from_polygon:

  1. Widen the area. The source becomes an area by the fetcher's rules (a country's boundary, a geometry as given, a frame's union, or points' hull, bounding box, or buffers), and the area is widened by 500 m, as osmnx widens what it downloads. The raw network's nodes in the widened area are kept; with truncate_by_edge=True, so are the nodes just outside that share an edge with one inside.
  2. Combine extracts. When a source needs several extracts, such as schools along a border, their raw networks are combined as if they were one file: a road that crosses between extracts is in both, and is kept once.
  3. Keep the largest connected part, and simplify, unless retain_all=True keeps every part.
  4. Cut to the area. The nodes in the area itself are kept, and the largest connected part again. street_count is the count on the simplified widened network, as osmnx sets it.

Simplifying the widened network before cutting it decides what happens to a road that leaves the area: its simplified edge runs to the next real junction outside, so the edge's far end is outside the area and the edge is dropped. That is what osmnx does, and the handler does the same, so a cropped load equals the fetcher's network for the same area. A country whose extracts are its own file, or its regional files, is not cropped at all.

docs.title: Saving and loading
docs.text:
save writes a network to a folder of three files: nodes.parquet, edges.parquet as GeoParquet, and network.json with whether the network is directed, its CRS, weight, and metadata. SpatialNetwork.load reads it back.

import os

started = time.perf_counter()
network.save("rwanda-with-schools")
print(f"Saved in {time.perf_counter() - started:.2f} s")
for name in sorted(os.listdir("rwanda-with-schools")):
    print(f"  {name}: {os.path.getsize(os.path.join('rwanda-with-schools', name)) / 1e6:.1f} MB")

started = time.perf_counter()
loaded = SpatialNetwork.load("rwanda-with-schools")
print(loaded, f"{time.perf_counter() - started:.2f} s")

Saved in 0.94 s
  edges.parquet: 48.3 MB
  network.json: 0.0 MB
  nodes.parquet: 2.9 MB
SpatialNetwork(nodes=125,494, edges=333,426, directed=True, weight='length') 0.71 s

The files are plain Parquet, compressed with zstd, so other tools read them directly: geopandas reads edges.parquet as a GeoDataFrame, and DuckDB, QGIS, and pandas read both tables without the library.

import geopandas as gpd

edges_on_their_own = gpd.read_parquet("rwanda-with-schools/edges.parquet")
print(edges_on_their_own.shape, edges_on_their_own.crs.to_string())

(333426, 21) EPSG:4326

Loading less. columns= names the edge columns to load, on top of the ones every network needs (u, v, key, length, kind, and the weight). With an empty list, only the topology and lengths load, which is the fastest way to get a network for routing:

started = time.perf_counter()
topology = SpatialNetwork.load("rwanda-with-schools", columns=[])
print(list(topology.edges.columns), f"{time.perf_counter() - started:.3f} s")

['u', 'v', 'key', 'length', 'kind'] 0.230 s

Remote data stores. save(path, data_store=...) and load(path, data_store=...) work with any of the library's data stores, such as Azure Blob Storage, through the same calls.

Why this format. We compared GraphML, pickle, GeoPackage, Feather, and Parquet on Rwanda's roads. For the unsimplified network, GraphML took 1.4 GB and 437 s to read, pickle 532 MB and 25 s, and these Parquet files 73 MB and 0.18 s. Pickle cannot be read safely from a data store you do not control, and GeoPackage turns OpenStreetMap's list attributes into strings. The details are in design decision 4.

Attributes on save. Parquet cannot store a column that mixes lists and single values, as osmnx's attributes do after simplification. The library normalises them when it builds a network: osmid becomes a list of integers on every edge, other lists become ;-joined text, and text becomes categorical. Networks from your own tables are normalised when you save them; the network itself does not change.

docs.title: GeoDataFrames
docs.text:
nodes_gdf and edges_gdf are the tables as GeoDataFrames in EPSG:4326, built once and cached; edges without geometry get straight lines. to_geodataframes(crs=) returns both, projected if you ask:

nodes_utm, edges_utm = network.to_geodataframes(crs="EPSG:32735")
print(nodes_utm.crs.name, edges_utm.crs.name)
print(edges_utm.geometry.length.sum() / network.total_length())

WGS 84 / UTM zone 35S WGS 84 / UTM zone 35S
0.9985940358403483

The projected lengths differ from the network's great-circle lengths by a fraction of a percent near the projection's centre. The network's length is what every algorithm uses.

docs.title: networkx
docs.text:
to_networkx() returns a networkx MultiDiGraph (or MultiGraph when the network is undirected, or with directed=False), with every attribute. It is built on each call and not cached, so keep it in a variable. from_networkx goes the other way and takes any osmnx graph.

started = time.perf_counter()
graph = network.to_networkx()
print(type(graph).__name__, f"{graph.number_of_edges():,} edges", f"{time.perf_counter() - started:.2f} s")

MultiDiGraph 333,426 edges 1.83 s

When to use it. For algorithms scipy does not have, such as betweenness centrality or community detection, and for libraries built on networkx, including osmnx's own functions. On a large network, centrality in networkx can take hours; run it on a clipped or reduced network.

docs.title: pandana
docs.text: to_pandana() returns a pandana network indexed by node ID, built once per weight and cached, on which pandana's own functions, such as aggregations of points within a distance of every node, become available. It needs the pandana extra, and node IDs that are all integers or all text. backend="pandana" (see Algorithms) does not need either restriction on IDs: it gives pandana node positions instead.

docs.title: Worked use cases
docs.text: This page puts the methods together for two applications, fibre planning and accessibility, and ends with how to turn network results into features for a statistical model. It continues the example: network is Rwanda's roads with the 200 schools, 5 fibre nodes, and 10 clinics inserted.

docs.title: Fibre backbone planning
docs.text:
The question. Which roads would carry fibre from the existing fibre nodes to the schools, how long would the cable be, what would it cost, and in which order should the schools be connected?

1. Price the network. The costs per metre from Editing are applied now, after the points are inserted, so that every split piece and connection gets its own cost:

planned = with_fibre_cost(network)
print(planned.edges.groupby("kind", observed=True)[["length", "cost"]].sum().round(0))

                 length          cost
kind                                 
road        106043551.0  1.293426e+09
split          184149.0  2.374447e+06
connection      29550.0  7.387490e+05

2. Compare plans. Each school can take its own shortest route to the nearest fibre node, or its own cheapest route. Or the schools can share one plan, connecting through each other where that saves cable, made by ConnectionPlanner with the fibre nodes as roots, by length or by cost, and improved:

from gigaspatial import ConnectionPlanner

by_length = ConnectionPlanner(planned, school_ids, roots=fibre_ids)
by_cost = ConnectionPlanner(planned, school_ids, roots=fibre_ids, weight="cost")
shortest = by_length.improve(by_length.plan())
cheapest = by_cost.improve(by_cost.plan())
plans = {
    "each school's shortest route to the nearest fibre node": by_length.plan("nearest_root").network,
    "each school's cheapest route to a fibre node": by_cost.plan("nearest_root").network,
    "one shared plan, shortest": shortest.network,
    "one shared plan, cheapest": cheapest.network,
}
for label, plan in plans.items():
    cost = (plan.edges["rate"] * plan.edges["length"]).sum()
    print(f"{label}: {plan.total_length() / 1000:.1f} km, cost {cost / 1e6:.2f} million")
by_cost.lower_bound(cheapest)
print(f"The cheapest shared plan costs at most {cheapest.gap:.1%} more than the best possible one.")

each school's shortest route to the nearest fibre node: 355.2 km, cost 5.52 million
each school's cheapest route to a fibre node: 365.3 km, cost 4.46 million
one shared plan, shortest: 244.1 km, cost 3.64 million
one shared plan, cheapest: 257.7 km, cost 3.19 million
The cheapest shared plan costs at most 1.3% more than the best possible one.

The plan's cost is the rate times the length of each of its edges. The plans are contracted networks, whose edges join many road segments, and a joined edge's rate is the length-weighted mean of its parts, so this total is exact (see Editing).

Sharing cuts the length by almost a third (244 against 355 km), and the cost by more than a quarter (3.19 against 4.46 million for each school's own cheapest route), because schools near each other share one trench instead of each running its own to a fibre node. Pricing by cost avoids main roads where a residential street does the job, at some extra length. Whether a shared plan is acceptable depends on how much a failure of one shared segment would matter. Joining the schools and the fibre nodes in one tree, without roots, would also be shorter than separate routes, but it pays to connect fibre nodes that the backbone already connects.

Open the interactive version of this map to check which roads the plan takes.

3. A phased rollout. A plan by shortest_path, the default, connects the schools one at a time, cheapest connection first, to everything connected so far. Each school's order and marginal_cost turn the plan into phases:

rollout = by_cost.plan()
phases = rollout.terminals.dropna(subset=["order"]).sort_values("order")
phases["students"] = planned.nodes.loc[phases.index, "students"].to_numpy()
phases["phase"] = pd.qcut(phases["order"].astype(int), 4, labels=["first", "second", "third", "fourth"])
summary = phases.groupby("phase", observed=True).agg(
    schools=("order", "size"), students=("students", "sum"), cost=("marginal_cost", "sum")
)
summary["cost per pupil"] = summary["cost"] / summary["students"]
summary["cost"] = summary["cost"] / 1e6
print(summary.round(2))

        schools  students  cost  cost per pupil
phase                                          
first        50   34373.0  0.62           18.14
second       49   34771.0  0.63           18.08
third        49   28388.0  0.81           28.47
fourth       49   30391.0  1.18           38.87

The first phases reach the schools nearest the fibre and those that connect through them, at about 18 per pupil; the last reaches the remote schools, at about 39. A school's marginal cost depends on what was connected before it: it is what this order adds, not what the school would cost alone.

4. Last-mile distances. The road distance from each school to its nearest fibre node decides which schools are worth connecting first. Weighting by students turns it into a statement about pupils:

last_mile = planned.nearest_by_network(school_ids, fibre_ids)
last_mile["students"] = planned.nodes.loc[last_mile["origin"], "students"].to_numpy()
bands = pd.cut(last_mile["distance"], [0, 2000, 5000, 10000, np.inf], labels=["under 2 km", "2-5 km", "5-10 km", "over 10 km"])
print(last_mile.groupby(bands, observed=False).agg(schools=("origin", "size"), students=("students", "sum")))

            schools  students
distance                     
under 2 km       10    7001.0
2-5 km           65   40515.0
5-10 km          92   62469.0
over 10 km       30   17938.0

What to check before trusting a plan. Schools that were skipped because they lie far from any road (see Inserting points) are missing from every plan, and schools with status unreachable are in no part of the network with fibre; bridge_cost= lets the plan cross such gaps by straight-line links. Roads missing from OpenStreetMap make routes longer than they are; connect_components and a look at the schools with the longest detours find most of them. A plan's gap says how far above the best possible plan it can be at most. And a plan along roads assumes the cable follows roads, which is the usual case but not the only one.

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text:
The question. Which schools have a clinic within reach by road, and which are left out?

nearest = planned.nearest_by_network(school_ids, clinic_ids)
within_5km = planned.count_within(school_ids, clinic_ids, 5000)
access = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "nearest_clinic_m": nearest.set_index("origin")["distance"],
        "clinics_within_5km": within_5km,
        "students": planned.nodes.loc[school_ids, "students"],
    }
)
print(access.describe().round(0))
share = (access["clinics_within_5km"] > 0).mean()
pupils = int(access.loc[access["clinics_within_5km"] == 0, "students"].sum())
print(f"Schools with a clinic within 5 km by road: {share:.0%}; pupils without one: {pupils:,}")

Road distance against straight-line distance. The same question asked with straight lines gives a rosier answer, because no road is shorter than the straight line:

straight_5km = features.set_index("origin")["straight"] <= 5000
road_5km = access["nearest_clinic_m"] <= 5000
print(pd.crosstab(straight_5km.rename("within 5 km straight"), road_5km.rename("within 5 km by road")))

within 5 km straight

The schools that are within 5 km in a straight line but not by road are the ones a straight-line indicator would misclassify. They are worth listing by name in any report on access.

Service areas. For a map of what each clinic serves, reachable(clinic_ids, 5000) lists every node within 5 km of each clinic, and the service area figure on the Algorithms page draws one. In a directed network the distances run from the clinic outwards; for walking, pass directed=False.

docs.title: Network distance as a model feature
docs.text:
Road distances, detours, and counts within reach are covariates like any other once they are in a table keyed by school. Here they are joined to the schools, ready for a model of, say, attendance or connectivity:

model_table = (
    schools.set_index("school_id")
    .join(access[["nearest_clinic_m", "clinics_within_5km"]])
    .join(features.set_index("origin")[["detour"]])
    .join(last_mile.set_index("origin")["distance"].rename("fibre_m"))
    .dropna()
)
print(model_table.head(3).round(2))
print(model_table[["nearest_clinic_m", "detour", "fibre_m", "students"]].corr().round(2))

nearest_clinic_m              1.00   -0.09     0.57     -0.08

A few things are worth knowing when you use them:

  • Road distances are long-tailed: a few schools are much farther than the rest. A logarithm, or distance bands as above, usually fits better than the raw metres.
  • The detour index is a ratio and is unstable for very short straight-line distances; for a school next to its clinic, a 300 m road around a block gives a large ratio for a small detour. Consider leaving out pairs under a few hundred metres.
  • Counts within a distance depend on the threshold. Report the threshold, and check that results do not hinge on it.
  • Directed and undirected distances answer different questions. A car obeys one-way streets; a pupil on foot does not.
  • The made-up points here are uniform at random; real schools cluster along roads, so real detours are smaller.

docs.title: Design: connection planning
docs.text:
This is the agreed design for ConnectionPlanner, which plans how to connect a set of points (schools, clinics, villages) to an existing network (fibre, a power grid, water mains) along a spatial network at the smallest shared cost. It records the decisions from the design round of 30 October 2026 and splits the work into sub-tasks. Each sub-task starts by reading this document, the glossary, ADR 0004, ADR 0008, and the spatial network design.

This page is not in the docs site navigation. The user-facing description will be in the spatial networks concept note, and the evidence in design and algorithm decisions.

docs.title: 1. The problem
docs.text:
Given a spatial network with a non-negative weight on every edge, a set of terminals that must be connected, and a set of roots that are already connected to each other through an existing network, find the set of edges of smallest total weight such that every terminal can reach some root. A terminal may reach a root directly or through other terminals, and an edge used by several terminals counts once.

Joining every root to one virtual root at weight 0 makes this the Steiner tree problem in graphs over the terminals and the root (ADR 0008). Removing the root from the tree leaves a forest whose every tree contains at least one root.

  • Directions are ignored. A cable or a duct does not follow one-way streets.
  • The cost is per edge used, paid once. That is trench length, or a cost per metre of trench through weight=. A cost per cable, which grows with the number of terminals behind an edge, is out of scope: it makes the problem fixed-charge network design.
  • The roots are one backbone. Reaching any root is enough. Separate networks, each terminal assigned to one of them, are deferred.
  • No roots gives an unrooted Steiner tree joining the terminals, as connecting_subnetwork(terminals) does today.

Complexity: NP-hard, and NP-hard to approximate within 96/95. The best known approximation is ln 4 + ε ≈ 1.39 (Byrka et al., 2010), through large linear programs. Mehlhorn's algorithm gives at most 2(1 − 1/ℓ) times the optimum for ℓ leaves in O(m + n log n), and is within a few percent in practice. SCIP-Jack solves instances of a few hundred thousand edges exactly, typically in minutes.

On the concept note's example (197 schools and 5 fibre nodes in Kigali, on Rwanda's roads):

Method Length Illustrative cost Each school to its nearest fibre node (today's sources=) 355 km 5.52 million One unrooted tree over schools and fibre nodes 265 km 3.92 million Rooted tree, fibre nodes as one root, by length 258 km 3.83 million Rooted tree, by cost 269 km 3.33 million

The rooted tree was computed with today's code by joining the fibre nodes with zero-length edges; it took 0.19 s.

docs.title: 2. Names and modules
docs.text:
Item Decision Classes ConnectionPlanner and ConnectionPlan in gigaspatial/processing/network/planning.py Public names from gigaspatial import ConnectionPlanner; gigaspatial.processing.ConnectionPlanner, ConnectionPlan (ADR 0003) Terms terminals, roots, bridges, connection plan. Glossary entries for Connection planner, Connection plan, and Root beside Connecting subnetwork Steiner routines _steiner_edges, _nearest_source_edges (renamed _nearest_root_edges), _all_pairs_edges, _forest_edges, _spanning_tree, and _prune_leaves move from reduction.py to planning.py; reduction.py keeps simplify Dependencies none new: numpy, scipy, pandas, shapely

The docs use fibre as the main example, but the names and docstrings stay generic, so the planner reads as naturally for a power grid or water mains.

docs.title: 3. API
docs.text:
planner = ConnectionPlanner(
    network,                    # a SpatialNetwork, with terminals and roots already inserted
    terminals,                  # node IDs to connect
    roots=(),                   # node IDs already connected to each other
    weight=None,                # edge column to minimise; the network's weight otherwise
    bridge_cost=None,           # weight per metre of a straight-line link; no bridges when None
    bridge_max_distance=5000,   # metres
)
plan = planner.plan(method="shortest_path")  # or "steiner", "nearest_root", "all_pairs"
plan = planner.improve(plan, time_limit=None)
bound = planner.lower_bound(time_limit=60)   # also sets plan.bound and plan.gap when given a plan

SpatialNetwork.connecting_subnetwork(terminals, roots=None, method="steiner", weight=None) builds a planner and returns planner.plan(method).network. Its sources= parameter becomes roots=, and method="nearest_source" becomes "nearest_root"; neither is released yet.

method Meaning "steiner" Mehlhorn's 2-approximation. With roots, the rooted tree (section 4); without, the unrooted tree joining the terminals "shortest_path" (default since sub-task 6, section 11) Takahashi and Matsuyama's heuristic: connect terminals one at a time, cheapest first, to everything connected so far. Gives the rollout order (section 5) "nearest_root" Each terminal's shortest path to its nearest root; the union of those paths. Today's behaviour of sources= "all_pairs" The shortest path between every terminal and every terminal or root, as the old Giga code did; grows with the square of the terminals

Inputs are node IDs of the network. Inserting points is the user's step (insert_points, then plan), so insertion's options and its skipped points stay visible. A root that is also a terminal is connected from the start. Unknown IDs raise KeyError. Weights must be present on every edge and not negative; zero is allowed.

docs.title: ConnectionPlan
docs.text:
Field Meaning network The connecting subnetwork, contracted with simplify(keep=terminals and roots), as connecting_subnetwork returns today. Undirected edges The chosen edges of the original network, uncontracted, one row per undirected edge with its attributes and geometry; bridges included with kind="bridge" terminals One row per terminal: status (connected, root, or unreachable), root (a root its tree reaches), distance (weight along the plan to the nearest root in its tree), bridged (whether its path uses a bridge), and for shortest_path order and marginal_cost cost The total weight of edges bound, gap Filled by lower_bound: the bound, and cost / bound - 1, so the plan costs at most 1 + gap times the optimum metadata Method, weight, bridge_cost, counts, and the time each step took

Order and marginal cost come only from shortest_path. A Steiner tree's shared trenches have no natural per-terminal marginal cost, and a made-up one would mislead.

docs.title: 4. The rooted Steiner tree
docs.text:
The adjacency matrix of the undirected network (_graph(weight, directed=False)) gets one extra node, the virtual root, joined to every root node. scipy's minimum spanning tree drops zero entries, so these joins get the smallest positive float, as zero weights already do. Mehlhorn's routine then runs unchanged with terminals ∪ {root}:

  1. One multi-source Dijkstra from terminals and root gives every node its nearest terminal. Because the virtual root is joined to every root node at (almost) zero, its Voronoi region is everything nearer to some root node than to any terminal.
  2. Edges between regions give candidate links; an MST over the cheapest link per pair of regions picks the pairs.
  3. The links are expanded into paths, a second MST removes cycles, and leaves that are neither terminals nor the root are pruned.
  4. The root and its joins are removed. What is left is the plan's edges.

The cost is the same as today's Steiner tree: one Dijkstra and two MSTs over a matrix with one more row.

docs.title: 5. The rollout order (method="shortest_path")
docs.text:
Takahashi and Matsuyama's heuristic, a 2-approximation, is the planner's model of a phased rollout. Start with the roots as the connected set. Repeatedly connect the unconnected terminal nearest (by weight) to anything connected so far, along its shortest path, and add that path to the connected set. A terminal's order is when it was connected, and its marginal_cost the weight of its path, which uses only new edges. Ties go to the terminal listed first, so plans are reproducible. Terminals that the connected set cannot reach are unreachable.

Implemented incrementally:

  • One multi-source Dijkstra from the connected set gives every node its distance to it.
  • After each addition, distances can only fall, and only near the new path. A Dijkstra from the new path's nodes, limited to the largest distance of any unconnected terminal (limit= in scipy), updates them. Nodes beyond the limit cannot become any terminal's best connection.
  • Terminals are kept in a heap by distance.

Sub-task 3 benchmarks this against the naive version (one full Dijkstra per terminal), and against a version that recomputes only when the nearest terminal's distance changed. A compiled Dijkstra would need a new build dependency and is not planned.

As built (benchmarks/connection_planning/rollout.py, results in benchmarks/connection_planning/results.md):

  • Ties go to the terminal listed first in terminals, not the lower ID: IDs may mix integers and text, which do not sort, and the order given is as reproducible. Without roots, the rollout starts from the first listed terminal it can connect, with order 1 and marginal_cost 0. A terminal that is a root has order 0; an unreachable one has none.
  • The update is a pruned Dijkstra in Python, not scipy's limited one. The limit above is the largest distance of any waiting terminal, which a few remote terminals keep at tens of kilometres, so each update searched about 40,000 nodes. Only nodes nearer to the new path than to anything connected before need updating, and a Dijkstra that stops wherever a distance does not fall searches only those: 6 million node updates in a whole 10,000-terminal rollout on Rwanda, against 455 million nodes searched. scipy's Dijkstra cannot stop that way, but even in Python the pruned update is much faster:
Terminals, 20 roots, Rwanda Naive scipy, limited Python, pruned 100 1.6 s 0.6 s 0.4 s 1,000 19.5 s 5.4 s 1.1 s 10,000 not run 58 s 4.4 s
  • The version that recomputes only when the nearest terminal's distance changed is not valid. Stale distances are upper bounds, since distances only fall, so the top of a heap of stale distances need not be the nearest terminal. It would need lower bounds, which the problem does not provide.
  • On Rwanda the rollout was shorter than Mehlhorn's rooted tree: 1,163 against 1,194 km for 100 terminals, 3,845 against 3,942 km for 1,000, and 10,760 against 10,954 km for 10,000, 1.8 to 2.6% shorter. Both are 2-approximations, and Takahashi and Matsuyama's is known to be the better of the two in practice. steiner stays the default for now, since it takes 0.2 s against 1.1 s; sub-tasks 4 and 6 measure both against the optimum before deciding.

docs.title: 6. Bridges
docs.text:
With bridge_cost=c, the planner may use straight-line links between the network's connected components, for terminals that no road connects to a root: microwave, wireless, or a planned road.

  • Candidates are found with a KD-tree on all nodes, on the unit sphere as connect_components does: for each component, its nearest node pairs to up to 5 other components within bridge_max_distance.
  • Each candidate gets the weight c times its great-circle length in metres, in the units of weight, and is added to the planner's internal network with kind="bridge" and a straight-line geometry.
  • Only links between components are offered. Within a component, the roads already connect.
  • The Steiner tree uses a bridge only when it is cheaper than the alternatives. A terminal unreachable even with bridges is unreachable.

As built:

  • A component with more than 2,000 nodes, or most of the network, gets its own KD-tree, queried once with every node outside it, as connect_components does. That gives its closest pair to every other component exactly. Smaller components query the KD-tree of all nodes with their nodes' 16 nearest neighbours, doubled while none lies outside the component and the farthest is within bridge_max_distance. The closest pair per pair of components is kept, and each component keeps its 5 nearest. On Rwanda's roads cut in two along a meridian (23 components, two of 70,000 and 55,000 nodes), finding the candidates takes 0.1 s.
  • Bridges join the planner's graph as extra entries, not as a new SpatialNetwork, so offering them costs no copy of the tables. A bridge's length stays its great-circle length; its weight is bridge_cost times that, stored in the weight column unless the weight is length. cost and distance always count bridges at their weight.
  • Bridge ends are kept as nodes when the plan is contracted, so a bridge stays one edge of kind bridge in plan.network.
  • bridged is whether a terminal's path to its root along the plan crosses a bridge. Without roots, it is whether the terminal lies outside the road component that holds the most planned terminals.

A network loaded through OSMRoadsHandler keeps only its largest connected part by default, so bridges matter for networks loaded with retain_all=True, combined with concat, or clipped.

docs.title: 7. Local search (improve)
docs.text:
improve(plan) applies two of Uchoa and Werneck's moves until neither improves the plan or time_limit passes. Neither ever makes a plan worse.

A key vertex is a node of the tree that is a terminal, a root, or a Steiner node of degree 3 or more; a key path is a path of the tree between two key vertices whose inner nodes are Steiner nodes of degree 2.

  • Key-path exchange. Remove one key path; the tree falls into two parts. Find the cheapest path joining the two parts, with a Dijkstra from one part limited to the removed path's weight. If it is cheaper, replace the key path with it.
  • Key-vertex elimination. Remove one Steiner key vertex and its key paths; the tree falls into three or more parts. A multi-source Dijkstra labelled by part, as in Mehlhorn's algorithm, gives the cheapest links between parts, and an MST over them reconnects all parts. If the reconnection is cheaper than what was removed, keep it.

Moves are tried cheapest-to-evaluate first (key paths in decreasing weight), and each Dijkstra is limited by the weight it must beat, so most searches stop early. Vertex insertion and elimination are deferred, until real data shows a large remaining gap. Sub-task 6 found none on roads: improved plans were within 0.86% of the optimum on Kigali.

As built (benchmarks/connection_planning/improve.py):

  • The plan is rebuilt as one tree first. With roots, the virtual root is joined to every root the plan touches, and a spanning tree with pruned dangling branches is taken. This alone never costs more, and turns a nearest_root or all_pairs plan, which may hold cycles, into a tree.
  • Key paths are listed once per pass. An earlier move can leave a listed path's end only continuing it; such a path is extended to the next key vertex before it is tried, and paths whose edges are gone are skipped.
  • Key-vertex elimination searches only near the removed nodes: its links start from the parts' nodes within the removed weight of them. Searching from every node left in the plan took 20 ms per vertex on Rwanda; the local search found plans within 0.01% of it on Kigali, in half the time.
  • A move must save a billionth of the weight it replaces, so rounding cannot make it loop.
  • On Rwanda with 1,000 terminals and 20 roots, a pass takes 5.8 s from steiner, and the plan improves 4.7%, from 3,942 to 3,755 km. From shortest_path it improves 2.2%, and from nearest_root 31.8%. All three end within 0.1% of each other, so with improve() the choice of first method matters little.

docs.title: 8. Lower bound (lower_bound)
docs.text:
Wong's dual ascent (1984) gives a lower bound on the optimum, and with it the gap of any plan.
