  • The undirected network becomes a directed one with both directions of every edge, rooted at the virtual root (or at one terminal when there are no roots). Each arc starts with its weight as its reduced cost.
  • Repeatedly, pick a terminal that cannot yet be reached from the root along arcs of reduced cost 0, and the set of nodes that reach it along such arcs. Raise the bound by the smallest reduced cost of the arcs entering that set, and lower those arcs' reduced costs by it.
  • Stop when every terminal is reachable along arcs of reduced cost 0.

The sum of the raises is a lower bound on the optimal tree's weight. Each round costs a search over arcs of reduced cost 0, and the number of rounds can be large, so time_limit stops early and returns the bound reached so far, which is still valid, only looser. Terminals unreachable from the root are left out of the bound and reported.

As built (benchmarks/connection_planning/bound.py):

  • Wong's rule chooses the terminal. Every step, the active terminal whose region (the nodes that reach it at reduced cost 0) has the fewest entering arcs raises the bound by their smallest reduced cost. A first version gave each terminal one whole turn, until its region held the root, nearest the root first; it was valid but much weaker. Against SteinLib's proven optima its bound was on average 9.7% below the optimum on set C, at worst 45%, against 0.42%, at worst 3.1%, for Wong's rule; on Rwanda with 1,000 terminals it left a gap of 10.9% to the improved plan, against 1.4%.
  • Regions are kept between steps. Reduced costs only fall, so a region only grows. Each terminal keeps its region and its entering arcs, and a step checks only those arcs for any that reached 0, growing the region from their tails. Recomputing each region every step gave the same bounds and took 41 s for 100 terminals on Rwanda, against 1.5 s.
  • A complete bound is kept by the planner, so the gap of every later plan costs nothing. A bound stopped by time_limit is still valid, only looser, and is recomputed on the next call.
  • On Rwanda with 20 roots the bound takes 1.7 s for 100 terminals, 5.0 s for 1,000, and 40.5 s for 10,000. Improved plans have gaps of 2.1%, 1.4%, and 0.6%.

docs.title: 9. Edge cases
docs.text:
• No roots: the unrooted tree over the terminals.
  • One terminal and no roots: an empty plan.
  • A terminal that is a root: status="root", distance 0.
  • A terminal unreachable, even through bridges: status="unreachable", left out of the plan and the bound.
  • Weights: zero allowed, negative or missing refused with ValueError, as the algorithms do today.
  • bridge_cost set without any component to bridge: no bridges, no warning.

docs.title: 10. Performance targets
docs.text:
On Rwanda's simplified network (125,058 nodes, 332,535 edges), with 1,000 terminals and 20 roots, on the benchmark laptop:

Step Target plan(method="steiner") under 1 s (today's Steiner tree: 0.18 s) plan(method="shortest_path") under 10 s; 10,000 terminals under 60 s improve(), one pass of both moves under 10 s lower_bound() under 60 s, with time_limit returning the best bound so far

docs.title: 11. Validation
docs.text:
• Tests. The rooted tree against networkx's steiner_tree on the virtual-root graph; every method on small graphs against brute-force optima; improve never worse, and better on constructed cases; the bound never above the brute-force optimum; and every edge case above.
  • Benchmarks. benchmarks/connection_planning/ writes instances in SteinLib's STP format and solves them exactly with SCIP-Jack, which is installed only there, never as a dependency. Instances: Kigali, and Rwanda with 100 and 1,000 terminals, by length and by cost. Reported for each method: its gap to the optimum, with and without improve; and the bound's gap. If SCIP-Jack cannot be built, networkx's steiner_tree gives another upper bound, and the planner's own bound the lower one.

As built, without SCIP-Jack, whose source code must now be requested from its developers:

  • SteinLib's sets B, C, D, and E (78 random sparse graphs of 50 to 2,500 nodes, every optimum proven; steinlib.py). Improved plans were on average 0.4 to 2.2% above the optimum, at worst 9%; the bound was on average 0.05 to 0.42% below it, at worst 4.4%. The first version of the dual ascent was 7 to 10% below on average, at worst 45%, which led to Wong's rule in sub-task 5.
  • Exact optima on Kigali's roads with scipy's milp (HiGHS) and the multi-commodity flow model, whose relaxation equals the directed cut relaxation (exact.py; 30 and 60 terminals, 3 roots, 5 draws each, 4 to 110 s each). Improved plans were 0.00 to 0.86% above the optimum, shortest_path 0.65 to 5.9%, steiner 3.0 to 8.8%, and the bound 0.07 to 1.1% below. The single-commodity flow model did not solve such an instance in 600 s.
  • Rwanda is too large for HiGHS; there the bound alone gives the gap: 2.1%, 1.4%, and 0.6% for improved plans of 100, 1,000, and 10,000 terminals.
  • The default method became shortest_path. Without improve() it was about twice as close to the optimum as steiner, on Kigali and on SteinLib, and it still takes seconds at country scale (4.4 s for 10,000 terminals on Rwanda, against 0.2 s). After improve(), both end within about 0.1% of each other.
  • exact.py also writes its instances in SteinLib's STP format, with the virtual root as the last node, so an exact solver can take them as they are; exact.py --rwanda 100 1000 10000 writes Rwanda's instances of bound.py without solving them.

docs.title: 12. Sub-tasks
docs.text:
Each sub-task is its own pull request on feat/connection-planner, stacked on #21.

# Sub-task Delivers 1 Planner and rooted Steiner tree ConnectionPlanner, ConnectionPlan; the virtual root in Mehlhorn's algorithm; connecting_subnetwork rewired with its four methods; the terminals table; public imports; tests against networkx on the virtual-root graph and against today's results; glossary entries 2 Bridges bridge_cost, bridge_max_distance; candidate links between components; kind="bridge"; unreachable terminals; tests 3 Rollout order method="shortest_path", incremental; order and marginal_cost; tests against the naive version; performance targets 4 Local search improve() with key-path exchange and key-vertex elimination; tests; performance target 5 Lower bound lower_bound(time_limit=) by dual ascent; bound and gap; tests against brute force; performance target 6 Validation and docs Benchmarks against exact optima (SteinLib, and HiGHS on Kigali; SCIP-Jack deferred, section 13); the default method; new decisions in the design and algorithm decisions document; the concept note's reduction and use-cases pages; changelog

docs.title: 13. Deferred
docs.text:
• Prize-collecting plans (prizes=, a value per terminal such as its pupils): connect only the terminals worth their cost, or the most value within a budget. Goemans and Williamson's 2-approximation, with Hegde, Indyk, and Schmidt's nearly linear version (pcst_fast), fits the planner's virtual root.
  • Capacities (demands= per terminal, capacities= per root): the capacitated Steiner tree, with the capacitated shortest-path heuristic (PLOS One, 2022); and Ito, Zhou, and Nishizeki's partitioning of a tree among capacitated roots as a second stage.
  • Separate root networks, each terminal assigned to one.
  • Cost per cable: fixed-charge network design or buy-at-bulk.
  • Vertex insertion and elimination in improve. On SteinLib's dense random graphs the improved plans were up to 9% above the optimum, so these moves would help there; on roads, within 0.86%.
  • SCIP-Jack as an exact column in the benchmarks, once its source code arrives from its developers: exact optima for the Rwanda-scale instances that HiGHS cannot solve, from the STP files exact.py writes.

docs.title: 14. Why "roots"
docs.text: The existing network's nodes are called roots, not sources. "Source" is already a glossary term: the place a dataset is requested for (a country, a geometry, points, a frame), which every handler and fetcher uses. Using it for fibre nodes would give one word two meanings in the same library. "Root" is the Steiner literature's term and matches the virtual root the roots join. connecting_subnetwork's sources= and method="nearest_source" become roots= and "nearest_root" in sub-task 1, before their first release. "Anchors" and "connected nodes" were considered and rejected as less precise.

docs.title: 15. References
docs.text:
• Mehlhorn, K. (1988). A faster approximation algorithm for the Steiner problem in graphs. Information Processing Letters 27(3).
  • Takahashi, H., and Matsuyama, A. (1980). An approximate solution for the Steiner problem in graphs. Math. Japonica 24.
  • Wong, R. T. (1984). A dual ascent approach for Steiner tree problems on a directed graph. Mathematical Programming 28.
  • Uchoa, E., and Werneck, R. F. (2012). Fast local search for the Steiner problem in graphs. ACM Journal of Experimental Algorithmics 17.
  • Byrka, J., Grandoni, F., Rothvoß, T., and Sanità, L. (2013). Steiner tree approximation via iterative randomized rounding. Journal of the ACM 60(1).
  • Gamrath, G., Koch, T., Maher, S., Rehfeldt, D., and Shinano, Y. (2017). SCIP-Jack: a solver for STP and variants with parallelization extensions. Mathematical Programming Computation 9.
  • Hegde, C., Indyk, P., and Schmidt, L. (2015). A nearly-linear time framework for graph-structured sparsity. ICML.
  • Ito, T., Zhou, X., and Nishizeki, T. (2005). Partitioning trees of supply and demand. International Journal of Foundations of Computer Science 16(4).
  • A construction heuristic for the capacitated Steiner tree problem (2022). PLOS One.

docs.title: Design: the OSM roads handler
docs.text:
This is the agreed design for OSMRoadsHandler, which builds country-scale road networks from Geofabrik's OpenStreetMap extracts. It returns the same SpatialNetwork as OSMRoadsFetcher, which queries Overpass and suits cities, districts, and areas around schools. It records the decisions from the design round of 28–29 October 2026 and splits the work into sub-tasks. Each sub-task starts by reading this document, GLOSSARY.md, the ADRs listed below, docs/design/spatial-network.md, and .agents/reference/handler-contract.md.

Read first:

  • GLOSSARY.md and CONTEXT.md (local files, gitignored): extract, road network, handler, source, data store.
  • ADR 0001: search key and search geometry; small leftovers for datasets published per country.
  • ADR 0003: public import paths and lazy loading.
  • ADR 0005: how a saved network is laid out.
  • ADR 0006: extracts stored by date, uncropped networks beside them, cropping at load.
  • ADR 0007: extracts chosen by polygon, with a curated list of multi-country extracts.

This page is not in the docs site navigation. Why each part was built the way it was, with the benchmarks behind it, is in design and algorithm decisions.

docs.title: 1. Why a handler
docs.text:
• Overpass is a shared service. A country-scale fetch takes many queries (osmnx splits areas above 2,500 km²), can take hours, runs into fair-use limits (roughly 10,000 queries and 1 GB a day), and needs osmnx's networkx graph in memory: about 2.3 GB for unsimplified Rwanda. Every public Overpass server was unreachable on 26–27 October 2026.
  • An extract is a file kept in a data store and reused, which the glossary calls a handler. Users need both small areas (the fetcher) and whole countries or provinces (this handler).
  • The handler reads extracts with pyosmium and builds the node and edge tables directly, without osmnx or networkx. On Rwanda, the handler builds the simplified drive_service network in 15 s; the route through OSM XML and osmnx took 300 s.

docs.title: 2. Names, modules, and dependencies
docs.text:
Item Decision Classes OSMRoadsConfig, OSMRoadsDownloader, OSMRoadsReader, OSMRoadsHandler in gigaspatial/handlers/osm/roads.py Package gigaspatial/handlers/osm/, grouped by provider as nasa/ and wri/ are: roads.py (the handler), geofabrik.py (the index, choosing extracts, dated files), pbf.py (building a network from a .pbf, and its header timestamp). geofabrik.py and pbf.py know nothing about the handler base, so other datasets in the same extracts can reuse them Public names from gigaspatial import OSMRoadsHandler; config, downloader, and reader from gigaspatial.handlers (ADR 0003) Dependency osmium (pyosmium) added to giga-spatial[roads], imported lazily with the usual ImportError naming the extra. Wheels exist for Python 3.10 to 3.14 on macOS, Linux, and Windows Data type a new DATA_TYPES key osm, so config.get_path("osm", "bronze") works Suffix .pbf added to DATA_FILE_SUFFIXES in gigaspatial/handlers/base/source.py; today "x.osm.pbf" is classified as a country

The handler follows the handler contract: the config's only required hook is get_relevant_data_units_by_key; the downloader implements download_data_unit; the reader implements load_from_paths; options are frozen dataclasses with no **kwargs.

docs.title: 3. Geofabrik facts (October 2026)
docs.text:
• https://download.geofabrik.de/index-v1.json (3.8 MB) lists 554 extracts, each with id, parent, name, urls.pbf, and a MultiPolygon. 191 carry iso3166-1:alpha2 codes; 71 carry iso3166-2. A lighter index-v1-nogeom.json exists.
  • Every country split into sub-regions also has a country file (China 33 regions, France 27, Spain 18, Germany 16, India 6, Brazil 5, and others). The US is a country file us plus 53 state extracts under north-america.
  • Multi-country extracts: gcc-states, haiti-and-domrep, israel-and-palestine, and senegal-and-gambia carry several codes; malaysia-singapore-brunei and ireland-and-northern-ireland carry one; south-africa-and-lesotho, dach, alps, britain-and-ireland, and sea carry none.
  • Code errors and gaps: polynesie-francaise, wallis-et-futuna, tokelau, american-oceania, and ile-de-clipperton are coded VU; pitcairn-islands is coded MH. Saudi Arabia, Singapore, Brunei, and about 33 other countries exist only inside larger extracts.
  • Sizes: Rwanda 65 MiB, Ethiopia 134 MiB, Kenya 335 MiB, South Africa 404 MiB, Mexico 618 MiB, Nigeria 680 MiB, India 1.6 GiB, Indonesia 1.7 GiB, Brazil 2.0 GiB, Germany 4.6 GiB, Africa 7.4 GiB.
  • -latest.osm.pbf redirects (307) to a dated file such as rwanda-261027.osm.pbf; some large files redirect to a mirror. .md5 files exist for both names. Daily dated files are kept about a week, then monthly and yearly snapshots. Files update daily around 21:00 CET. The PBF header carries the replication timestamp, so a stored file's age can be read offline.

docs.title: 4. Choosing extracts (ADR 0007)
docs.text:
• The index is downloaded once and stored at osm/geofabrik/index-v1.json, with its download time in index-v1.json.downloaded, refreshed with the same refresh and max_age_days options as extracts.
  • The search key is {"country": "RW"} for a country source and {"area": polygon} otherwise; the area is built by the fetcher's query_area, so buffer and area mean the same in both.
  • For a source's area, choose the smallest extracts that together cover it: take touching extracts from the smallest up while part of the area is uncovered, then drop any extract the others cover. A source that needs more than one extract, such as an area crossing a border, loads each and combines them with concat.
  • A country's ISO code is a fast path: when exactly one extract carries that one code and the extract is not on the multi-country list, it is the country's own file. A country without one (Palestine, Singapore, Malaysia) is covered by its AdminBoundaries polygon, and its units are cropped.
  • The curated lists live in the module and are tested against a stored copy of the index: MULTI_COUNTRY_EXTRACTS, and CODE_FIXES for territories the index mis-codes (French Polynesia, Wallis and Futuna, Tokelau and Pitcairn carry Vanuatu's or the Marshall Islands' code).
  • Continent extracts, root extracts without an ISO code, are used only when named with extracts=; an area only a continent covers raises an error saying so.
  • regions=False (default): a country source uses the country file. regions=True: it uses all of the country's sub-region files, each built and saved on its own and combined at load; these are the children of its extract, or the extracts coded with its ISO 3166-2 subdivisions (the US states). A country without regions uses its own file. extracts=[...] names Geofabrik extract IDs directly and overrides the choice.
  • Units are {"id", "url", "path", "matches_country"}, where path is the extract's place in Geofabrik's folders (africa/rwanda) and matches_country marks a country source's own file or one of its regions, which needs no crop.

docs.title: 5. Storage (ADR 0006)
docs.text:
osm/geofabrik/index-v1.json
osm/geofabrik/2026-10-27/africa/rwanda.osm.pbf
osm/geofabrik/2026-10-27/africa/rwanda.networks/drive_service-simplified/
osm/geofabrik/2026-10-27/south-america/brazil.osm.pbf
osm/geofabrik/2026-10-27/south-america/brazil/nordeste.osm.pbf
osm/geofabrik/2026-10-27/south-america/brazil/nordeste.networks/drive_service-simplified/
  • The date folder is the extract's own date as an ISO date; below it, the path mirrors Geofabrik's URL path. The date is the one in Geofabrik's dated file name (rwanda-261027.osm.pbf), which is the UTC date of the replication timestamp in the file's header and in the extract's -updates/state.txt.
  • The data unit is {id, date, url, path, matches_country}, with url the dated file; its stored path is the .pbf. The base's availability check covers the .pbf only.
  • Network folders are a cache the reader derives from the .pbf path, one per variant: the network type or a short hash of the tag filter, and simplified or raw. A missing network is built from the extract and saved; it never triggers a download.
  • A stored network always covers its whole extract, with every connected part. It is never cropped.
  • Loading uses the newest stored date holding the extract, unless date= pins one. Old dates are never deleted automatically.

docs.title: 6. Downloads
docs.text:
• The unit's date is chosen at resolution, so the downloader and the availability check need no options: date= when given; otherwise the newest stored date, found offline by listing the date folders; otherwise, or with refresh, or when the newest is more than max_age_days old, Geofabrik's latest.
  • Geofabrik's latest date comes from a HEAD of -latest without following the redirect: the Location names the dated file. Large extracts (Germany) redirect to a mirror under the -latest name; their date is read from -updates/state.txt. When max_age_days asks and Geofabrik cannot be reached, the stored extract is used with a warning; refresh raises.
  • The download is always the dated file from Geofabrik, which also serves the files it mirrors. It is streamed into the data store with fetch.stream_to_store, which checks the dated file's .md5 while streaming and removes the file on a mismatch, so a remote store is never read back. A dated file Geofabrik no longer keeps (404) raises FileNotFoundError saying how long files are kept.
  • date= takes YYYY-MM-DD or a datetime.date, and cannot be combined with refresh or max_age_days.
  • replication_timestamp(path, data_store) reads the header from the file's first 64 KiB through pyosmium's FileBuffer, so it works offline and on remote stores.
  • The network's metadata records the extract's ID, date, URL, and replication timestamp. Reproducing an old result needs the stored extract, since Geofabrik deletes daily files after about a week; the docs say so.

docs.title: 7. Building a network from an extract
docs.text:
The same network as osmnx for every network_type, tested against osmnx on the Kigali test extract: the same nodes, street_count, and node tags; the same (u, v, key) edges with the same lengths, way IDs, oneway, reversed, kept tags, and simplified geometries. The builder is gigaspatial/handlers/osm/pbf.py (build_road_network); OSMRoadsReader.build_network adds the extract's ID, date, and URL from its stored path.

  1. Read the file once, with pyosmium's node location index. pyosmium preselects ways by key in C++; Python applies the filter to each way, keeps its ID, node references, and kept tags, and has pyosmium write its line (every node, in order) as WKB. Nodes reach Python only when they carry a kept node tag.
  2. In numpy: drop consecutive repeated nodes, reverse ways that run against their node order, cut ways into edges, number parallel edges as networkx does, and compute lengths and street_count; build the SpatialNetwork; run simplify for the simplified variant.

Two reads (ways, then their nodes) were measured against one (benchmarks/osm_roads/read_strategies.py, results in benchmarks/osm_roads/results.md). Reading the referenced nodes through an ID filter in Python takes 12.2 s in all and 2.4 GB; reading the ways again with the location index takes 7.5 s and 1.0 GB; one read with the index takes 7.3 s and 1.0 GB. The location index is what saves the time. One read is kept because it is simpler (the filter, tags, and line come from the same way) and reads the file once, not because it is faster.

Rwanda (68 MB extract) Raw Simplified drive_service 2.3 M nodes, 4.6 M edges, 8.9 s 129 k nodes, 339 k edges, 15.4 s walk 3.8 M nodes, 7.8 M edges, 15.0 s 263 k nodes, 698 k edges, 27.3 s

drive_service peaks at 1.6 GB of memory (benchmarks/osm_roads/build_rwanda.py).

osmnx rules to reproduce exactly (osmnx 2.0.2):

  • Ways with nodes missing from the file are skipped with a warning; Geofabrik's extracts have none. osmnx would fail on them.
  • Every preset requires highway, excludes area=yes, and, except all, excludes access=private. The presets' excluded highway values and extra conditions are in osmnx/_overpass.py (drive 75–82, drive_service 85–92, walk 99–106, bike 110–115, all_public 119–123, all 127–130). Their conditions are Overpass !~ patterns: unanchored regular expressions, and a way without the key passes (so walk's motor also drops motorway).
  • tags= replaces Overpass's custom_filter: a dict of key to allowed values, such as {"highway": ["primary", "secondary"]}. A way must match every key; None allows any value. tags= networks are one-way where tagged, as osmnx's custom_filter networks are.
  • One-way: oneway in {"yes", "true", "1", "-1", "reverse", "T", "F"}, or junction=roundabout; walk is two-way everywhere. Reversed: oneway in {"-1", "reverse", "T"}, and the node order is reversed. Two-way ways get both directions, the reverse edges with reversed=True.
  • Kept tags: osmnx's useful_tags_way (access, area, bridge, est_width, highway, junction, landuse, lanes, maxspeed, name, oneway, ref, service, tunnel, width) and useful_tags_node (highway, junction, railway, ref). Consecutive duplicate nodes are dropped.
  • Lengths: great-circle per segment before simplification, summed by simplify. street_count per node as osmnx's count_streets_per_node.
  • The node coordinate index: pyosmium's in-memory flex_mem up to about 1 GiB of extract (about 16 bytes per node in the file, about 2 GB for Nigeria), and the disk-backed sparse_file_array above it. node_index= overrides the choice. Dense indexes are never used: on Rwanda's 64-bit node IDs they need about 115 GB.
  • Attributes are normalised with normalize_attributes(edges, int_lists=("osmid",)), as in the fetcher.

docs.title: 8. Loading for a source
docs.text:
OSMRoadsHandler.load_data(source) returns a SpatialNetwork; crop_to_source defaults to True. A cropped load gives what osmnx.graph_from_polygon gives for the same area, in its order (tested against osmnx on the Kigali extract, with and without truncate_by_edge, simplify, and retain_all):

  1. Clip each extract's raw network to the source's area widened by 500 m, as osmnx downloads it. The area follows the fetcher's rules (OSMRoadsConfig.source_area, sharing the fetcher's query_area): a country's boundary, a geometry as given, a frame's union, or points as hull, bounding box, or buffers widened by buffer meters. Nodes in it are kept, and with truncate_by_edge, nodes outside with a neighbour inside, as osmnx's truncate_graph_polygon does.
  2. Combine several extracts as if they were one file (pbf.combine_road_networks): a way in several extracts is kept once, and parallel edges are keyed again in way order. SpatialNetwork.concat would key parallel edges by whichever extract came first.
  3. Keep the largest connected part unless retain_all=True, and simplify.
  4. Clip to the area itself, keep the largest connected part again, and set street_count as counted on the simplified widened network, as osmnx does.

These are the steps of osmnx's graph_from_polygon after its download (osmnx 2.0.2), so a cropped load is the fetcher's network. Simplifying the widened area first means a road that leaves the area ends where its simplified edge ends, at a real junction outside, and is dropped with that edge, as osmnx drops it. A first version clipped the raw network to the area and simplified afterwards; it kept stubs of such roads (513 nodes against the fetcher's 478 for central Kigali) and its test, which replayed that order instead of osmnx's, did not notice. The test now replays osmnx's steps, and a live test compares the handler with the fetcher. Clipping the raw network costs about 1 s for Rwanda's 4.6 million edges.

No crop when the source is a country and every extract is its own file or one of its sub-region files (ADR 0007), accepting small leftovers across borders as ADR 0001 does. A single extract then uses its stored simplified network; several are combined raw and simplified. A country's boundary geometry as the source gives an exact crop. crop_to_source=False uses whole extracts for any source.

  • The decision needs the source and its units together, which the base's crop does not get, so OSMRoadsReader.load overrides the public entry (changing crop_to_source's default to True, as the contract allows) and units_match_country stays False. crop_to_geometry clips a network; anything else goes to the base's version.
  • Network folders are named by variant: the network type, or tags- and a hash of the tags filter, then -simplified or -raw. Building reads the extract once for its raw network and simplifies that, saving both; a stored raw network is simplified without reading the extract again. A network saved by an older BUILD_VERSION of the builder is built again.
  • pyosmium cannot read Python file objects. With a remote data store, the reader copies the extract to a local temporary file, reads it, and deletes it; a LocalDataStore path is read in place. Built networks are saved back to the data store.
  • Path sources: a .pbf path loads that extract through its network folders, with the largest part unless retain_all; a network folder path loads that network as it is. The handler's availability check treats every path as a file, so a folder path source needs sub-task 6 (or ensure_available=False).
  • Metadata records the extract (or extracts, for several), the build, and the load: cropped, area_bounds, retain_all, truncate_by_edge.
Rwanda (benchmarks/osm_roads/load_rwanda.py) Time Four school points, first load (builds the raw network) 11.1 s Four school points; a 30 × 22 km box around Kigali 1.4 s; 1.9 s The country, first load (simplifies the stored raw network) 9.8 s The country 0.44 s

Parameters, matching the fetcher where they overlap: network_type="drive_service", tags=None, simplify=True, retain_all=False, truncate_by_edge=False, buffer=2000, area="hull", regions=False, extracts=None, date=None, refresh=False, max_age_days=None, node_index=None.

docs.title: 9. Performance targets
docs.text: Operation Target Build Rwanda's network from its extract under 30 s (osmnx route: 300 s); drive_service 15.4 s Nigeria (680 MiB) on a 16 GB machine fits in memory with the default index Load a stored network under 1 s for Rwanda (ADR 0005 load: 0.48 s); the country 0.44 s, a cropped area 1.4 to 1.9 s Extracts over 1 GiB use the disk-backed index automatically

docs.title: 10. Tests and fixtures
docs.text:
• A stored subset of index-v1.json with the countries the tests need (Rwanda, Brazil and its regions, the multi-country extracts, a mis-coded territory), plus a test that checks the curated multi-country list against a full stored index.
  • A small Kigali .pbf cut from the Rwanda extract with pyosmium (a few hundred KB), and osmnx's network for the same file recorded beside it, built through graph_from_xml once by a script in benchmarks/.
  • Downloads mocked offline; one live test downloads Rwanda's extract.

docs.title: 11. Sub-tasks
docs.text:
Each sub-task is its own chat and pull request on feat/osm-roads-handler, stacked on feat/spatial-network until PR #18 merges. All six are implemented; the modules are in gigaspatial/handlers/osm/, and OSMRoadsHandler is public from gigaspatial.

# Sub-task Delivers 1 Scaffolding osmium in [roads]; .pbf in DATA_FILE_SUFFIXES; DATA_TYPES["osm"]; the module skeleton; the index subset and Kigali .pbf fixtures, with the scripts that make them 2 Choosing extracts storing the index; smallest covering extract by polygon with the ISO fast path; the own-country rule and curated multi-country list; regions= and extracts=; continents only when named 3 Downloads and storage -latest to the dated file; streaming and checksum; the date-first layout; refresh, max_age_days, date=; the offline replication timestamp 4 Building a network the single read with numpy assembly (planned as three passes); osmnx's filters, one-way rules, kept tags, lengths, and street_count; simplify; the node index by size; the equivalence test on the Kigali extract; Rwanda under 30 s 5 Loading for a source network folders per variant, built once and reused; clipping, the largest part, concat; the no-crop rule; local copies for remote stores; the reader's crop 6 Handler and docs wiring OSMRoadsHandler, import registration, a live test, a country-scale section in the road networks guide, the API reference, and the changelog

docs.title: 12. Deferred
docs.text:
• One entry point that picks the fetcher or the handler by area size.
  • Other OSM datasets from the same stored extracts, such as buildings or points of interest.
  • Updating stored extracts with Geofabrik's daily diffs (pyosmium-up-to-date) instead of downloading them again.

docs.title: Design: spatial networks and the OSM roads fetcher
docs.text:
This is the agreed design for two components: OSMRoadsFetcher, which fetches the road network of a source from OpenStreetMap, and SpatialNetwork, which holds any spatial network and offers editing, insertion of points, reduction, and network algorithms. It records the decisions from the design interview of October 2026 and splits the work into sub-tasks. Each sub-task starts by reading this document, the glossary, and ADRs 0003 to 0005.

Read first:

  • GLOSSARY.md and CONTEXT.md at the repository root (local files, gitignored): spatial network, road network, insertion, connecting subnetwork, fetcher, source.
  • ADR 0003: public import paths and lazy loading.
  • ADR 0004: a spatial network is held as tables; networkx and pandana are exports; edits return a new network.
  • ADR 0005: a saved network is a folder of Parquet files.

This page is not in the docs site navigation. The user-facing description is the road networks guide and the spatial networks API page. Why each part was built the way it was, with the benchmarks behind it, is in design and algorithm decisions.

docs.title: 1. Responsibilities
docs.text:
• OSMRoadsFetcher only acquires data. It turns a source into an area, queries Overpass through osmnx, normalises the attributes, and returns a SpatialNetwork. It never saves anything.
  • SpatialNetwork owns everything after that: accessors, editing, weights, insertion of points, simplification, algorithms, the networkx and pandana exports, and saving and loading.
  • The fetcher shares no static helpers with the network; it hands over a network object.
  • Application workflows stay in applications. The per-admin clustering, the school, fiber, and splitter node types, and the orchestration in the old OSMRoadGraphModel are not part of the library. The library provides the building blocks: fetch, insert_points, concat, connect_components, and connecting_subnetwork.

docs.title: 2. Modules, imports, and dependencies
docs.text:
Item Location SpatialNetwork gigaspatial/processing/network.py, possibly split into a gigaspatial/processing/network/ package if it grows past one module OSMRoadsFetcher gigaspatial/fetchers/osm/roads.py Public names from gigaspatial import SpatialNetwork, OSMRoadsFetcher; gigaspatial.processing.SpatialNetwork; gigaspatial.fetchers.OSMRoadsFetcher Lazy registration Add both to the attach dictionaries and the TYPE_CHECKING blocks, per ADR 0003. tests/test_public_api.py checks the two lists match and that every exported name resolves. SpatialNetwork is registered in sub-task 1; OSMRoadsFetcher is registered in sub-task 8, when it exists.

Dependencies:

  • giga-spatial[roads] adds osmnx>=2.0. On Python 3.10, pip resolves osmnx 2.0.x; on 3.11 and newer, 2.1.x. Use only API common to both, and test both.
  • giga-spatial[pandana] adds pandana>=0.8. It pulls in scikit-learn and PyTables, which is why it is a separate extra.
  • [all] includes both.
  • Core dependencies already cover the rest: numpy, pandas, geopandas, shapely, scipy, pyarrow, and networkx.
  • osmnx and pandana are imported only inside the functions that need them, following the Overture and DuckDB pattern: a module flag, and an ImportError naming the extra (pip install 'giga-spatial[roads]'). A bare import gigaspatial must not import either.
  • Python support stays at 3.10 and newer.

Configuration: add OVERPASS_URL to gigaspatial/config.py, with the default https://overpass-api.de/api/interpreter.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
The nodes table is a pandas DataFrame indexed by node_id. The index keeps the original IDs (OSM integers, user IDs such as giga_id, or negative integers for split nodes). IDs are unique.

Column Type Meaning x float64 longitude, EPSG:4326 y float64 latitude, EPSG:4326 kind categorical road, point, or split other any attributes, such as street_count from OSM or the columns of inserted points

The edges table is a pandas DataFrame with a default RangeIndex. An edge is identified by (u, v, key).

Column Type Meaning u, v node ID type endpoints, which must exist in the nodes table key int16 distinguishes parallel edges, as in osmnx length float64 meters (see section 4) kind categorical road, split, connection, point_link, component_link, added, or bridge (from a connection plan) geometry shapely LineString or missing optional; missing means a straight line between the endpoints other any OSM attributes after normalisation (section 8), or user attributes

Network-level fields:

  • directed (bool). In a directed network, a two-way road is two rows, one per direction, as osmnx returns it. In an undirected network, each edge is one row and the order of u and v has no meaning.
  • weight (str, default "length") is the default weight column for algorithms.
  • metadata (dict) holds provenance: fetch parameters, the source description, and the library version. It is saved to network.json.

docs.title: Immutability and caching
docs.text:
Every edit returns a new SpatialNetwork (ADR 0004). There is no inplace= option. Unchanged columns are shared between the old and new network, not copied. Never mutate a table that another network may share; build a new column or a new table instead.

Each instance caches its derived structures lazily:

  • the ID-to-position mapping (pd.Index.get_indexer, int32 positions);
  • the scipy CSR adjacency per weight and direction;
  • the KD-tree on node coordinates;
  • the STRtree on edge geometries;
  • nodes_gdf and edges_gdf;
  • a pandana network per weight.

Because networks never change, these caches never need to be invalidated.

docs.title: 4. Coordinates, distances, and lengths
docs.text:
• Nodes are stored in EPSG:4326. Constructors that receive another CRS convert to it.
  • Lengths are meters. Road edges keep the lengths osmnx gives them: the great-circle (haversine) distance with an Earth radius of 6,371,009 m, added up along the original edges during simplification.
  • Every edge the library creates gets its haversine length along its geometry, using the same formula and radius as osmnx. This covers connection edges, split pieces, from_points edges, component links, and point links. The calculation is a vectorized numpy function, shared by every module.
  • When a road is split, the lengths of the pieces are rescaled so they add up exactly to the original length. Inserting a point never changes the length of a route that passes through it.
  • Nearest-edge searches run in a UTM projection estimated from the network's extent (estimate_utm_crs_with_fallback). UTM is conformal, so the ranking of nearby candidates is right even outside the zone. Distance thresholds such as max_distance and snap_to_node are always checked with haversine distances, never projected ones.
  • Nearest-node searches use a cKDTree on 3D unit-sphere coordinates, with chord distances converted to great-circle meters. This is accurate everywhere and needs no projection.
  • Ellipsoidal (geodesic) distances were rejected because they would make new edges inconsistent with osmnx's road lengths. Haversine is within about 0.5% of the ellipsoid.
  • Accessors take crs= to return projected output. Coordinate arrays are always ordered (y, x), which is (lat, lon) in EPSG:4326.

docs.title: Constructors
docs.text:
• SpatialNetwork(nodes, edges, directed=True, crs="EPSG:4326", weight="length", metadata=None) validates and adopts the two tables. Validation checks that IDs are unique, edges reference existing nodes, x and y are present, and length is present or computable. Missing lengths are computed with haversine.
  • SpatialNetwork.from_networkx(G) takes osmnx graphs or any networkx graph whose nodes have x and y. directed comes from G.is_directed(), and the CRS from G.graph["crs"] (EPSG:4326 if absent). Missing keys become 0. Directed graphs are read from networkx's adjacency dictionaries rather than its edge views, attributes go through DataFrame.from_records, and Python's cyclic garbage collector is paused during the conversion (and in to_networkx): collections triggered by millions of new objects tripled the time on unsimplified Rwanda.
  • SpatialNetwork.from_points(points, connect="knn", k=5, max_distance=None, id_column=None, weight="length", weight_func=None) builds a network whose nodes are the points. connect="knn" joins each point to its k nearest neighbours. connect="distance" joins every pair within max_distance meters. Both use a cKDTree, like build_distance_graph, and never connect all pairs. Edges get length in meters. weight_func(nodes_u, nodes_v, length) -> array optionally computes another weight column at construction. The network is undirected.
  • SpatialNetwork.load(path, data_store=None) (section 7).

points, here and everywhere else, accepts what the library already understands as point input: a GeoDataFrame, a DataFrame with latitude and longitude columns (found with detect_coordinate_columns and converted with convert_to_geodataframe), or a list of (lat, lon) tuples, the same order the handlers use.

docs.title: Accessors
docs.text: Accessor Returns nodes, edges the tables; cheap nodes_gdf, edges_gdf GeoDataFrames in EPSG:4326, built on first access and cached; missing edge geometries are filled with straight lines in one vectorized call to_geodataframes(crs=None) (nodes_gdf, edges_gdf), projected if crs is given node_coordinates(ids=None, crs=None) numpy array of (y, x) degree(directed=None) Series of node degrees bounds (minx, miny, maxx, maxy) total_length(by=None) meters, optionally grouped by a column such as kind to_networkx(directed=None) a new networkx graph each call, not cached: MultiDiGraph or MultiGraph with all attributes to_pandana(weight=None) a pandana network with twoway set to not directed; IDs are validated first, because pandana raises a cryptic dtype error on unknown IDs adjacency(weight=None, directed=None) scipy CSR matrix; parallel edges keep the minimum weight node_index maps adjacency positions to node IDs and back clip(geometry, predicate="intersects") the edges matching the predicate and their endpoints len(), info(), repr size and summary

docs.title: Editing
docs.text:
Every method takes many items at once and returns a new network. They live in gigaspatial/processing/network/editing.py, a mixin of SpatialNetwork. Filters and attribute edits wrap their tables with _from_tables, passing remapped edge positions; additions (add_nodes, add_weighted_edges, concat) go through the validating constructor. Geometries are in EPSG:4326, or a GeoDataFrame or GeoSeries in any CRS.

  • nearest_nodes(points, max_distance=None, return_distance=False) returns a Series of the node IDs closest to coordinates, indexed like the points. Points with no node within max_distance get a missing ID (<NA> for integer IDs). The other "by coordinates" methods build on it.
  • filter_nodes(ids=None, mask=None, geometry=None, predicate="intersects") keeps the selected nodes and the edges between them. Exactly one selector is allowed.
  • remove_nodes(ids=None, points=None, geometry=None, max_distance=None) removes nodes and their edges. points are resolved with nearest_nodes.
  • set_node_attribute(name, values) takes a scalar, an array in node order, or a Series or dict keyed by node ID.
  • update_nodes(frame, by="id" | "coordinates", max_distance=None) updates several attributes. With by="coordinates", rows are matched to their nearest node.
  • add_nodes(frame, id_column=None, kind="point") adds nodes from a points input with IDs.
  • Attribute edits keep a column's dtype when nothing is lost (an int16 column stays int16), and text columns stay categorical. x and y cannot be set, and neither can u, v, and key.
  • For edges: filter_edges(mask=None, geometry=None, predicate=...) keeps every node; remove_edges(edges=None, mask=None), where edges are (u, v, key) or (u, v) tuples or a frame, and (u, v) removes every parallel edge; set_edge_attribute(name, values), keyed by (u, v, key); and update_edges(frame) keyed by (u, v, key). In an undirected network, (v, u) matches (u, v).
  • add_weighted_edges(u, v, weights, weight="length", kind="added", **attributes) mirrors networkx's add_weighted_edges_from, but takes arrays. Keys continue from the edges already between each pair. When weight != "length", length is computed with haversine.
  • Edge predicates describe the edge's relation to the area: intersects, within, crosses, touches. Node predicates are intersects and within.
  • drop_geometry() removes edge geometry to save memory.
  • to_undirected(weight=None) merges reverse and parallel edges into the one with the smallest weight (the network's weight by default), sets every key to 0, and records directed=False. It also collapses parallel edges of an undirected network.
  • SpatialNetwork.concat(networks) combines networks. Nodes with the same ID are the same node, as when separately fetched areas share boundary nodes, and the first occurrence wins. Edges are deduplicated on (u, v, key). All inputs must have the same directed value.

docs.title: Weights
docs.text: Algorithms take weight=None, which means the network's weight (by default "length"), and any edge column can be named. There are three ways to set weights: at construction (from_points(weight_func=...)), later with set_edge_attribute, or when adding edges with add_weighted_edges.

docs.title: insert_points
docs.text:
insert_points(points, id_column=None, max_distance=None, snap_to_node=5.0,
              chain=False, return_skipped=False) -> SpatialNetwork | tuple

return_skipped was return_unmerged in the interview; it was renamed because the glossary avoids "merging". The method lives in gigaspatial/processing/network/insertion.py, a mixin of SpatialNetwork.

  • IDs come from id_column, or from the frame's index if it is None. They must be unique and must not collide with existing node IDs; a collision raises.
  • The columns of the points frame are carried onto their nodes. A collision with reserved columns (x, y, kind) raises.
  • Each point is joined to its nearest edge at the foot of the perpendicular. The edge is split there, a split node is added (kind="split"), and a connection edge (kind="connection") joins the point (kind="point") to the split node.
  • If the foot is within snap_to_node meters (haversine) of one of the edge's endpoints, the point connects to that node instead and no split happens.
  • Points farther than max_distance from any road are left out. A warning gives their count, and return_skipped=True returns (network, skipped_points): the skipped rows of a frame, or the skipped items of a list.
  • With chain=True, points are handled in order of their distance to the road. A point connects to an already-inserted point (kind="point_link") when that point is closer than any road. This reproduces rule (i) of the old merge_points_to_graph. Candidates come from a KD-tree on the points, querying k neighbours and doubling k only for points whose k-th neighbour is still closer than their road.
  • Split nodes get negative integer IDs, decreasing from the lowest existing negative ID, as OSM does for new objects.
  • In a directed network, a two-way road is two rows with reversed geometries. Both rows must be split at the same split nodes, and connection edges are added in both directions.

  • Lengths follow section 4: haversine for connections, and split pieces rescaled to the original length.

  • Points join road edges only: edges of kind connection and point_link from earlier insertions are never split.

  • In a directed network, the other direction of a two-way road is the row from v to u whose geometry is the reverse (or both straight). One-way roads are split in their one direction only; connections still run both ways.
  • When the network's weight is not length, road pieces get their share of the road's weight in proportion to length, and connection edges get the weight equal to their length.
  • The UTM projection of the road edges and its STRtree are cached per network (_projected_roads), built on the first insertion. The EPSG:4326 STRtree used by clip is not used here: in degrees, a road 100 m east looks farther than one 150 m north at 60° latitude.

The work is done in one batch:

  1. Run one STRtree.query_nearest in UTM for all points.
  2. Compute positions along the edges with vectorized line_locate_point and line_interpolate_point.
  3. Group the points by edge and sort each group by position. Points with the same foot share one split node.
  4. Split each affected edge once, at all of its points.
  5. Append the new nodes and edges in one concatenation.

Python loops may run over affected edges, never over points with table operations inside.

Problems in the old merge_points_to_graph that must not come back:

  • the distance from each point to every earlier point, which grows with the square of the number of points;
  • a pd.concat per point, which also grows with the square;
  • the bare except that falls back to scanning every edge when two points share an edge;
  • projecting and copying the whole graph twice.

docs.title: simplify(keep=None, sum_columns=("length",))
docs.text:
• Removes nodes that only continue a road: nodes with two neighbours in an undirected network, or the osmnx rule for directed networks.
  • Never removes nodes of kind point or split, or nodes in keep.
  • Joins the edges across each removed node. Columns in sum_columns are added up, and so are any columns the user names as weights. Geometries are joined. Text attributes are ;-joined when they differ. osmid lists are concatenated. Other numeric columns take the length-weighted mean. That last rule is a default set in this spec; revisit it in the sub-task 6 pull request if it surprises anyone.
  • A two-way road stays two-way only when both directions can be joined.
  • Removable nodes follow osmnx's rule, with two deliberate differences. osmnx also removes nodes between duplicated parallel ways and keeps one way; here such nodes stay. osmnx deletes rings without any junction (remove_rings=True); here a ring keeps one node, so no road is lost. On the unsimplified Kigali fixture and on unsimplified Rwanda, the result has the same nodes, edges, and edge lengths as ox.simplify_graph.
  • Joined edges always get a geometry, as in osmnx, so a network without edge geometry gains a geometry column, missing for edges left as they were. Edges without geometry contribute their two node positions.
  • Implemented in gigaspatial/processing/network/reduction.py without walking chains in Python: each edge into a removable node is linked to the edge that continues it, chains are ranked by pointer jumping, and attributes are aggregated with reduceat per chain. Rings are found as connected components of removable nodes that touch no other node. Undirected networks run on half-edges and keep one of each mirrored chain.
  • Tests compare against tests/data/spatial_network/kigali_raw/ (the fixture box cut from unsimplified Rwanda, 8,266 nodes and 15,652 edges) and kigali_raw_osmnx.json, osmnx's result for it, both made by make_fixture.py raw.

docs.title: connecting_subnetwork(terminals, sources=None, method="steiner", weight=None)
docs.text:
Superseded by the connection planning design: sources= is now roots=, and with roots the default is the rooted Steiner tree. The record below is the design as first built.

This works on the undirected form of the network. The result is contracted to the terminals, the sources, and the branching nodes (degree 3 or more), with lengths added up and geometries joined.

  • method="steiner" (the default) uses Mehlhorn's 2-approximation of the Steiner tree. One multi-source Dijkstra run from the terminals (scipy dijkstra(min_only=True, return_predecessors=True)) finds each node's nearest terminal. Edges between different terminals' regions give candidate links. Then come an MST over the terminals, expansion of the links into paths, a second MST, and removal of leaves that are not terminals.
  • With sources= given, the result is the union of each terminal's shortest path to its nearest source, using one multi-source run from the sources.
  • method="all_pairs" is the union of shortest paths between every terminal and every node in terminals plus sources, the behaviour of the old create_cleaned_graph. Its cost grows with the square of the number of terminals, which is documented.
  • Paths are collected from Dijkstra predecessor arrays with a vectorized walk back to the roots, not one path at a time. The contraction is simplify(keep=terminals and sources) on an undirected network of the chosen edges, so lengths and geometries are joined the same way. Terminals that cannot reach the others stay as nodes without edges.

docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text:
Every algorithm uses scipy by default. backend="pandana" is available where noted, and requires [pandana]. Directed networks respect one-way roads unless directed=False is passed. The algorithms live in gigaspatial/processing/network/algorithms.py, a mixin of SpatialNetwork.

  • The adjacency matrix is cached per weight and direction, together with the edge row behind each entry, so routes can be drawn along edge geometries. Its transpose (for searches towards targets) and pandana networks are cached the same way.
  • Dijkstra runs in blocks of sources of at most CHUNK_BYTES (256 MiB) of distances, and shortest_path_lengths refuses result matrices over MAX_MATRIX_BYTES (1 GiB). Both are module constants.
  • Weights must be present and non-negative on every edge; zero weights are allowed. scipy's minimum spanning tree drops zero-weight entries, so they are replaced by the smallest positive float for that call only.
  • pandana reports unreachable pairs as 4294967.295; the library returns inf. pandana stores weights with limited precision (differences of about 0.02 m on the Kigali fixture). to_pandana refuses node IDs that mix integers and text; backend="pandana" indexes pandana's network by node position instead, so it works on any network.
  • connect_components uses Borůvka's method: each round, every component finds its nearest node outside it (a KD-tree on all nodes with a growing k for small components, a KD-tree on the component's own nodes for large ones). When the network's weight is not length, the links get that weight equal to their length.
Method Result shortest_path_lengths(origins, destinations=None, pairwise=False, weight=None, backend="scipy") a matrix DataFrame of origins by destinations, or a 1-D array when pairwise=True. Estimate the matrix size first and raise with advice to batch if it would exceed a limit. pandana is supported for the pairwise case. shortest_paths(origins, destinations, pairwise=True, weight=None, geometry=False) lists of node IDs, or a GeoDataFrame with one LineString per route and its length when geometry=True reachable(origins, max_distance, weight=None) a long table of origin, node ID, and distance, from dijkstra(limit=...) nearest_by_network(origins, targets, k=1, max_distance=None) origin, target, and distance. k=1 is one multi-source run from the targets (on the transposed matrix when directed). count_within(origins, targets, max_distance) a Series of counts per origin, running from whichever side is smaller connected_components(strong=False) a Series of component labels largest_component() a network connect_components(max_distance=None) a network with component_link edges from an MST over components, using the nearest node pairs from a KD-tree minimum_spanning_tree(weight=None) an undirected network

Deferred: isochrone polygons, centrality (available through to_networkx()), and travel speeds (osmnx's add_edge_speeds).

docs.title: 7. Storage (ADR 0005)
docs.text:
save(path, data_store=None) writes a folder through DataStore.open(..., "wb"), using in-memory buffers so remote data stores work:

  • nodes.parquet: plain Parquet, zstd. The node_id column holds the index, plus x, y, kind, and attributes. Categoricals are stored as dictionaries.
  • edges.parquet: GeoParquet 1.0, WKB geometry, zstd, with the file-level geo metadata written by the library (not through geopandas' private writer). When the geometry has been dropped, it is a plain Parquet file with no geometry column.
  • network.json: {"format": "gigaspatial.spatial_network", "format_version": 1, "directed", "crs", "weight", "node_ids", "metadata", "library_version", "created"}. It is written last, so a folder with network.json always holds complete tables.
  • Node IDs are stored natively when they are all integers or all text. When they mix both, as after inserting points with text IDs into an OSM network, node_ids is "mixed": node_id, u, and v are stored as text and a node_id_is_int column restores the integers on load. An integer and a text ID with the same digits (5 and "5") cannot be saved; other ID types raise.
  • The files carry no pandas metadata, so plain pd.read_parquet reads them; pandas would otherwise record dtype names it cannot parse back.
  • Before writing, normalize_attributes (gigaspatial/processing/network/attributes.py) makes every attribute column storable; the network itself is not changed. The fetcher calls the same function with int_lists=("osmid",).

load(path, data_store=None, columns=None) checks format and format_version, and raises a clear error for unknown versions. List columns such as osmid load as Arrow-backed columns (pd.ArrowDtype), so each value reads as a Python list and the column stays compact. columns= names edge attributes to read on top of u, v, key, length, kind, and the weight column; "geometry" is included only if it was saved. Reading a subset of columns is allowed (columns= for edges) for users who only need the topology.

docs.title: 8. OSMRoadsFetcher
docs.text:
The fetcher is a pydantic dataclass, like the other fetchers (@dataclass(kw_only=True), logger from config.get_logger).

OSMRoadsFetcher(network_type="drive_service", custom_filter=None, simplify=True,
                retain_all=False, truncate_by_edge=False, buffer=2000, area="hull",
                overpass_url=None, timeout=180, max_retries=3)
    .fetch(source) -> SpatialNetwork

How a source becomes the queried area:

Source Area Country the admin 0 boundary through AdminBoundaries.create(...), as handlers do Geometry used as given Frame of polygons the union of the polygons Points, or a frame of points area="hull" (default): convex hull; "bbox": bounding rectangle; "buffers": union of a buffer per point. Buffered by buffer meters through UTM (buffer_geodataframe), never degrees.
  • Point tuples are (lat, lon).
  • The library's source classification (classify_source) decides the kind. The body of BaseHandlerConfig.extract_search_geometry moved into source_geometry(source, crs, options) in gigaspatial/handlers/base/config.py; the method calls it, and so does the fetcher. Lines are buffered like points, and a single point or a line with buffer=0 raises. query_area(source) is public, so users can see what will be queried.
  • The query is ox.graph_from_polygon(polygon, network_type=..., simplify=..., retain_all=..., truncate_by_edge=..., custom_filter=...). Set ox.settings for the Overpass URL (overpass_url or config.OVERPASS_URL) and the timeout inside a context manager that restores the previous settings. osmnx's HTTP cache is left as the user configured it.
  • osmnx's overpass_url is the API base, while OVERPASS_URL is the full endpoint, so a trailing /interpreter is removed for osmnx.
  • Transient failures are retried up to max_retries times, pausing retry_delay seconds and doubling each time: connection errors and timeouts (requests.RequestException) and osmnx's ResponseStatusCodeError. osmnx already retries 429 and 504 itself. osmnx's InsufficientResponseError (no matching roads) becomes a ValueError and is not retried. The last error names the Overpass URL and suggests a mirror.
  • Warn when the area is large (above about 50,000 km²): Overpass is slow at country scale and has fair-use limits, and the Geofabrik handler will be the faster route.
  • Normalisation before building the network, with normalize_attributes(edges, int_lists=("osmid",)), so saving does not repeat it (ADR 0005):
  • osmid becomes a list of int64 on every edge.
  • List-valued text attributes (highway, name, maxspeed, lanes, ref, and the like) become ;-joined strings, stored as categoricals.
  • oneway and reversed become booleans. A list of oneway values is true only if every value is true; a list of reversed values is true if any value is true. The test fixture uses the same rules (benchmarks/spatial_network/make_fixture.py).
  • The network is built with the column-wise extraction of from_networkx. The fetch parameters and the source description go into metadata.
  • directed=True is what OSM returns. Users call to_undirected() when they need it.

docs.title: 9. Performance targets
docs.text:
Measured on an Apple M1 Pro (8 cores, 17 GB) with the Geofabrik Rwanda extract. The full results and scripts are in benchmarks/spatial_network/.

Network Nodes Edges Kigali, simplified 18,547 47,499 Rwanda, simplified 125,058 332,535 Rwanda, unsimplified 2,224,948 4,526,967

Targets on the simplified Rwanda network unless stated. A pull request that misses one explains why.

Operation Target Baseline measured load under 0.5 s lean Parquet 0.17 s, 0.29 s with geometry decoded; GraphML 12.0 s save under 1 s lean Parquet 0.26 s Memory, tables with geometry under 400 MB 229 MB with WKB, 393 MB decoded; networkx 731 MB node_coordinates() under 5 ms 0.6 ms from the table; 43 ms from networkx clip of 4% of the area under 0.1 s 0.03 s; 1.6 to 3.0 s from networkx adjacency() under 0.3 s 0.14 s to_networkx() under 3 s 2.5 s Conversion from an osmnx graph under 2 s 0.81 s; 14.5 s for unsimplified Rwanda (4.5 million edges), once 49 s; 4.0 s with graph_to_gdfs shortest_path_lengths, 100 by 1,000 under 3 s with scipy scipy 2.4 s; pandana 1.4 s build plus 0.19 s; networkx about 29 s insert_points, 10,000 points under 10 s 1.8 s, plus 1.3 s once per network for the UTM road index; the old function took 292 s for 1,000 points simplify of unsimplified Rwanda faster than osmnx osmnx simplify_graph 197 s; simplify 9.1 s, same result

docs.title: 10. Tests and benchmarks
docs.text:
• Unit tests run offline, on synthetic networks and on a small saved Kigali network fixture under tests/data/ (a few hundred KB of Parquet). Build the fixture once from the benchmark data with a script kept in benchmarks/.
  • The fetcher's tests mock osmnx and AdminBoundaries.create. One test marked @pytest.mark.live calls Overpass for a small area.
  • Each sub-task tests its own methods, including the cases called out above: two-way roads in directed networks, points sharing a split position, ID collisions, list attributes in storage, and unknown IDs given to pandana.
  • The benchmark scripts live in benchmarks/spatial_network/. They are run by hand, not by pytest. Sub-tasks 2 to 7 rerun the relevant script and report the numbers in the pull request.

docs.title: 11. Sub-tasks
docs.text:
Each sub-task is its own chat and pull request, with tests, in this order. The fetcher comes late because everything else can be tested on saved networks.

# Sub-task Delivers 1 Scaffolding the [roads] and [pandana] extras; OVERPASS_URL; SpatialNetwork registered for import and covered by the public API test; an empty SpatialNetwork module; benchmark scripts tidied in benchmarks/spatial_network/; the Kigali fixture in tests/data/spatial_network/kigali/ (1,209 nodes, 2,802 edges, 264 KB) 2 Core tables, validation, the ID-to-position mapping, constructors (__init__, from_networkx, from_points), accessors, to_networkx, info, caching, haversine helper 3 Storage save and load, and attribute normalisation (shared with the fetcher) 4 Editing nearest_nodes, filter, remove, update and add for nodes and edges, add_weighted_edges, clip, drop_geometry, to_undirected, concat 5 Algorithms adjacency, shortest paths, reachable, nearest_by_network, count_within, components, connect_components, MST, to_pandana and the pandana backend 6 Reduction simplify, connecting_subnetwork 7 Insertion insert_points in one batch, including chain=True, benchmarked against the old merge_points_to_graph 8 Fetcher OSMRoadsFetcher: source to area, osmnx, normalisation, SpatialNetwork, retries, live test, and its import registration 9 Docs user guide page, API reference pages, changelog entry, README mention

docs.title: 12. Deferred
docs.text:
• A Geofabrik handler for country-scale road networks from .osm.pbf extracts, returning the same SpatialNetwork. Its design is now in osm-roads-handler.md, with ADRs 0006 and 0007; the notes below are the starting point it was designed from. This comes next, decided on 28 October 2026:
  • Users need both small areas and whole countries or provinces. Overpass suits the small ones; a country-scale Overpass fetch can take hours, exceed fair-use limits, and needs osmnx's networkx graph in memory (about 2.3 GB for unsimplified Rwanda).
  • It is a separate handler, not an option on OSMRoadsFetcher: an extract is a file kept in a data store and reused, which the glossary calls a handler.
  • It reads extracts with pyosmium (osmium), added to giga-spatial[roads]; pyosmium has wheels for Python 3.10 to 3.14 on macOS, Linux, and Windows (pyrosm needs 3.11 or newer). It builds the node and edge tables directly, without osmnx or networkx, and uses simplify. The benchmark's route through OSM XML and osmnx took 300 s for Rwanda, most of it in osmnx; pyosmium filtered the extract in 22.5 s, and simplify takes 9 s.
  • Open questions for its design round: the class name; whether it returns exactly what OSMRoadsFetcher returns for the same area, which means reproducing osmnx's network-type filters and one-way rules; clipping to admin areas smaller than an extract; Geofabrik's split and combined countries (its index-v1.json lists ISO codes); and keeping stored extracts up to date.
  • The road networks guide says country-scale networks from Geofabrik are planned.
  • Isochrone polygons, centrality measures, and travel speeds.
  • Dropping Python 3.10 (end of life in October 2026) is a library-wide decision, outside this work.

docs.title: Spatial networks and OSM roads: design and algorithm decisions
docs.text:
This document explains how I built SpatialNetwork, OSMRoadsFetcher, OSMRoadsHandler, and ConnectionPlanner, and why. For each decision it gives the question I faced, the options I considered, what I measured, what I chose, and what that choice costs. It is meant for colleagues who use these classes and want to know how far they can trust them, and for whoever changes them next.

It does not repeat the implementation specs or the API. For those, read:

  • the spatial network design, the OSM roads handler design, and the connection planning design, which say what was built;
  • the ADRs under Design decisions, which record single decisions in a few lines: 0004 (tables), 0005 (storage), 0006 (extract storage), 0007 (extract choice), and 0008 (connection planning);
  • the spatial networks concept note, which explains how to use each method;
  • the benchmark scripts in benchmarks/spatial_network/, benchmarks/osm_roads/, and benchmarks/connection_planning/, with their last results beside them.

Every number below comes from those scripts. Where a number explains a decision I took earlier, I give the run it came from; everything else is from the run of 29 October 2026 on the code as it is now.

docs.title: Environment and data
docs.text:
All benchmarks ran on one laptop:

Machine Apple M1 Pro, 8 CPU cores, 16 GiB of memory, internal SSD System macOS 15.7 Python 3.10.11 numpy 2.2.6, pandas 2.3.0, scipy 1.15.2, shapely 2.1.2, geopandas 1.1.4, pyarrow 17.0.0, networkx 3.3, osmnx 2.0.2, pandana 0.7, igraph 1.0.0, pyosmium 4.3.2 Python 3.14.6 numpy 2.5.2, pandas 3.0.3, scipy 1.18.0, shapely 2.1.2, geopandas 1.1.4, pyarrow 23.0.1, networkx 3.6.1, pyosmium 4.3.2

The spatial network benchmarks run on Python 3.10, where osmnx, pandana, and igraph are installed for the comparisons. The OSM road benchmarks run on Python 3.14, with pandas 3. The library supports both, and the test suite runs on both.

The test networks are all Rwanda's drivable roads (osmnx's drive_service network type), from Geofabrik's Rwanda extract:

Network Built by Nodes Edges Kigali, simplified osmnx, cut to the box 29.98, -2.03 to 30.20, -1.89 18,547 47,499 Rwanda, simplified osmnx's graph_from_xml 125,058 332,535 Rwanda, unsimplified osmnx's graph_from_xml(simplify=False) 2,224,948 4,526,967 Rwanda's extract Geofabrik, 26 October 2026 65 MiB file

Rwanda is a useful size: big enough that slow code shows (the unsimplified network has 4.5 million edges), small enough to run every comparison on a laptop. Timings are wall-clock times, the mean of three runs unless a table says otherwise. Costs paid once per network, such as building a spatial index, are reported separately from the calls that use them. Memory is the resident set size of the process, or tracemalloc's count where stated.

To reproduce, see benchmarks/spatial_network/README.md and benchmarks/osm_roads/README.md. A full run takes about ten minutes, most of it osmnx's own simplify_graph.

docs.title: Decision 1: tables, not networkx graphs
docs.text:
Question. What should hold a network in memory? osmnx returns a networkx MultiDiGraph, and the original Giga code worked on those directly.

Options. A networkx graph; an igraph graph; or two tables, one of nodes and one of edges, with the structures that algorithms need (a sparse adjacency matrix, spatial indexes) derived from them and cached.

Evidence. Measured on simplified Rwanda (partB.py, 27 October 2026):

networkx graph tables Memory, with edge geometry 731 MB 229 MB (geometry as WKB), 393 MB (as shapely objects) All node coordinates 42.7 ms 0.61 ms The edges of a box covering 4% of the country 1.63 s 0.037 s Shortest paths from one source to every node 292 ms 24.1 ms (scipy)

networkx keeps a Python dictionary per node and per edge, so every accessor loops in Python. igraph is compact and fast, but it is one more compiled dependency, and its routing sat between scipy's and pandana's (decision 5).

Decision. A SpatialNetwork holds a pandas table of nodes, indexed by node ID, and a table of edges identified by (u, v, key). scipy's sparse graph routines work on an adjacency matrix built from the edge table on demand. networkx and pandana are export formats: to_networkx() and to_pandana().

On the current code, a built network of simplified Rwanda takes 350 MB with its tables, all node coordinates come back in 0.38 ms, clipping the same 4% box takes 0.066 s, and the adjacency matrix is built in 0.062 s. Converting from osmnx takes 0.85 s and back to networkx 1.35 s, so the bridge to networkx stays cheap for anyone who needs it.

Consequences and limits. Editing one node or edge at a time in a Python loop is slow, so every editing method takes many items at once. Algorithms that scipy does not offer, such as centrality, are reached through to_networkx().

docs.title: Decision 2: edits return a new network
docs.text:
Question. Should edits change the network in place, as networkx and many pandas methods do, or return a new one?

Options. In-place edits; an inplace= option; or always a new network.

Evidence. An in-place option saves no memory, because a new network shares every column it did not change with the old one. It would also make caching dangerous. A network caches its adjacency matrix per weight and direction, a KD-tree on nodes, an R-tree on edges, a projected index of roads for insertion, a pandana network, and its GeoDataFrames. Every in-place edit would have to invalidate the right ones, and missing one gives wrong shortest paths without any error. Returning a new network is cheap: keeping 10,000 nodes by ID takes 0.004 s and setting an attribute 0.004 s. Adding 10,000 edges, which validates the whole network again, takes 0.34 s.

Decision. Every edit returns a new SpatialNetwork, and there is no inplace= option. We discussed keeping one for familiarity, and I left it out for the reasons above.

Consequences and limits. The nodes and edges properties return shallow copies of the tables. Adding a column to them is safe, but changing their values in place could reach another network that shares the column, so the docs say not to.

docs.title: Decision 3: lengths by haversine, with osmnx's Earth radius
docs.text:
Question. How should the library measure the edges it creates, such as connections to inserted points, split pieces of roads, links between points, and links between components?

Options. Great-circle (haversine) distance with osmnx's Earth radius of 6,371,009 m; ellipsoidal (geodesic) distance; or distance in a projected CRS such as UTM.

Evidence. osmnx measures road edges with haversine and that radius, so any other formula would make new edges inconsistent with the roads they join. Haversine is within about 0.5% of the ellipsoid. Projected distances drift with distance from the projection's centre: on 1,000 points inserted into Rwanda's roads, the old code's connections added up to 67,985 m in UTM metres, against 68,187 m by haversine.

Decision. Every length is haversine in metres, with osmnx's formula and radius, computed by one vectorised function. When a road is split, the pieces are rescaled so they add up exactly to the road's length, so inserting a point never changes the length of a route through it. Searches use whatever ranks candidates correctly: the nearest edge is found in UTM, which is conformal, and the nearest node with a KD-tree on points on the unit sphere, which needs no projection at all. Distance thresholds are always checked in haversine metres.

Consequences and limits. Lengths can differ from a geodesic measurement by up to about 0.5%, in exchange for consistency with osmnx's road lengths.

docs.title: Decision 4: a folder of Parquet files for storage
docs.text:
Question. How should a network be saved?

Options. GraphML or pickle of a networkx graph, as is common with osmnx; a GeoPackage with two layers; GeoParquet written by geopandas; Feather; or our own layout of Parquet tables.

Evidence. partA.py, 27 October 2026. Read times are the fastest reader for each format:

Format Simplified Rwanda Unsimplified Rwanda size read size read GraphML 216 MB 12.0 s 1,389 MB 437 s pickle 121 MB 1.9 s 532 MB 25 s GeoPackage 167 MB 0.47 s Feather, zstd 62 MB 0.14 s 64 MB 0.11 s Our Parquet tables, zstd 64 MB 0.17 s 73 MB 0.18 s

GeoParquet written straight from osmnx's GeoDataFrames failed: simplified osmnx edges mix lists and single values in one column (osmid is a number on some edges and a list on others), which Parquet cannot store. GeoPackage and stringified GeoParquet turn those lists into strings. Pickle cannot be read safely from an untrusted data store, or by any other tool.

Decision. save writes a folder: nodes.parquet, edges.parquet as GeoParquet with WKB geometry and zstd compression, and network.json with whether the network is directed, its CRS, weight, metadata, and the format version. network.json is written last, so a folder that has it holds complete tables. Feather was as fast but is read by fewer tools; GeoPandas, DuckDB, QGIS, and pandas all read these Parquet files directly. On the current code, simplified Rwanda saves to 64.9 MB and loads in 0.47 s, or 0.022 s for the topology alone (load(columns=[])).

Consequences and limits. Saving a network fresh from osmnx takes 1.2 s, above my 1 s target, because its attributes are normalised first (decision 9). A network that was loaded or built by this library saves in 0.62 s. Node IDs that mix integers and text are stored as text with a flag that restores the integers.

docs.title: Decision 5: scipy for routing, pandana as an option
docs.text:
Question. Which engine should compute shortest paths and the searches built on them?

Options. networkx; igraph; scipy's sparse graph routines (scipy.sparse.csgraph); pandana, which uses contraction hierarchies.

Evidence. On simplified Rwanda, 100 origins by 1,000 destinations (partB.py, 27 October 2026):

Engine Set-up 100 by 1,000 Per pair Agreement with scipy networkx none about 29 s 292 µs within 0.003 m igraph 0.28 s graph build 1.33 s 13.3 µs exact scipy 0.14 s adjacency build 2.41 s 24.1 µs pandana 1.42 s contraction hierarchy 0.19 s 1.9 µs median 0.15 m, at most 0.47 m

scipy is already a dependency of the library. pandana is the fastest once built, but it pulls in scikit-learn and PyTables, stores weights with limited precision, reports unreachable pairs as 4294967.295, and fails with a cryptic dtype error on an unknown node ID. It is maintained: version 0.8 came out in August 2026. igraph would have been one more compiled dependency for a middle speed.

Decision. Every algorithm uses scipy by default. backend="pandana" is available where it helps, through the giga-spatial[pandana] extra. The backend gives pandana node positions rather than IDs, so it works on any network, including one whose IDs mix OpenStreetMap's integers with the text IDs of inserted schools, and it returns inf for unreachable pairs. to_pandana(), for pandana's own functions, keeps node IDs and so still needs them all integers or all text. My first version passed IDs to pandana in both cases, which ruled out the backend on exactly the networks people build; writing the concept note's examples showed it. networkx is only an export. I did not add igraph.

How the algorithms use scipy, on the current code:

Operation, simplified Rwanda Time shortest_path_lengths, 100 by 1,000, scipy 2.58 s the same with pandana, after a 1.43 s build 0.24 s reachable, 100 origins, 5 km 0.080 s nearest_by_network, 10,000 origins to 100 targets 0.046 s count_within, 1,000 origins, 100 targets, 5 km 0.039 s minimum_spanning_tree 0.069 s

The searches are fast because they avoid computing a full matrix. reachable stops Dijkstra at the distance limit. nearest_by_network with one target per origin runs a single multi-source Dijkstra from all the targets, on the reversed graph when the network is directed. count_within runs from whichever side is smaller. Dijkstra runs in blocks of at most 256 MiB of distances, and shortest_path_lengths refuses result matrices over 1 GiB, with advice to batch.

Consequences and limits. scipy's cost grows with the number of origins (about 25 ms per origin on Rwanda), and pandana's with the number of pairs. pandana's 1.43 s build costs as much as about 55 origins of scipy work; below that, scipy is faster end to end. scipy's minimum spanning tree ignores zero-weight edges, so zero weights are replaced by the smallest positive float for that call only.

docs.title: Decision 6: our own simplification
docs.text:
Question. osmnx's simplify_graph removes nodes that only continue a road. Should the library call it, or implement the same rule on tables?

Options. Convert to networkx and call osmnx; or implement it on the tables.

Evidence. On unsimplified Rwanda (reduction.py simplify, current code):

Time Nodes Edges Total length ox.simplify_graph 147.5 s 125,058 332,535 106,220,098.3 m SpatialNetwork.simplify 7.1 s 125,058 332,535 106,220,098.3 m

The two give the same nodes and the same edge lengths, 21 times faster. The first run, on 27 October, measured 9.1 s against 197 s.

Decision. simplify uses osmnx's rule for which nodes can go, and never walks a chain of edges in Python. Each edge into a removable node is linked to the edge that continues it; chains are ranked by pointer jumping; attributes are aggregated per chain with numpy's reduceat. Joined edges get the sum of their lengths (and of the weight column), one geometry, text joined with ; where it differs, osmid lists concatenated, oneway true only if every part is one-way, reversed true if any part is, the length-weighted mean of other numbers, and the kind of their longest part.

Consequences and limits. I made two deliberate differences from osmnx. osmnx also removes the nodes between two duplicated parallel ways and drops one of the ways; simplify keeps them, so no road is lost. osmnx deletes rings with no junction at all; simplify keeps one node of the ring. Neither case occurs in Rwanda's roads, which is why the results above are identical. Nodes of kind point and split, and nodes passed in keep, are never removed, so simplify can run after points are inserted.

docs.title: Decision 7: connecting subnetworks with Mehlhorn's Steiner approximation
docs.text:
Question. Fibre planning needs the roads that connect a set of points, such as schools, at the smallest total length. That is the Steiner tree problem, which is NP-hard. How should the library approximate it, and what else should it offer?

Options. networkx's steiner_tree, after a conversion to networkx; Kou's algorithm, which needs the shortest-path distance between every pair of terminals; Mehlhorn's algorithm, which needs one multi-source Dijkstra; and the old Giga approach, which kept the shortest path between every pair of points (create_cleaned_graph).

Evidence. On simplified Rwanda (reduction.py subnetwork, current code):
