Method Time Result Steiner tree, 100 terminals 0.108 s 1,537 km Steiner tree, 1,000 terminals 0.178 s 4,070 km Each of 1,000 terminals to its nearest of 20 sources 0.178 s 5,802 km Shortest paths between all pairs, 50 terminals and 20 sources 1.54 s 6,453 km

The test suite checks that our tree on the Kigali fixture is no longer than the shorter of networkx's Mehlhorn and Kou trees.

Decision. connecting_subnetwork works on the undirected network and offers three methods:

  • method="steiner" (the default) is Mehlhorn's 2-approximation. One multi-source Dijkstra from the terminals gives each node its nearest terminal. Every edge between two terminals' regions is a candidate link between those terminals, and an MST over the cheapest links, expanded back into road paths, gives a tree. A second MST and pruning of leaves that are not terminals finish it. Its length is at most twice the optimum, and in practice close to it.
  • With sources=, each terminal takes its shortest path to its nearest source. This is the right model when every school must reach some fibre node, and the cost is one multi-source Dijkstra.
  • method="all_pairs" keeps the shortest path between every terminal and every terminal or source, as the old code did. Its cost grows with the square of the number of terminals, which is why it is not the default.

The result is contracted to the terminals, the sources, and the branching nodes, with lengths added and geometries joined, using simplify(keep=...).

Consequences and limits. The Steiner tree is an approximation, not the optimum. It ignores one-way restrictions, which suits cables laid along roads. Terminals that cannot reach the others stay in the result without edges.

Later change. connecting_subnetwork became the network of ConnectionPlanner (Part 4). sources= became roots=; with roots, a plan is the rooted Steiner tree, in which a terminal may connect through another one, and each terminal's path to its nearest root is method="nearest_root". The default method became shortest_path (decision 25); Mehlhorn's tree is method="steiner".

docs.title: Decision 8: inserting points in one batch
docs.text:
Question. The old merge_points_to_graph joined schools to roads one at a time. How should insertion work at country scale?

Options. Keep the old algorithm; or insert all points in one batch.

Evidence. On simplified Rwanda (insertion.py; the old function was timed on 27 October 2026, one run each):

1,000 points 2,000 points 10,000 points Old merge_points_to_graph 291.7 s 542.8 s not run insert_points, current code 0.66 s 1.83 s

insert_points also builds a projected index of the road edges once per network, in 1.36 s. The old function compared each point with every earlier point and concatenated a table per point, so its cost grew with the square of the number of points. It fell back to scanning every edge when two points shared an edge, and projected and copied the whole graph twice.

Decision. insert_points does all points at once. One nearest-edge query in UTM finds each point's road; vectorised line_locate_point finds where along the road each point falls; points are grouped by edge and sorted by position; each affected road is split once, at all of its points; and the new nodes and edges are appended in one step. Python loops run only over affected edges. A point within snap_to_node metres (5 by default) of a road's end connects to that node instead of splitting the road. In a directed network, both directions of a two-way road are split at the same new nodes. chain=True reproduces the old rule that a point may connect to an already inserted point when that point is closer than any road; candidates come from a KD-tree on the points, querying more neighbours only for points that need them.

Consequences and limits. Points join roads only, never earlier connections. The 10,000-point time stays far below my 10 s target, so I did not optimise the per-edge loop further.

Writing the concept note's figures showed a bug in the first version. The two directions of a two-way road are split together, so each road row is mapped to its reverse twin, and a one-way road, which has none, was recorded with the twin -1. The remapping took -1 for a lower row and moved every point on a one-way road onto the edge table's last row: in the example, five schools across Kigali shared one split node, and the pieces took the geometry of a road 25 km away. Connection lengths were right, which is what the tests checked; the split nodes' positions and the pieces' geometries were not. The tests now check both, and the fix changed the timings above by less than their noise.

docs.title: Decision 9: normalising attributes
docs.text:
Question. osmnx attributes mix lists and single values in one column after simplification, and Parquet cannot store that (decision 4). What should those columns become?

Options. Stringify the lists, as GeoPackage does; keep Python objects, which cannot be saved; or normalise each column to one storable type.

Evidence. Stringified lists lose their types (an osmid list becomes the string "[123, 456]") and cannot be filtered or joined. Two library changes made this harder than it looked. pandas 3 reads text as its new str dtype rather than object, which my first version did not recognise as text. And Arrow list columns made pandas write metadata to the Parquet files that pandas could not read back, so the library writes the GeoParquet metadata itself and leaves out pandas' metadata. Normalising simplified Rwanda's osmnx attributes takes 0.52 s.

Decision. normalize_attributes gives every attribute column one type. osmid becomes a list of integers on every edge (an Arrow list column). Other list columns become lists of integers when they hold only integers, and ;-joined text otherwise, without repeats. oneway is true only if every value is, and reversed if any is. Text columns become categoricals. The fetcher and the handler normalise once, when they build a network, so saving does not repeat it.

Consequences and limits. A joined text value such as "primary;secondary" no longer says which part of the edge is which. That is the same information osmnx gives, as a string.

docs.title: Decision 10: fast conversion from networkx
docs.text:
Question. Converting osmnx graphs is how most existing work will enter the library. How fast can it be?

Evidence. On unsimplified Rwanda (core.py convert), my first from_networkx took 49 s. Reading networkx's adjacency dictionaries directly instead of its edge views, building attributes with DataFrame.from_records, and pausing Python's cyclic garbage collector during the conversion brought it to 14.5 s, and to between 12.9 and 14.6 s in the latest runs. The garbage collector was the largest part: the millions of small objects created during a conversion kept triggering collections over everything already alive. On simplified Rwanda, from_networkx takes 0.85 s, against 4.0 s for osmnx's own graph_to_gdfs, and to_networkx 1.35 s.

Decision. Both conversions pause the garbage collector for their duration and restore it afterwards, including when they fail. They create no reference cycles, so nothing is left for the collector.

docs.title: Decision 11: osmnx and Overpass for small areas
docs.text:
Question. How should users get the roads around a set of schools, a district, or a city?

Options. osmnx's graph_from_polygon over the Overpass API; our own Overpass client, like OSMLocationFetcher's; or a Geofabrik extract even for small areas.

Evidence. osmnx is the reference most people working with OSM roads already know, and it is maintained. Its network types, one-way rules, and simplification define what "the road network" means in most published work. Downloading a whole country's extract (Rwanda is 65 MiB, Nigeria 680 MiB) to get one district is wasteful. I did not time Overpass: it is a shared public service whose speed depends on its load, and osmnx caches its responses.

Decision. OSMRoadsFetcher turns a source into an area and calls graph_from_polygon:

  • a country becomes its boundary, a geometry is used as given, and a frame of polygons becomes their union;
  • points and lines become their convex hull (area="hull"), bounding box ("bbox"), or buffers ("buffers"), widened by buffer metres in UTM, never in degrees;
  • query_area(source) shows the area before anything is downloaded.

Failed requests are retried with growing pauses, and the last error names the Overpass server and suggests a mirror. A query that finds no roads raises ValueError and is not retried. Areas above 50,000 km² log a warning that points to the handler. The osmnx settings for the server and timeout are set for the call and restored afterwards.

Consequences and limits. The fetcher needs the internet and Overpass's goodwill. osmnx splits areas over 2,500 km² into several queries, and a country can take hours, which is why decision 12 exists. On Python 3.10 pip resolves osmnx 2.0, and on 3.11 and later 2.1, so the fetcher uses only what both provide.

docs.title: Decision 12: Geofabrik's extracts for countries
docs.text:
Question. How should users get a whole country's roads?

Options. Overpass through osmnx, with the area split into parts; or Geofabrik's daily .osm.pbf extracts, one file per country or region.

Evidence. A country through Overpass can take hours and run into its fair-use limits. Even with the data in hand, osmnx's route is slow: building simplified Rwanda from the extract through OSM XML and graph_from_xml took 300 s (step0.py, 27 October 2026), and its unsimplified networkx graph held about 2.3 GB. Geofabrik updates every extract daily and keeps the files for download.

Decision. A separate handler, OSMRoadsHandler, downloads extracts, stores them, and builds the network from them. It is a handler rather than a fetcher option because an extract is a file kept in a data store and reused, which is what our handlers do.

Consequences and limits. A small area inside a large country still needs the whole country's file. The fetcher stays the better tool for small areas, and the guide says so.

docs.title: Decision 13: choosing extracts by polygon
docs.text:
Question. Which extracts does a source need?

Options. Look countries up by ISO code; or choose by the extracts' polygons, from Geofabrik's index.

Evidence. Geofabrik's index (index-v1.json, 554 extracts) gives each extract a polygon, and ISO codes for 191 of them. The codes are not reliable enough to rely on alone. French Polynesia, Wallis and Futuna, Tokelau, American Oceania, and Clipperton carry Vanuatu's code, and Pitcairn carries the Marshall Islands'. Twelve extracts hold several countries, such as israel-and-palestine and malaysia-singapore-brunei, and several of them carry one country's code or none. About 36 countries, among them Saudi Arabia, Singapore, and Brunei, exist only inside such larger extracts.

Decision. Extracts are chosen by polygon (ADR 0007):

  • A country's ISO code is a fast path: if exactly one extract carries only that code and is not on a curated list of multi-country extracts, it is the country's own file.
  • A country without one is covered through its boundary.
  • Any other source gets the smallest extracts that together cover its area: touching extracts are taken from the smallest up while part of the area is uncovered, then any extract the others already cover is dropped.
  • regions=True uses a country's regional extracts. Continents are used only when named in extracts=.

The curated lists, of multi-country extracts and of corrected codes, are tested against a stored copy of the whole index: every extract with several codes must be on the list, and no country may end up with two files of its own.

Consequences and limits. The curated lists need checking when Geofabrik changes its index. The test runs against the stored copy, so it catches mistakes in our lists but not changes on Geofabrik's side; refreshing the stored copy reveals those.

docs.title: Decision 14: storing extracts by date
docs.text:
Question. How should extracts be stored and kept up to date?

Options. Country folders with dates below them; or date folders with Geofabrik's own folders below them. Always download the latest file; or reuse what is stored.

Evidence. Geofabrik keeps daily files for about a week, then the files of the 1st of each month and of 1 January. A dated snapshot is what users keep, compare, or delete together, so the date is the first thing they need to see. -latest URLs redirect to the dated file (such as rwanda-261028.osm.pbf), except for large extracts like Germany's, which redirect to a mirror under the -latest name. For those, the date comes from the extract's replication state file. The date in a file's name is the UTC date of the replication timestamp in its header, which can be read from the file's first 64 KiB.

Decision. Extracts are stored as osm/geofabrik/<date>/<Geofabrik path>.osm.pbf, with each network saved beside its extract and always covering the whole extract (ADR 0006). The newest stored date is used without contacting Geofabrik. refresh=True uses Geofabrik's latest, max_age_days does when the stored file is older, and date= pins a date. Downloads are checked against Geofabrik's .md5 files while they stream, so a multi-gigabyte file on a remote data store is never read back to check it. A file that fails the check is removed.

Consequences and limits. Old dates are never deleted automatically, and extracts take space (Brazil is 2.0 GiB). Reproducing an old result needs its stored extract, since Geofabrik deletes daily files after a week.

docs.title: Decision 15: building the network with pyosmium and numpy
docs.text:
Question. How should the handler turn an extract into the same network osmnx would build?

Options. osmnx's graph_from_xml, after converting the extract to OSM XML; pyrosm; quackosm; or pyosmium to read the file, with our own code reproducing osmnx's rules.

Evidence. The osmnx route took 300 s for simplified Rwanda: 22.5 s to filter the extract and write 314 MB of XML, and the rest in osmnx. pyrosm needs Python 3.11 or newer, and the library supports 3.10. quackosm converts extracts to GeoParquet features through DuckDB, a heavier dependency, and the network would still have to be built from those features. pyosmium is a thin layer over the C++ library libosmium, with wheels for Python 3.10 to 3.14 on macOS, Linux, and Windows. I only checked pyrosm's and quackosm's versions and wheels; I did not time them.

How to read the file, on Rwanda's extract (read_strategies.py, one process each):

Strategy Time Peak memory Read the ways, then read only their nodes through an ID filter 12.2 s 2,351 MB Read the ways, then read them again with pyosmium's node location index 7.5 s 1,047 MB Read once with the location index 7.3 s 1,042 MB

Most of the cost of the first strategy is Python handling 3.8 million node objects. With the location index, pyosmium keeps every node's coordinates while it reads, and writes each way's line as WKB in C++, so Python touches each way but no node.

Decision. build_road_network reads the extract once with the location index. For each way that passes osmnx's filter for the network type, it keeps the way's ID, node references, and osmnx's kept tags, and has pyosmium write its line. The rest is numpy: drop consecutive repeated nodes, reverse ways that run against their node order, cut ways into edges, number parallel edges as networkx does, measure lengths, and count streets per node. osmnx's rules are reproduced exactly: the network-type filters, including the fact that Overpass's !~ patterns are unanchored (so walk's exclusion of motor also excludes motorway), the one-way values including -1, T, and F, the kept tags, and street_count.

I measured two reads first and expected one read to be faster. It is not, by much: the location index is what saves the time. I kept one read because it is simpler, with the filter, the tags, and the line coming from the same way, and because it reads the file once.

The result on Rwanda's extract, current code:

Network Nodes Edges Time drive_service, raw 2,270,376 4,615,754 8.4 s drive_service, simplified 129,073 338,550 13.5 s (fresh process, 2.5 GB peak) walk, raw 3,799,166 7,770,848 13.7 s walk, simplified 262,964 698,444 24.4 s

That is 22 times faster than the osmnx route, and both network types are under my 30 s target. walk is the largest of osmnx's presets except all, which I did not time.

Consequences and limits. The library now owns osmnx's rules, so a change in osmnx would not reach it automatically. Decision 18 describes the tests that guard them. When the builder's output changes, BUILD_VERSION in pbf.py must be raised so stored networks are built again.

docs.title: Decision 16: the node location index
docs.text:
Question. Which of pyosmium's location indexes should the build use?

Evidence. Dense indexes reserve space for every possible node ID; with OSM's 64-bit IDs that is about 115 GB even for Rwanda. The in-memory flex_mem index takes about 16 bytes per node in the file, so about 2 GB for Nigeria. On Rwanda, on this laptop's SSD:

Index Time Peak memory flex_mem, in memory 7.3 s 1,042 MB sparse_file_array, on disk 7.2 s 846 MB sparse_mem_array, in memory 7.3 s 1,025 MB

Decision. flex_mem up to 1 GiB of extract, and the disk-backed sparse_file_array above it, in a temporary file. node_index= chooses another, and dense indexes are refused.

Consequences and limits. The disk index was as fast as memory and lighter on Rwanda, so the threshold is not about speed on a machine like this one. I kept flex_mem as the default for smaller extracts because it needs no temporary disk space. Whether the disk index should be the default everywhere is an open question; it has not been measured on large extracts or slow disks.

docs.title: Decision 17: cropping in osmnx's order, and combining extracts as one file
docs.text:
Question. A stored network covers a whole extract. How should it be cut to a source, so that the result equals what the fetcher would return for the same area?

Options. Clip the stored simplified network, which is small and fast; clip the raw network to the area and simplify afterwards; or replay osmnx's graph_from_polygon step by step. For several extracts: SpatialNetwork.concat, or a combination that treats them as one file.

Evidence. osmnx 2.0.2's graph_from_polygon downloads the area widened by 500 m, keeps the largest connected part of that, simplifies it, and only then keeps the nodes inside the area itself and the largest part again. It counts streets on the simplified widened network. Simplifying the widened area first means a road that leaves the area ends where its simplified edge ends, at a real junction outside, and is dropped with that edge.

I first implemented the second option, believing it was osmnx's order, and tested it against my own replay of that order. Writing the concept note's examples showed the mistake: for central Kigali (a 2 by 2 km box), the handler returned 513 nodes and the fetcher 478, from identical raw data (2,824 nodes and 5,117 edges in both). Clipping the raw network first kept the stubs of roads that leave the area. Replaying osmnx's steps on the stored extract gives the fetcher's network exactly: the same 478 nodes and 1,074 edges. The handler now does that, and the tests replay osmnx's steps (decision 18).

For extracts, neighbouring files share the ways that cross between them, with the same IDs, but each numbers parallel edges in its own way order. concat keeps one edge per (u, v, key), so depending on which extract came first it can keep a duplicate and drop a different way.

Loading times on Rwanda, from stored networks (load_rwanda.py, current code):

Load Time Four school points with a 2 km buffer 1.43 s A 30 by 22 km box around Kigali 1.85 s The whole country 0.44 s The first load of a source, which builds and saves the raw network 11.1 s

Decision. A cropped load replays graph_from_polygon: it clips each extract's raw network to the source's area widened by 500 m, combines several extracts with combine_road_networks, keeps the largest connected part, simplifies, clips to the area itself, keeps the largest part again, and sets street_count as counted on the simplified widened network. retain_all and truncate_by_edge apply at the same steps as in osmnx. The combination keeps a way's edges once and numbers parallel edges again in way order. A country whose extracts are its own file or its regions is not cropped at all.

Consequences and limits. A cropped load reads the raw network, 4.6 million edges for Rwanda, and simplifies the widened area, which together cost 1.4 to 1.9 s for a city-sized area; the first version took about 1 s, for a wrong result. street_count near the edge of the widened area counts only the streets inside it, as osmnx's does.

docs.title: Decision 18: how equivalence with osmnx is tested
docs.text:
Question. The handler claims to return osmnx's network. How is that checked?

Decision. The test suite compares against osmnx itself wherever it can:

  • osmnx's networks for a small Kigali extract, built once through graph_from_xml and stored as fixtures, for drive_service raw and simplified, drive, walk, and all. Nodes, street_count, node tags, edges by (u, v, key), way IDs, oneway, reversed, kept tags, and simplified geometries must all match. Raw lengths must be bit-identical.
  • The filter presets against osmnx's own filter strings.
  • A small made-up extract with every one-way case, repeated nodes, parallel ways, and node tags, against graph_from_xml, for a one-way and a two-way network type.
  • Cropped loads against osmnx's graph_from_polygon, replayed with osmnx's own functions after the download (projection, 500 m buffer, truncate_graph_polygon, largest_component, simplify_graph, count_streets_per_node), with and without truncate_by_edge, raw and simplified, and with retain_all.
  • Kigali split in two at a meridian and stored as two extracts, combined in either order, against the whole.
  • A live test (pytest -m live) that loads central Kigali through the handler and through the fetcher, and requires them to share at least 98% of their nodes, allowing for edits made to OpenStreetMap since the extract's date.

The tests that need osmnx run on Python 3.10, where it is installed, and are skipped elsewhere. One cross-check needs no test: the handler's whole-country load of Rwanda, which keeps the largest connected part, has 125,058 nodes and 332,535 edges, exactly the simplified network osmnx built from the same extract.

The lesson of decision 17 is in the third point: a test that replays my understanding of osmnx can only confirm that understanding. Replaying osmnx's own code, and comparing with the fetcher live, is what catches a wrong understanding.

docs.title: Part 4: ConnectionPlanner
docs.text: The benchmarks of this part are in benchmarks/connection_planning/, with their results in results.md beside them, and ran on Python 3.14 on 30 October 2026. Rwanda is the simplified network above, with 20 random roots. The design is in the connection planning design, and the reasons for a planner object in ADR 0008.

docs.title: Decision 19: connecting points to an existing network is a rooted Steiner tree
docs.text:
Question. A fibre planner's real question is not which roads join the schools to each other, but how to connect every school to the existing fibre at the smallest shared cost, where a school may connect through another school and a trench used by several schools is paid once. Is that a known problem, and how should the library solve it?

Options. Each school's shortest path to its nearest fibre node, which connecting_subnetwork(sources=...) did; one unrooted Steiner tree over the schools and the fibre nodes; a rooted Steiner tree, with every fibre node joined to one virtual root at cost 0; and an exact solver.

Evidence. On the concept note's example, 197 schools and 5 fibre nodes in Kigali: the nearest fibre node for each school took 355 km, one tree over schools and fibre nodes 265 km, and the rooted tree 258 km, in 0.19 s. On Rwanda with 1,000 terminals, the rooted tree took 4,037 km against 5,802 km for the nearest roots, in 0.19 s.

Decision. Joining every root to a virtual root makes the problem the Steiner tree problem in graphs, over the terminals and that root. Removing the root leaves a forest whose every tree reaches the existing network. ConnectionPlanner holds the problem (network, terminals, roots, weight, bridges) and its solvers, and returns a ConnectionPlan with the contracted network, the chosen edges, the cost, and each terminal's status, root, and distance along the plan. connecting_subnetwork stays as the planner's network. The existing network's nodes are called roots, since "source" already means the place a dataset is requested for.

Consequences and limits. The problem is NP-hard, so the planner returns approximations and a lower bound (decisions 22 and 23). Directions are ignored, and the cost is per edge used, not per cable: a cost that grows with the number of schools behind an edge makes it fixed-charge network design, which is out of scope.

docs.title: Decision 20: bridges between parts of the network
docs.text:
Question. A clipped network, or one loaded with retain_all=True, has parts that no road joins, and schools there cannot be connected. How can a plan cross such gaps, by microwave or a planned road?

Options. Join the parts beforehand with connect_components, which adds one spanning tree of links whatever they cost; or offer the planner candidate links at a cost per metre, and let it use one only where it is cheaper than the roads.

Evidence. On Rwanda cut in two along longitude 30°E (23 parts, the two largest of 70,000 and 55,000 nodes), with all roots in the west, 416 of 1,000 schools could be connected without bridges. With bridges at 10 per metre all 1,000 were, using 2 links of 961 m; at 1,000 per metre, 1 link of 35 m. Finding the 50 candidates took 0.1 s, and the whole plan 0.34 s.

Decision. bridge_cost offers each part straight-line links to its 5 nearest other parts within bridge_max_distance. A part with more than 2,000 nodes, or most of the network, gets its own KD-tree, queried with every node outside it, which gives its closest pair to every other part exactly; smaller parts query a KD-tree of all nodes with their nodes' nearest neighbours, more of them while none lies outside the part. Bridges join the planner's sparse graph as extra entries, not a new network, keep their great-circle length, and count at their cost.

Consequences and limits. For two small parts, the search stops at the first outside neighbour, so a small part can miss one of its 5 nearest; the tests check that every part gets its nearest, and the largest its 5 nearest.

docs.title: Decision 21: the rollout order by a pruned Dijkstra
docs.text:
Question. Takahashi and Matsuyama's heuristic connects the terminal nearest to everything connected so far, one at a time, which is also a model of a phased rollout: each school gets an order and a marginal cost. Run naively, it is one Dijkstra per terminal. How can it run at country scale?

Options. The naive version; scipy's Dijkstra from each new path, limited to the largest distance of a waiting terminal; a version that recomputes only when the nearest terminal's distance changed; and a Dijkstra from each new path that stops wherever a distance does not fall, written in Python.

Evidence. On Rwanda:

Terminals Naive scipy, limited Python, pruned 100 1.6 s 0.6 s 0.4 s 1,000 19.5 s 5.4 s 1.1 s 10,000 not run 58 s 4.4 s

A few remote terminals keep scipy's limit at tens of kilometres, so each update searched about 40,000 nodes: 455 million in the 10,000-terminal run, against 6.2 million nodes updated by the pruned search.

Decision. The pruned search in Python. Ties go to the terminal listed first, since node IDs may mix integers and text. The version that recomputes only when the nearest terminal's distance changed is not valid: stale distances are upper bounds, so the top of a heap of them need not be the nearest terminal.

Consequences and limits. It is the slowest method, 5 to 20 times slower than Mehlhorn's, but still seconds at country scale. The tests check it, order for order, against the naive version.

docs.title: Decision 22: local search with two moves, the second kept local
docs.text:
Question. Both heuristics are 2-approximations, and in practice a few percent above the optimum. How can a plan be shortened, without risk of making it worse?

Options. Uchoa and Werneck's moves: key-path exchange (replace a path between key vertices by the cheapest path between the two parts it joins), key-vertex elimination (remove a branching node and reconnect the parts by their cheapest links), and key-vertex insertion; and an exact solver.

Evidence. On Rwanda with 1,000 terminals, the first version of key-vertex elimination searched for links from every node left in the plan, 20 ms per vertex, and stopped at a 60 s limit after four passes. Searching only from the parts' nodes within the removed weight of the removed nodes gave plans within 0.01% of it on Kigali, in half the time. With it:

First method Plan Improved Saved Longest pass steiner 3,942 km 3,755 km 4.7% 5.8 s shortest_path 3,845 km 3,759 km 2.2% 5.8 s nearest_root 5,510 km 3,759 km 31.8% 9.4 s

Decision. improve() applies key-path exchange and the local key-vertex elimination until neither saves anything or time_limit passes; a move must save a billionth of the weight it replaces. Key paths are listed once per pass, and a path whose end an earlier move left only continuing it is extended to the next key vertex first. Key-vertex insertion is deferred.

Consequences and limits. All three first methods end within 0.1% of each other, so after improve() the first method matters little. On Kigali's roads improved plans were within 0.86% of the optimum (decision 24); on SteinLib's dense random graphs they were up to 9% above it, where insertion would help.

docs.title: Decision 23: the lower bound by Wong's dual ascent, following Wong's rule
docs.text:
Question. Without the optimum, a plan cannot say how good it is. How can every plan state how far above the optimum it can be at most?

Options. The linear relaxation of a Steiner tree model, solved by an LP solver; and Wong's dual ascent on the directed form of the network, which approximates the directed cut relaxation from below with only shortest-path-like searches. For the dual ascent, which terminal grows next decides the bound: one whole turn per terminal until it reaches the root, nearest first, or Wong's rule, one step at a time for the terminal whose region has the fewest entering arcs.

Evidence. The first version gave whole turns, nearest the root first at the current reduced costs. It was valid, but against SteinLib's proven optima it was on average 7.0% below the optimum on set B and 9.7% on set C, at worst 45%. Wong's rule was 0.05% and 0.42% below, at worst 3.1%. On Rwanda the improved plans' gaps fell from 5.5%, 10.9%, and 12.0% to 2.1%, 1.4%, and 0.6%, for 100, 1,000, and 10,000 terminals. Recomputing each region every step took 41 s for 100 terminals on Rwanda; keeping them between steps gave the same bounds in 1.7 s, and 40.5 s for 10,000.

Decision. lower_bound() follows Wong's rule. Each terminal keeps its region and its entering arcs between steps, since reduced costs only fall and regions only grow, and a step checks only those arcs. The planner keeps a complete bound; one stopped by time_limit is still valid, only looser.

Consequences and limits. A plan's gap is an upper limit on its distance from the optimum. On Kigali the bound was 0.07 to 1.1% below the optimum, so most of the gap there is real.

docs.title: Decision 24: validation without SCIP-Jack
docs.text:
Question. The design planned to validate the planner against SCIP-Jack, an exact Steiner tree solver, whose source code must now be requested from its developers. How else can the heuristics and the bound be checked against exact optima?

Options. SteinLib's test sets with their proven optima; an exact model in scipy's milp (HiGHS); and the planner's own bound alone.

Evidence. SteinLib's sets B, C, D, and E (78 random sparse graphs of 50 to 2,500 nodes): improved plans were on average 0.4 to 2.2% above the optimum, at worst 9%; the bound 0.05 to 0.42% below it, at worst 4.4%. On Kigali's roads with 30 and 60 terminals and 3 roots (10 instances), the multi-commodity flow model solved each instance in 4 to 110 s: improved plans were 0.00 to 0.86% above the optimum, and the bound 0.07 to 1.1% below. The weaker single-commodity flow model did not solve one in 600 s.

Decision. steinlib.py scores every method and the bound on SteinLib, and exact.py on Kigali against HiGHS; both run only in the benchmarks, so neither SteinLib nor an exact model is a dependency. exact.py writes its instances, and Rwanda's, in SteinLib's STP format, so SCIP-Jack can be added as a column when its code arrives.

Consequences and limits. HiGHS cannot solve Rwanda-scale instances, so there the bound alone gives the gap. SteinLib's graphs are random, not roads.

docs.title: Decision 25: the default method
docs.text:
Question. Which method should plan() and connecting_subnetwork() use by default?

Options. steiner, Mehlhorn's algorithm, the fastest; and shortest_path, Takahashi and Matsuyama's.

Evidence. Without improve(), shortest_path was 0.65 to 5.9% above the optimum on Kigali and steiner 3.0 to 8.8%; on SteinLib 2.6 to 4.7% and 3.4 to 9.9% on average. On Rwanda, shortest_path took 1.1 s for 1,000 terminals and 4.4 s for 10,000, against 0.2 s.

Decision. shortest_path: about twice as close to the optimum out of the box, still seconds at country scale, and its order and marginal costs come with it. steiner stays one argument away for very large inputs, and improve() brings either within about 1% of the optimum on roads.

docs.title: Known limits and open questions
docs.text:
Differences from osmnx:

  • simplify keeps the nodes between duplicated parallel ways and one node of a ring without junctions, where osmnx removes them (decision 6).
  • pandana's distances can differ from scipy's by up to about 0.5 m on Rwanda (decision 5).
  • An uncropped load counts streets on the whole extract, where graph_from_xml sets no street_count at all; this follows graph_from_polygon, which counts them.

Untested or unmeasured:

  • Memory for a large country. Rwanda's simplified drive_service build peaks at 2.5 GB; I have not built Nigeria (680 MiB) or larger extracts, so the 16 GB target for Nigeria is an estimate.
  • Remote data stores. Loading and building through Azure Blob Storage or another remote store is tested for correctness but not timed.
  • pyrosm and quackosm were compared by their requirements, not timed.
  • Every benchmark ran on one laptop with a fast SSD.

Open questions:

  • Whether the disk-backed node index should be the default for every extract size (decision 16).
  • walk is the slowest network type at 24 s for Rwanda, most of it in simplify. A larger country will take proportionally longer.
  • How far the planner's plans are from the optimum at country scale: HiGHS solved Kigali-size instances exactly, but on Rwanda only the bound measures the gap (decision 24). SCIP-Jack would give exact optima there.
  • On dense random graphs, improved plans were up to 9% above the optimum (decision 22); key-vertex insertion is the next move to add if real data shows such gaps.
  • SpatialNetwork.concat keeps one edge per (u, v, key). That is right for networks that share no ways, but OSM networks from overlapping areas should be combined like extracts are, and concat does not yet do that for networks from the fetcher.

Deferred from the designs: isochrone polygons, centrality measures, and travel speeds; prize-collecting and capacitated connection plans, separate root networks, and a cost per cable; one entry point that chooses the fetcher or the handler by the size of the area; and dropping Python 3.10, which reached its end of life this month and is a decision for the whole library.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Install the package, run the tutorial on one country, see which datasets are built in, and set your data directory or API keys.

  • InstallationInstall giga-spatial and optional extras such as roads, gee, bq, azure, and snowflake.

  • TutorialBuild H3 cells for Rwanda and attach WorldPop population to each cell.

  • DatasetsHandlers, fetchers, sources, cropping, and the full table of built-in datasets.

  • ConfigurationSet the local data directory, remote data stores, and API keys.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Paths and credentials come from the environment, or from a .env file in the project root.

docs.title: Data directory
docs.text:
Variable Default What it holds ROOT_DATA_DIR . The directory the others sit under BRONZE_DIR bronze Files a handler has downloaded SILVER_DIR silver Files you have processed GOLD_DIR gold Results you keep CACHE_DIR cache Temporary files

A handler builds its own folder under BRONZE_DIR. With ROOT_DATA_DIR=/data, WorldPop files land in /data/bronze/worldpop.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
Set these only for the datasets you use. WorldPop, GHSL, OpenStreetMap, and Ookla do not need a key for ordinary access.

Variable Used by MAPBOX_ACCESS_TOKEN Mapbox images MAXAR_API_KEY Maxar images EARTHDATA_USERNAME, EARTHDATA_PASSWORD NASA SRTM OPENCELLID_ACCESS_TOKEN OpenCellID HEALTHSITES_API_KEY Healthsites.io GEOREPO_API_KEY, GEOREPO_USER_EMAIL UNICEF GeoRepo boundaries GIGA_SCHOOL_LOCATION_API_KEY Giga school locations GIGA_SCHOOL_PROFILE_API_KEY Giga school profiles GIGA_SCHOOL_MEASUREMENTS_API_KEY Giga school connectivity measurements GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT, GOOGLE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT, GOOGLE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_KEY_PATH Google Earth Engine ADLS_CONNECTION_STRING, ADLS_CONTAINER_NAME Azure Data Lake

docs.title: Services
docs.text: Variable Default Used by OVERPASS_URL https://overpass-api.de/api/interpreter OpenStreetMap road networks. Set a mirror when the main server is down.

docs.title: Data stores
docs.text: LocalDataStore is the default. ADLSDataStore, SnowflakeDataStore, and DeltaSharingDataStore are the remote stores. Pass one as data_store= to a handler or a generator. They are documented in the API reference.

docs.title: Datasets
docs.text: A dataset is a named product the library can acquire, such as WorldPop population or Google Open Buildings.

docs.title: Handler
docs.text:
A handler is a dataset published as files. It keeps those files in a data store and loads them for a source.

A source is the place you load for, or an explicit list of stored files. A place is a country, a geometry, points, or a frame.

from gigaspatial import GHSLDataHandler

population = GHSLDataHandler(product="GHS_POP", year=2020, resolution=1000)
frame = population.load_into_dataframe("RWA")

The first call downloads the tiles that cover Rwanda. load_data and load_into_dataframe take the source as the first argument.

crop_to_source=True cuts the loaded data to that source. A path source is not cropped. A country source is not cropped when the dataset is already one file for that country. An unknown keyword raises TypeError.

frame = population.load_into_dataframe("RWA", crop_to_source=True)

docs.title: Built-in handlers
docs.text:
Every handler is importable from gigaspatial. See Handlers for method signatures and options.

Dataset Handler What it acquires WorldPop WPPopulationHandler Country population rasters, age and sex structures, school-age and under-18 population, and degree of urbanisation Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL) GHSLDataHandler Population (GHS_POP), built-up surface (GHS_BUILT_S), settlement model (GHS_SMOD), building height (GHS_BUILT_H), and building volume (GHS_BUILT_V) Google-Microsoft combined buildings GoogleMSBuildingsHandler Country and S2-partitioned building footprints from Google Open Buildings and Microsoft Global Buildings in GeoParquet Google Open Buildings GoogleOpenBuildingsHandler Building footprint polygons and points by S2 tile Microsoft Global Buildings MSBuildingsHandler Building footprint polygons by country and quadkey OpenStreetMap roads OSMRoadsHandler Country-scale road networks built from Geofabrik OpenStreetMap extracts, returned as a SpatialNetwork Meta Relative Wealth Index (RWI) RWIHandler Relative wealth index tiles per country from HDX Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX) HDXHandler Datasets and resources published on HDX Ookla Speedtest OoklaSpeedtestHandler Fixed and mobile network performance tiles OpenCellID OpenCellIDHandler Crowd-sourced cell tower locations by country NASA SRTM NasaSRTMHandler 30 m digital elevation model tiles Copernicus GloFAS GlofasHandler Global river flood hazard depth and water masks by return period WRI Aqueduct AqueductFloodHandler Coastal and riverine flood hazard rasters Administrative boundaries AdminBoundaries Country and subnational administrative boundary polygons

docs.title: Fetcher
docs.text:
A fetcher is a dataset served as a query, from an API or a database. It returns records, or a road network. It does not store the dataset as files.

from gigaspatial import OSMLocationFetcher

clinics = OSMLocationFetcher(country="RWA", location_types=["clinic"]).fetch_locations()

MLabFetcher queries M-Lab speed tests in BigQuery. OSMRoadsFetcher returns a road network instead of records; see Road networks.

docs.text:
Every fetcher is importable from gigaspatial. See Fetchers for method signatures.

Dataset Fetcher What it queries OpenStreetMap places OSMLocationFetcher Points of interest (schools, clinics, hospitals, amenities) from the Overpass API OpenStreetMap roads OSMRoadsFetcher Road networks from the Overpass API, returned as a SpatialNetwork Giga schools GigaSchoolLocationFetcher, GigaSchoolProfileFetcher, GigaSchoolMeasurementsFetcher, GigaCountriesFetcher School locations, profiles, connectivity measurements, and country metadata from the Giga API Healthsites.io HealthSitesFetcher Health facility locations and attributes Overture Maps OvertureAmenityFetcher Amenity places from Overture Maps UNICEF SDGs UnicefDataFetcher UNICEF indicator and SDG datasets M-Lab MLabFetcher NDT7 internet speed test records in BigQuery Google Earth Engine GEEProfiler Raster and vector collections in Google Earth Engine

docs.title: Data store
docs.text:
A data store is where a handler keeps its files. LocalDataStore is the default. It may also be remote (ADLSDataStore, SnowflakeDataStore, DeltaSharingDataStore). A client, such as BigQueryClient, queries a database and is not a data store.

Pass data_store= when you construct a handler or a generator to choose the store. Paths and credentials are in Configuration.

docs.title: Installation Guide
docs.text: This guide will walk you through the steps to install the gigaspatial package on your system. The package is compatible with Python 3.10 and above.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before installing gigaspatial, ensure you have Python installed on your system. You can check your Python version by running:

python --version

If Python is not installed, you can download it from the official Python website.

docs.title: Installing from PyPI
docs.text:
The easiest way to install gigaspatial is directly from PyPI using pip:

pip install giga-spatial

This will install the latest stable version of the package along with all its dependencies.

docs.title: Optional extras
docs.text:
Some datasets and tools need packages that most users don't. Install them with an extra, such as pip install "giga-spatial[roads]", or all of them with giga-spatial[all].

Extra Adds Used by roads osmnx, osmium (pyosmium) OSMRoadsFetcher and OSMRoadsHandler, for OpenStreetMap road networks pandana pandana SpatialNetwork.to_pandana and backend="pandana" gee earthengine-api, geemap Google Earth Engine bq google-cloud-bigquery and its auth packages BigQueryClient, MLabFetcher azure azure-storage-blob ADLSDataStore snowflake snowflake-connector-python SnowflakeDataStore delta delta-sharing DeltaSharingDataStore db SQLAlchemy, trino, dask DBConnection duckdb duckdb OvertureAmenityFetcher unicef unicefdata UnicefDataFetcher elevation itur Refractivity in gigaspatial.processing.elevation maxar OWSLib MaxarImageDownloader hdx hdx-python-api HDXHandler

docs.title: Installing from Source
docs.text:
If you need to install a specific version or want to contribute to the development, you can install from the source:

  1. Clone the Repository: 

    git clone https://github.com/unicef/giga-spatial.git
cd giga-spatial

  2. Install the Package: 

    pip install .

docs.title: Installing in Development Mode
docs.text:
If you plan to contribute to the package or modify the source code, you can install it in development mode. This allows you to make changes to the code without reinstalling the package:

pip install -e .

docs.title: Installing Dependencies
docs.text:
The package dependencies are automatically installed when you install gigaspatial. However, if you need to install them manually, you can use:

pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: Verifying the Installation
docs.text:
After installation, you can verify that the package is installed correctly by running:

python -c "import gigaspatial; print(gigaspatial.__version__)"

This should print the version of the installed package.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If you encounter any issues during installation, consider the following:

  • Ensure pip is up-to-date: 

    pip install --upgrade pip

  • Check for conflicting dependencies: If you have other Python packages installed that might conflict with gigaspatial, consider using a virtual environment.

  • Use a Virtual Environment: To avoid conflicts with other Python packages, you can create a virtual environment: 

    python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate  # On Windows, use `venv\Scripts\activate`
pip install giga-spatial  # or pip install . if installing from source

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
Once the installation is complete, you must configure your storage and API credentials before running complex analyses.

  1. Configuration Guide: Set up your .env file, storage backends (Local, ADLS, or Snowflake), and API keys.
  2. Quick Start Guide: Learn how to perform your first spatial query.

docs.title: Tutorial
docs.text:
This tutorial builds H3 cells for Rwanda and attaches WorldPop population to each cell. The result is a view.

The first run downloads the country's population raster into the data store. That can take a few minutes. Later runs read the stored files. WorldPop does not need an API key.

docs.title: Build the view
docs.text:
from gigaspatial import H3ViewGenerator

zones = H3ViewGenerator(source="RWA", resolution=6)
view = zones.map_wp_pop(country="RWA")
print(view.head())

source is the country the cells cover. resolution=6 is the H3 size: about 36 km² per cell. map_wp_pop loads the WorldPop raster for that country and sums it onto the cells. view is a table of cells with a population column and a geometry.

S2ViewGenerator and MercatorViewGenerator follow the same pattern: construct them with a country, then call map_wp_pop.

docs.title: What happened
docs.text:
A handler acquired the WorldPop files and stored them. The generator mapped that dataset onto zones. The view is those zones with population attached. That attachment is enrichment.

The next pages name those pieces, then show other uses:

  • Datasets: handlers, fetchers, and cropping to a source
  • Points and nearest buildings
  • Processing a raster or a table, when you want the files themselves rather than a view

docs.title: User guide
docs.text:
These guides assume you have run the tutorial.

  • Combining datasets for a country. WorldPop population, Google and Microsoft building footprints, and OpenStreetMap places on an H3 grid or as tables.
  • Points and nearest buildings. Your own points, Giga school locations, and country building footprints.
  • Population around points. Sum WorldPop inside a radius around schools, clinics, or other points.
  • OSM points of interest. A fetcher for OpenStreetMap points of interest.
  • Road networks. OSM roads around schools, routes, and the roads that connect them.
  • Processing a raster or a table.
  • Settlement. GHSL settlement class.
  • Infrastructure files. Partner files, not a published dataset.

docs.title: Combining datasets for a country
docs.text: This guide combines WorldPop population, Google and Microsoft building footprints, and OpenStreetMap places for a country in a few lines of Python. You can map all three onto an H3 hexagonal grid as a single view, or load each dataset directly as its own table.

docs.title: Map population, buildings, and OSM places onto H3 hexagons
docs.text:
H3ViewGenerator builds the H3 cells covering a country and attaches attributes from each dataset to the same view. The first run downloads the WorldPop raster and the Google-Microsoft building files into your data store.

from gigaspatial import H3ViewGenerator, OSMLocationFetcher

zones = H3ViewGenerator(source="RWA", resolution=6)
zones.map_wp_pop(country="RWA")
zones.map_buildings(country="RWA")

schools = OSMLocationFetcher(country="RWA", location_types=["school"]).fetch_locations()
zones.add_variable_to_view(zones.map_points(schools), "school_count")

view = zones.view
print(view[["zone_id", "population", "building_count", "school_count"]].head())

view is a GeoDataFrame with one row per H3 cell, its polygon geometry, the summed WorldPop population, the building_count from Google and Microsoft building footprints, and the OpenStreetMap school_count.

You can attach additional datasets to the same view before reading zones.view:

  • zones.map_rwi(country="RWA") attaches the mean Meta Relative Wealth Index (rwi)
  • zones.map_smod() attaches the GHSL settlement model class (smod_class)
  • zones.map_ghsl_pop() attaches GHSL population (ghsl_pop)

The same workflow applies to S2ViewGenerator, MercatorViewGenerator, and AdminBoundariesViewGenerator.

docs.title: Load each dataset directly for a country
docs.text:
When you want the datasets themselves as DataFrames or GeoDataFrames rather than aggregated onto zones, call each handler and fetcher directly with the country ISO3 code:

from gigaspatial import (
    GoogleMSBuildingsHandler,
    OSMLocationFetcher,
    WPPopulationHandler,
)

population = WPPopulationHandler(year=2020, resolution=1000).load_into_geodataframe("RWA")
buildings = GoogleMSBuildingsHandler().load_data("RWA")
schools = OSMLocationFetcher(country="RWA", location_types=["school"]).fetch_locations()
  • WPPopulationHandler.load_into_geodataframe("RWA") downloads the WorldPop raster for Rwanda into the data store and returns a GeoDataFrame of grid cells and population counts (load_into_dataframe returns a plain DataFrame with coordinates).
  • GoogleMSBuildingsHandler().load_data("RWA") downloads the combined Google Open Buildings and Microsoft Global Buildings GeoParquet files for Rwanda and returns a GeoDataFrame of building footprints.
  • OSMLocationFetcher(country="RWA", location_types=["school"]).fetch_locations() queries OpenStreetMap via the Overpass API and returns the matching places as a GeoDataFrame.

docs.title: Infrastructure files
docs.text:
Partner files, such as a KMZ of fibre nodes, are not a published dataset. This guide reads a file you already have and validates it as transmission nodes.

TransmissionNodeTable.from_file reads the file, cleans column names and coordinates, and validates each row. Cleaning is on by default.

from gigaspatial.core.schemas import TransmissionNodeTable

nodes = TransmissionNodeTable.from_file("partner_nodes.gpkg")
print(nodes.to_dataframe().head())

read_dataset is the same reader, without validation. Use it when you want the table as the partner sent it.

from gigaspatial import read_dataset

raw = read_dataset("partner_nodes.gpkg")

To clean a table you already loaded, use TransmissionNodeProcessor and then from_dataframe:

from gigaspatial.core.schemas import TransmissionNodeProcessor, TransmissionNodeTable

cleaned = TransmissionNodeProcessor().process(raw, country="RWA")
nodes = TransmissionNodeTable.from_dataframe(cleaned, clean=False)

The same pattern exists for the other partner tables in gigaspatial.core.schemas: WirelessSiteTable, WirelessAccessServiceTable, BuildingFootprintTable, MobileCoverageTable, and AdminBoundaryTable, each with its processor. A validated table can be passed to PoiViewGenerator as the points in Points and nearest buildings.

docs.title: OSM points of interest
docs.text:
OpenStreetMap points of interest, such as clinics, schools, and shops, come from a fetcher. OSMLocationFetcher queries the Overpass API and returns a table of records. It does not store the dataset as files. The public Overpass instance needs no API key.

from gigaspatial import OSMLocationFetcher

clinics = OSMLocationFetcher(
    country="RWA",
    location_types=["clinic", "hospital"],
).fetch_locations()
print(clinics.head())

location_types is a list of OSM values, or a dict of key to values such as {"amenity": ["clinic", "hospital"]}.

To limit the query to one admin area, pass admin_level and admin_value instead of relying on the whole country. A country-sized query can take several minutes.

fetch_locations_changed_between returns places edited in a date range. fetch_by_osmid loads particular OSM ids.

docs.title: Points and nearest buildings
docs.text:
This guide maps building footprints onto points you already have. The result is a table with the nearest building and the distance to it.

The points are (latitude, longitude) pairs. find_nearest_buildings downloads Microsoft and Google building files for the country on the first run.

from gigaspatial import PoiViewGenerator

points = [(-1.9441, 30.0619), (-1.9500, 30.1000)]
places = PoiViewGenerator(points)
nearest = places.find_nearest_buildings(country="RWA", search_radius=1000)
print(nearest.head())

search_radius is in meters. A point with no building inside that radius is still in the table, with no nearest building.

PoiViewGenerator also accepts a DataFrame or a GeoDataFrame. Set poi_id_column when the table already has an id column.

docs.title: Giga school locations
docs.text:
The same mapping works for schools from the Giga API. That call needs GIGA_SCHOOL_LOCATION_API_KEY. See Configuration.

from gigaspatial import GigaSchoolLocationFetcher, PoiViewGenerator

schools = GigaSchoolLocationFetcher(country="RWA").fetch_locations(process_geospatial=True)
nearest = PoiViewGenerator(schools).find_nearest_buildings(country="RWA", search_radius=1000)

fetch_locations is a fetcher: it returns records from the API and does not store a schools dataset. The building files are still acquired by a handler.

docs.title: Download and load building footprints for a country
docs.text:
When you want the building footprints themselves as a GeoDataFrame for a country or a geometry, call one of the three building handlers directly:

  • GoogleMSBuildingsHandler acquires the combined Google Open Buildings and Microsoft Global Buildings dataset in GeoParquet format.
  • GoogleOpenBuildingsHandler acquires Google Open Buildings polygons or points by S2 tile.
  • MSBuildingsHandler acquires Microsoft Global ML Building Footprints by country and quadkey.
from gigaspatial import (
    GoogleMSBuildingsHandler,
    GoogleOpenBuildingsHandler,
    MSBuildingsHandler,
)

combined = GoogleMSBuildingsHandler().load_data("RWA")
google_buildings = GoogleOpenBuildingsHandler().load_polygons("RWA")
ms_buildings = MSBuildingsHandler().load_data("RWA")

For large countries where you only need building coordinates, GoogleMSBuildingsHandler(partition_strategy="s2_grid").load_centroids("RWA") caches and returns a NumPy array of building centroids.

To count building footprints inside H3 hexagons for a country, use H3ViewGenerator.map_buildings:

from gigaspatial import H3ViewGenerator

zones = H3ViewGenerator(source="RWA", resolution=6)
view = zones.map_buildings(country="RWA")
print(view[["zone_id", "building_count"]].head())

docs.title: Population around points
docs.text:
The tutorial sums WorldPop onto H3 cells. This guide sums it inside a radius around each point, such as schools or clinics in a country. The result is a view: your points, with a population column.

from gigaspatial import PoiViewGenerator

points = [(-1.9441, 30.0619), (-1.9500, 30.1000)]
places = PoiViewGenerator(points)
view = places.map_wp_pop(country="RWA", map_radius_meters=1000)
print(view.head())

map_radius_meters is the buffer around each point in meters. The first run downloads the WorldPop raster for the country into the data store.

docs.title: Estimate how many people live near each school in a country
docs.text:
Pass a GeoDataFrame of schools or clinics directly to PoiViewGenerator to estimate the population living within a catchment radius of each place.

With schools or clinics from OpenStreetMap (no API key required):

from gigaspatial import OSMLocationFetcher, PoiViewGenerator

schools = OSMLocationFetcher(country="RWA", location_types=["school"]).fetch_locations()
view = PoiViewGenerator(schools).map_wp_pop(country="RWA", map_radius_meters=1000)
print(view[["population"]].head())

With school locations from the Giga API (requires GIGA_SCHOOL_LOCATION_API_KEY; see Configuration):

from gigaspatial import GigaSchoolLocationFetcher, PoiViewGenerator

schools = GigaSchoolLocationFetcher(country="RWA").fetch_locations(process_geospatial=True)
view = PoiViewGenerator(schools, poi_id_column="giga_id_school").map_wp_pop(
    country="RWA",
    map_radius_meters=1000,
)
print(view[["giga_id_school", "population"]].head())

For school-age or under-18 population, pass WorldPop options such as school_age=True or under_18=True to map_wp_pop. See Points and nearest buildings to also attach the nearest building footprint to each school.

docs.title: Processing a raster or a table
docs.text: The tutorial and the other guides stop at a view. This page uses the stored files and the vector helpers directly.

docs.title: A raster
docs.text:
GHSLDataHandler downloads the tiles that cover a country. load_into_dataframe turns those tiles into a table of pixel values. The first run downloads the files.

from gigaspatial import GHSLDataHandler

population = GHSLDataHandler(product="GHS_POP", year=2020, resolution=1000)
frame = population.load_into_dataframe("RWA")
print(frame.head())

For a file you already have, TifProcessor reads it, clips it, and samples it.

from gigaspatial import TifProcessor

raster = TifProcessor("bronze/ghsl/your-file.tif")
print(raster.get_raster_info())
pixels = raster.to_dataframe()

clip_to_geometry cuts the raster to a Shapely geometry. sample_by_coordinates reads values at points. to_geodataframe returns the pixels as polygons.

docs.title: A table
docs.text:
These helpers take a DataFrame or a GeoDataFrame:

  • convert_to_geodataframe builds a GeoDataFrame from coordinate columns
  • buffer_geodataframe buffers geometries in meters
  • aggregate_points_to_zones and aggregate_polygons_to_zones summarize features onto zones
  • calculate_distance returns the distance between two latitude/longitude pairs
  • map_points_within_polygons finds which polygon contains each point
import pandas as pd
from gigaspatial import convert_to_geodataframe, buffer_geodataframe

points = pd.DataFrame({"latitude": [-1.9441], "longitude": [30.0619]})
places = convert_to_geodataframe(points)
buffered = buffer_geodataframe(places, buffer_distance_meters=500)

buffer_distance_meters is the argument name on buffer_geodataframe. Check the processing reference if you call the others.

docs.title: Road networks
docs.text:
This guide fetches the OpenStreetMap roads around a set of schools, joins the schools to the roads, and finds the roads that connect them to a fiber node. The road network is a SpatialNetwork: two tables, one of nodes and one of edges, with lengths in meters.

OSMRoadsFetcher is a fetcher. It queries the Overpass API through osmnx and returns the network; it does not save it. You save the network yourself, into any data store. For whole countries and regions, OSMRoadsHandler builds the same network from Geofabrik's extracts instead (see Whole countries). Install the roads extra first:

pip install "giga-spatial[roads]"

docs.title: Fetch the roads
docs.text:
import pandas as pd
from gigaspatial import OSMRoadsFetcher

schools = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "giga_id": ["school-1", "school-2", "school-3"],
        "lat": [-1.9441, -1.9536, -1.9580],
        "lon": [30.0619, 30.0588, 30.0750],
    }
)
roads = OSMRoadsFetcher(network_type="drive_service", buffer=2000).fetch(schools)
print(roads)

The source can be points, a frame of points or polygons, a shapely geometry, or a country. Points become their convex hull, widened by buffer meters. Set area="bbox" for the bounding box, or area="buffers" for a circle around each point. fetcher.query_area(source) returns the area before anything is downloaded.

network_type is an osmnx network type, such as "drive", "drive_service", "walk", or "all". custom_filter takes an Overpass filter instead. The network is directed, as OSM is: a two-way road is two edges, one per direction.

docs.title: Which areas suit Overpass
docs.text:
Overpass is a shared public service. It handles a city, a district, or the area around a group of schools well, usually in seconds to minutes.

  • osmnx splits an area larger than 2,500 km² into several queries. The fetcher warns above 50,000 km². A whole country can take hours and run into Overpass's fair-use limits; use OSMRoadsHandler for it (see Whole countries).
  • osmnx caches every response, in a cache folder in the current directory. When a large fetch fails part-way, run it again: the queries that already succeeded come from the cache. Set osmnx.settings.cache_folder to keep the cache elsewhere, or osmnx.settings.use_cache = False to turn it off.
  • Failed requests are retried max_retries times, waiting retry_delay seconds and doubling the wait each time. When the main Overpass server is down, point the fetcher at a mirror, either for one fetcher or for every fetch through the OVERPASS_URL setting (see Configuration):
roads = OSMRoadsFetcher(overpass_url="https://overpass.kumi.systems/api/interpreter").fetch(schools)

docs.title: Whole countries
docs.text:
OSMRoadsHandler downloads Geofabrik's OpenStreetMap extracts, one .osm.pbf file per country or region, stores them, and builds the road network from them with pyosmium. The result is the network OSMRoadsFetcher returns for the same area, with the same nodes, edges, and attributes, but a country takes seconds to minutes instead of hours, and works offline once stored.

from gigaspatial import OSMRoadsHandler

handler = OSMRoadsHandler()
rwanda = handler.load_data("RWA")
around_schools = handler.load_data(schools, buffer=2000)

The first call downloads Rwanda's extract (65 MiB), builds its network (about 15 s), and saves both. Later calls read the saved network: the whole country in under a second, the area around a set of schools in about a second. The options are the fetcher's, plus those that choose the extract:

  • network_type, simplify, retain_all, truncate_by_edge, buffer, and area work as in the fetcher. tags={"highway": ["primary", "secondary"]} replaces network_type with the allowed values of each OSM key.
  • A country uses its own extract, whole. regions=True uses its regional extracts instead, such as Brazil's five, which are smaller downloads. A country without an extract of its own, such as Singapore inside malaysia-singapore-brunei, is cut from the extract that holds it along its boundary.
  • Any other source uses the smallest extracts that cover its area, such as both Rwanda and Uganda for schools along their border, and is cropped to that area as the fetcher would. extracts=["africa"] names extracts yourself; continents are used only when named.
  • crop_to_source=False returns whole extracts for any source.

docs.title: Storage and freshness
docs.text:
Extracts are stored by date, in Geofabrik's own folders, under base_path (by default osm/geofabrik in the bronze data folder). Each extract's networks are saved beside it, one folder per network type and simplification:

osm/geofabrik/index-v1.json
osm/geofabrik/2026-10-28/africa/rwanda.osm.pbf
osm/geofabrik/2026-10-28/africa/rwanda.networks/drive_service-raw/
osm/geofabrik/2026-10-28/africa/rwanda.networks/drive_service-simplified/
osm/geofabrik/2026-10-28/south-america/brazil/nordeste.osm.pbf

A stored network always covers its whole extract; cropping happens when loading. Pass data_store= to store everything in a remote data store, such as Azure Blob Storage.

The newest stored date is used, without contacting Geofabrik. refresh=True uses Geofabrik's latest extract instead, and max_age_days=30 does when the stored one is older than that. date="2026-10-01" pins a date, stored or downloaded. Geofabrik updates its extracts daily and keeps the daily files for about a week, then those of the 1st of each month and of January 1st; to reproduce an old result, keep its stored extract. Old dates are never deleted for you. Extracts take space: Nigeria is 680 MiB, Brazil 2.0 GiB, and Germany 4.6 GiB.

A network's metadata records its extract's ID, date, URL, and the time its data was taken from OpenStreetMap:

rwanda.metadata["extract"]
# {'id': 'rwanda', 'date': '2026-10-28', 'url': 'https://download.geofabrik.de/africa/rwanda-261028.osm.pbf', ...}

Building reads the extract once, with a node location index that pyosmium keeps in memory for extracts up to 1 GiB (about 2 GB of memory for Nigeria) and on disk above that; node_index= chooses it yourself. A saved network folder, or a stored .pbf file, can also be passed to load_data as the source.

docs.title: Join the schools to the roads
docs.text:
fiber = pd.DataFrame({"fiber_id": ["fiber-1"], "lat": [-1.9490], "lon": [30.0700]})

network = roads.insert_points(schools, id_column="giga_id", max_distance=1000)
network = network.insert_points(fiber, id_column="fiber_id", max_distance=1000)

Each point becomes a node, joined to its nearest road at the foot of the perpendicular. The road is split there at a new node of kind split, and a connection edge joins the point to it. A point within snap_to_node meters (5 by default) of a road's end connects to that end instead. The split pieces add up exactly to the road's length. Points farther than max_distance from any road are skipped, with a warning; return_skipped=True also returns them.

chain=True joins a point to an already inserted point when that point is closer than any road, nearest the road first. The frame's other columns become node attributes. Every edit returns a new network; the original does not change.

docs.title: Shortest paths
docs.text:
school_ids = schools["giga_id"].tolist()

lengths = network.shortest_path_lengths(school_ids, ["fiber-1"], directed=False)
nearest = network.nearest_by_network(school_ids, ["fiber-1"], directed=False)
routes = network.shortest_paths(school_ids, ["fiber-1"] * 3, geometry=True, directed=False)

lengths is a table of meters, one row per school. routes is a GeoDataFrame with one line per route. A directed network follows one-way roads; directed=False ignores them, which suits a cable laid along a road. reachable lists every node within a distance, and count_within counts targets within a distance, such as clinics within 5 km by road.

For very many origin-destination pairs, backend="pandana" is faster once its index is built (pip install "giga-spatial[pandana]").

docs.title: The roads that connect the schools
docs.text:
to_fiber = network.connecting_subnetwork(school_ids, roots=["fiber-1"])
print(to_fiber.total_length())

tree = network.connecting_subnetwork(school_ids)
branches = tree.degree()[tree.degree() >= 3]

A connecting subnetwork keeps only the roads that join the points, contracted to the points and the nodes where the paths branch. With roots, nodes already connected to each other such as fibre nodes, the schools are joined to the roots at close to the smallest total length: a school may connect through another school, and a road shared by several schools counts once. Without roots, the schools are joined by a tree of close to the smallest total length. Both are Steiner tree approximations. method="nearest_root" gives each school its own shortest path to its nearest root instead, and method="all_pairs" the shortest path between every pair; its cost grows with the square of the number of points.

tree.edges_gdf is the result as lines, ready to map or export.

ConnectionPlanner makes the same plans and says more about them: each school's status (connected, itself a root, or unreachable), the root it reaches and its distance along the plan, the plan's uncontracted edges, and its cost.

from gigaspatial import ConnectionPlanner

plan = ConnectionPlanner(network, school_ids, roots=["fiber-1"], weight="length").plan()
print(plan.cost, plan.terminals["status"].value_counts())

The default method, shortest_path, also models a phased rollout: schools are connected one at a time, nearest first, to everything connected so far, and the terminals table gives each school's order and marginal_cost, the cost its connection added. plan("steiner") uses Mehlhorn's faster approximation, a few percent longer on roads.

planner.improve(plan) shortens any plan by local search, and never makes it worse; time_limit= stops it after that many seconds. On Kigali's roads, improved plans came within 0.9% of the optimum.

planner.lower_bound(plan) computes a cost no plan can go below, and sets plan.bound and plan.gap: the plan costs at most 1 + gap times the best possible one.

Schools on roads that do not join the rest, such as an island or a clipped corner, are unreachable. bridge_cost lets the plan use straight-line links between such parts, such as microwave links, at a weight per metre and up to bridge_max_distance metres (5,000 by default). A link is used only where it is cheaper than the roads:

plan = ConnectionPlanner(network, school_ids, roots=["fiber-1"], bridge_cost=3.0).plan()
links = plan.edges[plan.edges["kind"] == "bridge"]

docs.title: Save and load
docs.text:
from gigaspatial import SpatialNetwork

network.save("roads/kigali")
network = SpatialNetwork.load("roads/kigali")
topology = SpatialNetwork.load("roads/kigali", columns=[])

A saved network is a folder of three files: nodes.parquet, edges.parquet as GeoParquet, and network.json. GIS tools, DuckDB, and pandas read the Parquet files directly. Pass data_store= to save to or load from a remote data store. columns= loads only some edge columns: with an empty list, only the topology and lengths, which is fastest.

docs.title: More
docs.text:
• simplify() removes nodes that only continue a road, as osmnx does. clip(area) keeps the roads in an area.
  • connected_components(), largest_component(), and connect_components() find and join the disconnected parts.
  • nodes_gdf and edges_gdf are GeoDataFrames; to_networkx() and to_pandana() convert the network for other libraries.

The spatial network API lists every method.

docs.title: Settlement
docs.text:
GHSL's settlement model (GHS_SMOD) classifies each cell as a kind of built-up area, from rural to urban centre. Mapping it onto points attaches that class to each point. The result is a view.

The first run downloads the settlement raster. It does not need an API key.

from gigaspatial import PoiViewGenerator

points = [(-1.9441, 30.0619), (-1.9500, 30.1000)]
places = PoiViewGenerator(points)
view = places.map_smod()
print(view[["smod_class"]].head())

map_smod uses the 2020 release at 1000 m. stat="median" is the class at the point.

The same method exists on a zone generator. After the tutorial, zones.map_smod() adds smod_class to the H3 view.

To load the raster yourself, construct the handler:

from gigaspatial import GHSLDataHandler

settlement = GHSLDataHandler(product="GHS_SMOD", year=2020, resolution=1000)
frame = settlement.load_into_dataframe("RWA")
